Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Those whom Heaven and Earth value are human beings;
that which the Sages esteem is righteousness;
that which perfects virtue and righteousness is wisdom;
and that which clear-sighted wisdom seeks is learning and inquiry.
Although there may be a supreme Sage,
he is not born with wisdom;
although there may be supreme talent,
it is not born with ability.
Thus the *Zhì* says:
Huáng Dì took Fēng Hòu as his teacher;
Zhuānxū took Lǎo Péng;
Dì Kù took Zhù Róng;
Yáo took Wù Chéng;
Shùn took Jì Hòu;
Yǔ took Mò Rú;
Tāng took Yī Yǐn;
Wén and Wǔ took Jiāng Shàng;
Zhōu Gōng took Shù Xiù;
Kǒng Zǐ took Lǎo Dān.
If these words are believed,
then people cannot but seek a teacher.
These eleven rulers
were all superior Sages,
yet they still relied on learning and inquiry
for their wisdom to become broad
and their virtue to become great.
How much more so for ordinary people?
For this reason, "a craftsman who wishes to do his work well
must first sharpen his tools";
a scholar who wishes to proclaim his righteousness
must first read his books.
The *Yì* says:
"The superior man, by recording many words and deeds of the past, cultivates his virtue."
Thus, a person's having learning
is like an object's having refinement.
Therefore, the Huáng-jade of Xià Hòu
and the Bì-jade of Hé of Chǔ,
though they had the quality of raw jade like that of Biàn Hé,
if not carved and polished,
they would not be separated from common stones.
The Hú and Guǐ ritual vessels
and the sacrificial robes of the court,
in their beginning,
were merely wood from the mountains and silk from cocoons.
If the skilled Chuí applies the marking cord and plumb line and crafts them with axe and adze,
and female artisans apply the five colors and craft them with the loom and shuttle,
then they all become vessels for the ancestral temple and patterned robes of state,
which can be presented to the spirits
and worn by kings and dukes.
How much more so for the solid and upright substance
and the keen and quick talent of a superior man?
If he is supported by good friends,
taught by enlightened teachers,
refined by the *Lǐ* and *Yuè*,
led by the *Shī* and *Shū*,
assisted by the *Zhōu Yì*,
and enlightened by the *Chūn Qiū*,
will he not achieve success?
The *Shī* says:
"Look at that wagtail,
now flying, now singing.
Every day I advance,
every month I journey.
Rising early and sleeping late,
do not disgrace those who gave you life."
For this reason, "The superior man is active and vigilant all day long,
advancing in virtue and cultivating his work."
This is not simply for the sake of broadening oneself;
rather, it is to think of continuing the good reputation of one's ancestors
and thereby making one's parents illustrious.
Kǒng Zǐ said:
"I once spent the whole day without eating
and the whole night without sleeping
in order to think.
It was of no use;
it is better to learn."
"In farming,
hunger may be found within it;
in learning,
official emolument may be found within it.
The superior man worries about the Way and not about poverty."
Jì Zǐ set forth the Six Extremes,
and the *Guó Fēng* sang the "Běi Mén";
this is what is meant by not worrying about poverty.
Is it that they liked poverty and did not worry about it?
It is because their will was focused on something specific,
making clear what they considered important.
For this reason, the superior man's pursuit of abundance
is not for fine food, beautiful clothes, excessive music, or sensual pleasures;
rather, it is to establish his Way and advance his virtue.
The Way is perfected through learning and preserved in books;
learning advances through encouragement and fails through hardship.
For this reason, Dǒng Zhòngshū never inquired about family matters throughout his life,
and Jǐng Jūnmíng did not leave his courtyard for years.
That they were able to sharpen their focus on their studies and make their achievements manifest
was because their families were wealthy.
To be as wealthy and leisurely as they were
and yet able to be as diligent and focused as this
makes them talented men.
Nì Kuān worked as a laborer in the capital's alleys,
and Kuāng Héng sold himself as a servant;
this was because they were personally poor.
To be as poor and destitute as they were
and yet able to advance in learning like this
makes them outstanding scholars.
In the present age, scholars are always counted by the tens of thousands,
yet those who complete the path do not number even several dozen.
What is the reason for this?
The wealthy allow their riches to tarnish their focus,
while the poor allow their lack of resources to change their plans,
or they take mourning and disorder to consume their years.
This is why they lose the achievements of their youth upon reaching adulthood and remain as children.
Therefore, without the talent of Dǒng or Jǐng,
or the will of Nì or Kuāng,
those who wish to forcibly sacrifice themselves, leave their homes, and spend their days at a teacher's gate
will certainly be few.
These four gentlemen
were keen of ear and eye,
loyal, trustworthy, incorruptible, and brave;
they were not necessarily without peers.
Yet when it came to achieving fame and establishing accomplishments,
with their virtuous reputation and good name never ceasing,
there was a reason for it.
What was the cause?
It was simply because they were able to entrust themselves to the scriptures of the former Sages
and bind their hearts to the bequeathed teachings of the Master.
Thus, though Zào Fù could run swiftly,
he would be exhausted after a hundred paces;
but by entrusting himself to a carriage,
he could reach a thousand lǐ while sitting.
Though a sailor can float on a beam,
if he lets go of the rope he will drown;
but by entrusting himself to a boat and oar,
he can cross rivers and streams while sitting.
Therefore, the superior man
does not have a nature that surpasses the world,
but he is good at entrusting himself to things.
Human nature and disposition
do not differ by a hundredfold,
yet in wisdom and intelligence, there is a ten-thousand-fold difference.
This is not due to their true innate talent;
it must be attained by relying on something.
The nature of the superior man
is not necessarily all-illuminating,
but when he learns,
his hearing and sight are without obstruction,
and his mind and wisdom are without blockage.
He records the emperors and kings of the past
and looks back to determine the patterns of a hundred generations.
This is the brilliance of the Way,
and the superior man is able to rely on it to make himself manifest.
For this reason, the Way is to the heart
as fire is to the human eye.
In a deep pit or a secluded room,
it is dark and nothing can be seen;
but when a bright candle is set out,
then all things are revealed.
This is the radiance of the fire,
not the light of the eye,
yet when the eye relies on it,
it becomes sight for oneself.
The Way of Heaven and Earth
and the workings of the spiritual light
cannot be seen.
But by studying the sacred scriptures
and contemplating the arts of the Way,
they all come into view.
This is the substance of the Way,
not the brilliance of the heart,
yet when a person relies on it,
it becomes knowledge for oneself.
Therefore, for one seeking an object in a dark room at night,
nothing is better than fire;
for one seeking the Way in the present age,
nothing is better than the scriptures.
The *Diǎn* are the *Jīng*.
They were created by the former Sages.
The former Sages obtained the essence of the Way to conduct their lives,
and they wished for worthy people to exert themselves to enter the Way.
Therefore, the Sages created the Classics to leave them to later worthies,
just as the skilled Chuí made the compass, square, level, and plumb line to leave them to later craftsmen.
In the past, the skill of Chuí was such that
his eyes were proficient with circles and squares,
and his heart was set on levelness and straightness.
He also created the compass, the cord, the square, and the ink-line to instruct later generations.
If one were to try to make the likes of Xī Zhòng or Gōng Bān
cast aside these four measures
and imitate Chuí by creating on their own,
they would surely be unable to do so.
Yet ordinary workers and reckless artisans,
by holding the compass and grasping the square,
applying the level and pulling the cord,
possess a skill equal to that of Chuí.
Therefore, Chuí used his heart to create the compass and square;
later workers use the compass and square
to align with Chuí’s heart.
Thus, workers who follow these measures
are nearly equal to Chuí.
The wisdom of the former Sages
reached divine brilliance in their hearts,
and their natures were aligned with the Way and Virtue.
They also created the classics and scriptures to leave behind for later generations.
If one were to try to make worthy men and gentlemen
cast aside learning and inquiry
and act solely on their raw nature,
they would surely not be complete.
But when they follow a teacher and pursue learning,
acting according to the classics,
the brilliance of intelligence and understanding
and the principles of virtue and righteousness
will also be nearly attained.
Therefore, the Sages used their hearts to create the classics;
later generations follow the classics to align with the Sages’ hearts.
Thus, worthies who cultivate the classics
have virtue close to that of the Sages.
The *Shī* says:
"The high mountain, I look up to it;
the great road, I travel it."
And it says: "Daily progress and monthly advancement;
learning has a continuous brilliance leading to light."
Therefore, for all who wish to manifest great achievements and spread glorious deeds,
nothing is better than learning.
In the general essence of governing,
nothing is better than restraining the secondary and striving for the fundamental,
and nothing is worse than departing from the fundamental and decorating the secondary.
He who rules a state takes enriching the people as the fundamental
and takes correct learning as the foundation.
When the people are rich, they can be taught;
when learning is correct, they attain righteousness.
When the people are poor, they turn their backs on goodness;
when learning is corrupt, they turn to deceit and falsity.
If they enter into learning, they will not be in disorder;
if they attain righteousness, they will be loyal and filial.
Therefore, the law of an enlightened ruler
strives for these two things,
using them as the foundation for achieving great peace
and bringing about the auspicious signs of prosperity.
As for enriching the people,
agriculture and sericulture are the fundamental,
while frivolous occupations are the secondary.
For the various craftsmen,
practical utility is the fundamental,
while intricate decoration is the secondary.
For merchants,
circulating goods is the fundamental,
while selling curiosities is the secondary.
If these three keep to the fundamental and depart from the secondary, the people will be rich;
if they depart from the fundamental and keep to the secondary, the people will be poor.
When they are poor, they are distressed and forget goodness;
when they are rich, they are joyful and can be taught.
As for instruction,
the Way and righteousness are the fundamental,
while cunning rhetoric is the secondary.
As for speech,
trustworthiness and compliance are the fundamental,
while deceptive beauty is the secondary.
For the ranks of scholars,
filial piety and brotherly respect are the fundamental,
while social networking is the secondary.
For filial piety and brotherly respect,
providing nourishment is the fundamental,
while grand appearance is the secondary.
For ministers,
loyalty and uprightness are the fundamental,
while fawning and seeking favor are the secondary.
If these five keep to the fundamental and depart from the secondary, benevolence and righteousness will flourish;
if they depart from the fundamental and keep to the secondary, the Way and virtue will collapse.
Being careful about the fundamental and neglecting the secondary is still acceptable;
abandoning the fundamental to strive for the secondary is evil.
To use the Way of Heaven
and divide the benefits of the Earth,
raising the six domestic animals according to the seasons
and gathering the hundred things in the wilds—
this is the fundamental of enriching the state.
Frivolous occupations and secondary matters
used to gather the people's profits—
this is the source of impoverishing the nation.
Loyalty, trustworthiness, and prudence
are the foundation of virtue and righteousness.
Emptiness, nothingness, and deceitful trickery
are the roots of the Way's disorder.
Therefore, diligent farming is the means to enrich the state.
Now, the people leave agriculture and sericulture
to rush into frivolous occupations,
seeking various profits
and gathering them into one household;
although there is wealth for the private family,
the public accounting becomes even poorer.
The various craftsmen are those employed to provide tools.
Tools are good if they are convenient for work
and superior if they are sturdy and firm.
Now craftsmen like to make carved and polished items,
decorating them with clever falsity
to deceive the people and take their wealth;
although it is profitable for the treacherous craftsman,
the state’s planning becomes even more diseased.
Merchants are the means to circulate goods.
Goods take utility as their essence
and durability as their capital.
Now merchants compete to sell useless goods and extravagant currencies,
deluding the people and taking their property;
although the corrupt merchant gains,
the state’s planning loses even more.
These three things,
outwardly although they have the private reputation of diligent effort and enriching the family,
inwardly they have the public reality of harming the people and impoverishing the state.
Therefore, those who govern
should clearly supervise industry and commerce
and not allow them to be corrupt or false;
they should distress and disgrace frivolous occupations
and not allow them to seize profit at will.
Be lenient toward the fundamental agriculture
and favor and advance the learned scholars;
then the people will be rich and the state will be at peace.
As for instruction,
it is the means to advance the arts of the Way and revere virtue and righteousness.
Now the men of learning
like to speak of empty and nihilistic matters
and compete to write carved and beautiful essays
to seek to appear different from the world.
People of little knowledge
follow and regard them highly;
this harms the reality of the Way and virtue
and is one of the greatest delusions for the ignorant.
As for poetry and rhapsodies,
they are the means to praise the virtue of the good and the bad
and to release the feelings of sorrow and joy.
Therefore they should be gentle and elegant to broaden culture,
using analogies to fully express meaning.
Now the followers of rhapsodies and praises
indulge in verbose and convoluted rhetoric,
competing to display false and groundless matters
to seek to appear strange to the world.
Foolish men and dull scholars
follow and think them marvelous;
this perverts the thoughts of children
and encourages insincere speech.
Exhausting filial piety and brotherly respect toward parents
and rectifying conduct within the household
are the ways to become a meritorious man.
Now many strive for social networking to form factions and groups,
stealing from the world and pilfering fame to achieve their ends;
the followers of boastful secondary matters
follow and honor them.
This pressures the integrity of upright men
and dazzles the hearts of the common world.
Nourishing life and following parents' will
are the ways to practice filial piety.
Now many go against that will and are stingy in nourishment,
restricting life to wait for the end;
after the end and death,
they then extravagantly decorate the funeral rites to speak of filial piety
and lavishly feast guests to seek fame.
The followers of false goodness
follow and praise them;
this disorders the true practice of filial piety and brotherly respect
and is a painful error for future generations.
Serving the lord with loyalty and uprightness
and governing subordinates by being faithful to the law
are the reasons for holding office.
Now many use treachery and flattery to gain favor
and twist the law to benefit the sycophants.
The followers of improper gain
follow and consider them worthy;
this extinguishes the conduct of the upright and good
and opens the source of disorder and danger.
These five things,
outwardly although they have the empty reputation of promoting worthy talents,
inwardly they have the reality of harming the ultimate Way and virtue.
All these eight items
are the pursuits of a declining age
and what a dark ruler clings to.
Even if they do not immediately lead to usurpation or regicide,
they are nonetheless the gradual arrival of the way of chaos.
The struggle between the flourishing and decaying of fundamentals and non-essentials
all lies with the ruler;
it is not something the common people can change.
The people naturally follow what the ruler likes
and pursue profit to sustain their lives.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ says:
That wealth and riches are not many,
that food and clothing are not sufficient,
that music and beauty are not exquisite,
and that majesty and power are not exercised
are not the concerns of a Jūnzǐ.
That good deeds are not many,
that the expression of the Way is not clear,
that integrity and resolve are not established,
and that virtue and righteousness are not manifest
—of these, the Jūnzǐ is ashamed.
For this reason, when the worthy and the wise deal with their descendants,
they encourage them with resolve
and not with deceit;
they urge them with righteousness
and not with deceit;
they show them frugality
and not luxury;
they leave them with words
and not with wealth.
Thus, Dǒng Zhòngshū never inquired about family matters throughout his life,
and Shū Guǎng did not leave behind his bestowed gold.
If descendants are worthy,
they do not need much wealth;
if they are not worthy,
then much wealth will only lead to the accumulation of resentment.
Therefore it is said:
To have great wealth without virtue
is the womb of calamity.
In the past, Cáo Jī had a saying:
“To guard what Heaven has gathered,
one must practice virtue and righteousness.
If virtue and righteousness are not practiced,
what is gathered will surely be depleted.”
Now, if a household is wealthy but stingy toward those in need,
fails to provide for the poor,
or show pity for the sick and suffering,
then they surely will not remain wealthy for long.
The Yì says:
“The Way of Heaven diminishes the full to supplement the humble.”
Thus, for what is spent on others through benevolence and righteousness,
Heaven rewards it here;
for what is taken through wickedness beforehand,
Heaven causes it to decline thereafter.
Hence, the way to maintain fullness
is to ladle out and diminish it;
then one may also avoid the regret of the Kànglóng and the errors of Qiánkūn.
Therefore, if one focuses on the fundamental, even hypocritical people will return to the fundamental;
if one occupies the non-essential, even sincere and respectful people will turn toward the non-essential.
Moreover, where there is cold and hunger,
the people cannot but leave;
where there is warmth and satiety,
the people cannot but stay.
Thus, in a declining and dark age,
those who follow the fundamental or the non-essential
are not necessarily worthy or unworthy;
it is because of the location of disaster and fortune
that the situation cannot be otherwise.
Therefore, when an enlightened ruler governs a state,
he must exalt the fundamental and suppress the non-essential
to check the sprouts of chaos and danger.
This is truly a perilous sign for governance
that must be scrutinized.
In the arguments of the world,
none do not value integrity and yielding while disparaging wealth and profit;
yet when it comes to their actions,
many abandon integrity and hanker after profit from others.
They only know that the former can benefit themselves,
but do not know that their gaining the former
will also make them a target for others seeking profit.
They know that fat and wax can light a lamp,
but do not know that too much of it will extinguish it.
They know that profit can amuse themselves,
but do not know that it must be commensurate with virtue to be possessed.
Former people suffered from this,
yet later people compete for it;
this is the folly of the common people and the peak of a declining and dark age.
I therefore sigh and say:
Why is this not scrutinized?
I wish they would reflect in the Way
and not reflect in water.
The elephant is burned for its tusks;
the mussel’s body is split for its pearl;
an ordinary man is innocent,
but carrying a jade disc is his crime.
Alas!
For those who are rich and noble without virtue,
one may certainly offer condolences in advance.
Furthermore, all beneficial things are the wealth of Heaven.
Heaven’s management of this wealth
is like a ruler’s possession of treasuries.
Taxing, rewarding, seizing, and giving
each have their proper amounts;
how could the people forcibly take more?
Therefore, if a person is rich and noble without virtue,
they are like wicked people who steal official positions and rob the treasuries;
they will eventually be discovered,
and once discovered, they will surely be punished.
A thief of men is surely punished;
how much more so a thief of Heaven?
How could they not suffer calamity?
Dèng Tōng died without even a hairpin;
Shèng and Guì brought destruction upon themselves.
Thus, the Tiānzǐ cannot defy Heaven to enrich those without merit,
and the feudal lords cannot defy the Dì to generously encourage private interests.
It is not just defying the Dì,
nor just defying Heaven.
The Dì takes Heaven as his standard,
and Heaven takes the people as its heart;
whatever the people desire,
Heaven will surely follow.
Therefore, those who seek fullness without performing service for the people
have never failed to fall forcefully;
those who have merit and virtue for the people yet remain humble
have never failed to be glorious.
From ancient times to the present,
from the Tiānzǐ above
down to the commoners,
there has never been one who loved profit and did not perish,
nor one who loved righteousness and did not become manifest.
In the past, Zhōu Lì Wáng loved to monopolize profit;
Ruì Liángfū remonstrated with him, but he would not listen.
Ruì retired and composed the poem Sāngróu to satirize him,
saying that this was a great wind
that would surely reach its end;
that these were greedy people
who would surely ruin their own kind.
The king still did not realize his error,
and thus he was eventually exiled and died in Zhì.
Yú Gōng lost his state because of repeated greed;
Gōngshū Shù turned bribes into a crime;
Huán Tuí was assassinated because he did not moderate his food and drink.
All these brought about their own ruin through goods
and destroyed themselves through wealth.
Chǔ Dòu Zǐwén served as Lìngyǐn three times
but had the look of hunger;
his wife and children suffered from cold and hunger,
and they lived from hand to mouth.
Jì Wénzǐ served as minister to four rulers,
yet his horses were not fed grain
and his concubines did not wear silk.
Zǐhǎn returned the jade;
Yànzǐ returned the house.
All these men were able to abandon profit and restrain themselves;
therefore, they faced no resentment from the people.
For generations, they enjoyed Heaven’s bounty
and their good reputations never ceased.
Bóyí and Shūqí starved at Shǒuyáng;
Báijū and Jiè Tuī fled to the mountain valleys;
Yán, Yuán, and Gōngxī suffered from hunger in the wilds.
They maintained their resolve with great firmness
and held to their integrity without compromise.
Favors and emoluments could not bind them,
and power and prestige could not sway them.
Even if they had the majesty of the ruler or the rank of duke or marquis,
if virtue and righteousness were endangered,
if ritual and righteousness were not distributed fairly,
and if they had to bend their resolve like common herbs
or betray their hearts like fragrant plants,
they certainly would not do it.
Therefore, even the master of the four seas cannot compare with them in fame,
and the rulers of various states cannot match them in weight.
They maintained their resolve within a single hut,
yet their righteousness overflowed beyond the Jiǔzhōu;
their trustworthiness was established a thousand years ago,
and their names are passed down through a hundred generations.
What is called a “worthy man” or a “Jūnzǐ”
does not necessarily refer to those with high positions, generous emoluments, wealth, and glory;
while these are what a Jūnzǐ should appropriately have,
they are not what make him a Jūnzǐ.
What is called a “petty man”
does not necessarily refer to those who are poor, lowly, cold, hungry, distressed, humiliated, or in dire straits;
while these are the conditions in which a petty man should appropriately dwell,
they are not what make him a petty man.
How can this be clarified?
Now, Jié and Zhòu
were the kings of Xià and Yīn;
Chónghóu and Èlái
were the Three Ducal Ministers of the Son of Heaven,
yet they still could not avoid being petty men
because their hearts and conduct were evil.
Bóyí and Shǔqí
were starving men,
Fù Yuè was a convict laborer,
and Jǐng Jiù was a slave;
yet the world still considers them gentlemen
because their will and integrity were beautiful.
Therefore, if the evaluation of a scholar is fixed upon their will and conduct
and not judged by the fate they encounter,
then even possessing the world is not enough to be considered important,
and having no use is not enough to be considered slight;
dwelling as a slave or stableman is not enough to be a disgrace,
and comforting the Four Seas is not enough to be a glory.
How much more so for those whose differences are not as vast as these?
Thus it is said:
"A favored position is not enough to honor me,
and lowliness is not enough to debase myself."
Indeed, a fine reputation arises from oneself,
while the two fates descend from Heaven.
The *Shì* says:
"Heaven truly did it;
what can be said about it!"
Therefore, a gentleman is not necessarily wealthy and noble,
and a petty man is not necessarily poor and lowly.
Sometimes a hidden dragon is not yet used,
and sometimes an overbearing dragon is in the sky;
it has been thus since ancient times.
Now, observing the discussions of vulgar scholars,
they promote virtue based on clan
and name the worthy based on position.
This can be said to have captured one aspect of discussion,
but it has not obtained the pure truth of the ultimate discussion.
Yáo was a sagely father,
but Dān was fierce and arrogant;
Shùn was a sagely son,
but Sǒu was stubborn and evil;
Shūxiàng was a worthy elder brother,
but Fù was greedy and violent;
Jìyǒu was a worthy younger brother,
but Qìngfù was debauched and rebellious.
If evaluation must be by clan,
then Dān should have succeeded the throne and Shùn should have been executed,
Fù should have been rewarded and Jìyǒu should have been exterminated.
That evaluation cannot certainly be by clan is like this.
Formerly, Qí Xī had a saying:
"Gǔn was executed and Yǔ rose;
Guǎn and Cài were put to death,
while Zhōugōng assisted the King."
Therefore, the *Shū* says: "Father, son, and brothers are not implicated by one another."
The nobility of Yōu and Lì
was that of the Son of Heaven,
and they were wealthy with the Four Seas.
The lowliness of Yán and Yuán
was that of commoners,
and they were often freezing, hungry, and empty-handed.
If evaluation must be by position,
then these two kings were worldly scholars,
and the two in seclusion were foolish and lowly.
That evaluation cannot certainly be by position
is also like this.
Therefore it is said:
Benevolence is heavy while power is light;
position is slight while righteousness is glorious.
Those who discuss things today
mostly do the opposite of this,
and moreover judge by the nine degrees of kin
or by where one comes from;
thus they are far from obtaining the truly worthy.
Long ago, even Zhōugōng did not demand perfection from one person;
how much more so when one's virtue and righteousness have already been raised—
can they then be rejected because of other reasons?
Yóuyú was born among the Wǔdí,
Yuè Xiàng was produced among the Bāmán,
yet their achievements reached Qí and Qín,
and their virtue was established among the Zhūxià.
Their fine names and beautiful reputations
are recorded in maps and books
and have not been extinguished to this day.
Zhāng Yí was a person of the Zhōngguó,
Wèi Yāng was a grandson of Kāngshǔ,
yet both were slandering, sycophantic, and treacherous,
causing mutual disorder throughout the Four Seas.
Viewing it from this,
the goodness or evil of a person
does not necessarily depend on a hereditary clan;
the worthiness or lowliness of one's nature
does not necessarily depend on worldly customs.
Inside the hall may grow useless weeds,
while in the wild mountains may grow orchids and angelica.
The Jade of Héshì
came from a rough stone;
the Pearl of Suíshì
was produced from a clam.
The *Shì* says:
"Gathering turnip greens and radish greens,
do not reject them because of their lower parts."
Therefore, if there is great beauty that can be esteemed by the world,
then even if there are minor conducts or small flaws, how could they be enough to be a burden?
Thus, in employing a scholar, one does not worry that he is not a state scholar,
but worries that he is not loyal;
the world does not worry about having no ministers,
but worries that they are not worthy.
There should be no constraints on origin.
Chén Píng and Hán Xìn were captives of Chǔ,
yet Gāozǔ made them his flanking assistants,
and they truly pacified the Four Seas
and secured the Hàn House;
Wèi Qīng and Huò Qùbìng
were personal servants of Píngyáng,
yet Wǔdì made them Commanders,
and they truly repelled the Běidí
and established commanderies in Héxī.
It only depends on their appointment;
what does lowliness or distance have to do with it?
However, the reason why those not from this land
or not from a lineage of generals and ministers are looked upon with difficulty
is that people fear they occupy this position without this ability,
dwell in this nobility without this virtue,
and have no way for me to respect them yet they hold power.
The reason the world is not well-governed
is because the worthy face difficulties.
What is called the difficulty of the worthy
does not just refer to having a bright and intelligent body and practicing virtue and righteousness.
This is the difficulty of finding the worthy,
not the difficulty faced by the worthy person.
Therefore, what is called the difficulty of the worthy
is to say that if one follows goodness, one is envied;
if one acts worthily, one is jealously disliked;
and one must encounter troubles and hardships.
The reason Yú Shùn was persecuted
and the reason Zǐxū was executed—
even supreme sages and great worthies still cannot avoid jealousy and envy,
how much more so for the people of a middle age?
This is why outstanding scholars, though they have worthy talent and beautiful quality,
still cannot walk the straight path
and fulfill their ambitions.
Scholars in seclusion cannot straighten their conduct,
and court officials cannot straighten their speech;
this is why social customs decline
and dark rulers become isolated.
The Marquis of Qí lost his state,
and the Duke of Lǔ was driven into exile;
they were all so busy with failure and being overwhelmed that they had no leisure;
how could they manage to govern?
Therefore, those with thin virtue hate to hear of beautiful conduct;
those with chaotic government hate to hear of governing speech;
this is why the falling Qín executed those who spoke in pairs and buried the scholars of techniques.
Now, among the vulgar people of this age,
there are not a few who are disrespectful to their own kin yet hate others for respecting them,
and who are neglectful of their own kin yet hate others for loving them.
Is it only the common people?
Worthy talents occasionally do this as well.
Dèng Tōng was favored by Wéndì;
he devoted his heart and did not disobey,
even sucking the Emperor's abscesses without a look of hesitation.
When the Emperor was ill and unhappy,
he asked casually:
"Who in the world loves me most?"
Dèng Tōng wanted to praise the Crown Prince's filial piety,
so he replied:
"None is like the Crown Prince who loves Your Majesty most."
When the Crown Prince came to inquire about the illness,
the Emperor ordered him to suck the abscess.
He had a look of difficulty,
and the Emperor was displeased and sent the Crown Prince away.
Later, when he heard that Dèng Tōng often sucked the abscesses,
he was ashamed and resented him.
When he succeeded to the imperial throne,
he eventually charged Tōng with a crime and caused him to starve to death.
Thus, for Dèng Tōng, his actions were meant to exhaust his heart and strength without harming others,
and his words were meant to praise the Crown Prince and manifest filial piety and kindness.
The Crown Prince himself could not live up to the praise,
but instead formed a grudge and placed the blame there.
Praising another's strengths
in a desire to illustrate their filial piety
still resulted in a crime;
how much more so for those who clarify people's shortcomings to correct the world?
Furthermore, for any scholar, the reason they are considered worthy
is because of their words and deeds.
Loyal and upright words
do not merely consist of praising others;
they must necessarily involve confrontation.
The conduct of a filial son
does not merely consist of sucking on sores;
it must necessarily involve correction.
This being the case, then for those scholars who follow such conduct and engage in such discourse,
to not meet with a reputation that invites jealousy
and to escape the blame that leads to punishment and execution
is a matter of sheer luck.
This is why Bǐ Gān had his heart cut open,
why Jī Zǐ was made a slave,
why Bó Zōng met with death,
and why Xiè Wàn went into exile.
Indeed, a state is never lacking in jealous men,
just as a household is never lacking in jealous women.
Since recent times,
from the court to the commoners,
is it rare for people to compete for merit and fame and be jealous of those who surpass them?
Do you think that just because two people are both worthy, it is appropriate that they do not harm each other?
That is not the case.
Fàn Juī demoted Bái Qǐ;
Gōngsūn Hóng suppressed Dǒng Zhòngshū.
Was this only because they were in the same court serving the same ruler and competing for favor and salary?
Can only those in different states and on different paths, whose interests do not interfere, escape this?
Even so, it is not guaranteed.
Sūn Bìn cultivated his abilities in Chǔ,
and Páng Juān in Wèi changed countenance out of jealousy,
luring him in to have his feet amputated.
Hán Fēi brought enlightened governance to Hán,
and Lǐ Sī in Qín harbored thoughts of jealousy,
causing him to be brought there and killed.
Alas! Is the mutual jealousy among scholars really as severe as this?
Is it because they have not reached the ruler that they suffer calamity?
Can one be trusted just because one is known to the ruler?
It is not necessarily so.
Jīng Fáng several times debated with Yuán Dì
and was made to establish a system for evaluating merit and selecting officials;
Cháo Cuò was traditionally known by Jǐng Dì
and was made to revise the laws of Hàn without causing chaos.
Regarding these two men’s relationship with their rulers,
it could be said they were deeply known and exceptionally favored,
yet Jīng Fáng died a wrongful death without the Emperor ever knowing,
and Cháo Cuò was already executed before the Emperor felt regret.
Was it because their talent and intelligence were insufficient to protect themselves that they met with disaster?
Can only Great Sages avoid being burdened by such things?
Not so.
Dì Yǐ was imprisoned because of righteousness;
Wén Wáng was detained because of benevolence.
Those who embody the highest benevolence and righteousness
and occupy the positions of teachers and high officials facing south,
still cannot avoid difficulties.
Thus, Fǔzǐ had his traces erased,
Shū Xiàng was bound in chains,
Qū Yuán was banished and drowned,
Jiǎ Yì was demoted and dismissed,
Zhōnglí was discarded,
Hé Chǎng was bound,
Wáng Zhāng was convicted,
and Píng'ā was cast out;
these are the ones among scholars who were treated lightly.
The Shī says:
"Though innocent and blameless,
the mouths of slanderers are clamorous."
"The hearts of those people,
where will they not reach?"
From this perspective,
the attacks of the jealous and fawning
are indeed skillful!
The existence of the worthy and the sage in the world
is indeed perilous!
Therefore, what is called "the difficulty of being worthy"
does not mean that being worthy itself is difficult;
it is escaping harm that is difficult.
Those Great Sages and various worthy ones,
with accomplishments achieved and names established,
some with titles of Marquis or Count,
some in the positions of the Three Ducal Ministers or Nine Ministers,
holding high heavenly offices,
selected in the Emperor's heart,
attending banquets day and night,
with names widely known—even they still face such things.
Then how much more so for the commoners in the fields or the recluses in the valleys,
who only reach others through intermediaries
and are only believed after public discussion?
This is why wise men clamp their mouths and tie their tongues,
closing their bags and remaining silent together.
Furthermore, among the common people of the lanes,
how could they have special discernment?
They merely watch the dust and parrot the sounds.
Observing their discussions,
they are unable to base them on the actual deeds within the private gates
or examine the reality of praise or blame;
they simply consider those who praise them to their faces as wise,
those who flatter them as benevolent,
those who deal in treacherous profit as having good conduct,
and those who steal salaries and positions as worthy.
How could they still know the source of filial piety and brotherly respect,
the uprightness of loyalty,
the transformation of social order,
or the destination of the fundamental path?
This is why Bào Jiāo stood until he withered by the roadside,
and why Xú Yǎn drowned himself in the blue sea.
The proverb says:
"One dog barks at a shape,
and a hundred dogs bark at the sound."
The world has suffered from this for a long time!
I am pained by the world's failure to examine the true nature of authenticity and falsehood.
Therefore, I set forth a hypothetical argument to illustrate its heart, saying:
Now, observing how the high officials select scholars,
it is similar to the Sīyuán clan's hunting.
Formerly, there was a man of the Sīyuán clan
who set a fire to hunt in the middle of a field.
A deer ran toward the east,
and Sīyuán chased it with shouting.
A crowd to the west was chasing a pig;
hearing Sīyuán's shouting,
they vied to raise their voices in harmony with him.
Sīyuán, hearing the voices of the crowd,
then conversely stopped his own pursuit and went to lie in wait there,
where he encountered a common, ugly pig.
Sīyuán was delighted,
thinking himself that he had captured a white auspicious sign or a precious beast.
He exhausted his fodder and livestock, emptying his granaries to raise it.
The pig looked up and down, making grunting sounds,
and composed its appearance and voice.
Sīyuán treasured it even more.
After a short while,
a fierce wind rose and marsh rains fell,
drenching the huge pig and washing away the foul mud.
Startled and afraid during the chase,
its true voice came out,
and then he knew it was merely an old boar from a household.
This is the error of following sounds and chasing echoes;
the crowd encountered it and believed in it before even approaching.
The rulers of the present age toward scholars
are such that when their eyes see the worthy, they dare not use them,
but when their ears hear of the worthy, they regret not reaching them.
Even if they have their own knowledge,
they still cannot take them,
but must wait for the recommendations of the various officials.
Thus they also fear losing a Qílín or a deer and obtaining an old boar.
Why is it that they cannot distinguish them?
It is because they have not encountered the changes of wind and rain.
If one morning extraordinary policies were to be implemented together,
then the treacherous and narrow-minded,
and those of mediocre quality,
would be distinguished.
Indeed, when small men form cliques to secure their positions,
and slanderous and jealous groups bark and bite at the worthy,
is the resulting calamity and ruin rare?
The Three Eras were overturned because of this,
and various states were destroyed because of this.
Later generations are still unable to reform;
this is why the various officials frequently fail in their duties
and why the Mandate of Heaven often shifts.
The Shī says:
"The state has been utterly cut down,
why do you not oversee it!"
Alas!
The rulers of the time and the common masters do not examine this.
That by which a state is governed is the ruler's clarity;
that by which it is in chaos is the ruler's darkness.
That by which a ruler is clear is listening to all;
that by which he is dark is partial belief.
For this reason, if a ruler communicates, he must listen to all,
then his sagacity will broaden daily;
if he listens to mediocre talk and believes partially,
then his folly will increase daily.
The Shī says:
"The people of old had a saying:
'Consult even the grass and firewood cutters.'"
In the governance of Yáo and Shùn,
they opened the gates in all four directions,
cleared their vision in all four directions,
and extended their hearing to all four directions.
Therefore, the world converged upon them like spokes to a hub, and there was nothing the sages did not illuminate;
thus, the likes of Gòng and Gǔn could not block them,
and those of glib speech and perverse conduct could not deceive them.
Qín Èrshì,
strove to hide himself
and cut himself off from the hundred officials;
he distanced himself from and discarded those of humble and distant status and placed his trust in Zhào Gāo.
Consequently, his hearing was blocked by noble and powerful ministers,
and his vision was obscured by arrogant and envious people.
Thus, when the world broke into rebellion,
he did not hear of it.
All were killed by Zhào Gāo,
and no one dared to speak of it.
Only when Zhōu Zhāng reached Xì did he first become alarmed;
only when Yán Lè stepped forward to admonish him did he then feel regret,
but was it not already too late!
Therefore, if a ruler listens to all and accepts those below,
then noble ministers cannot slander others,
and distant people cannot deceive him;
but if he treats the humble with contempt and trusts only the noble,
then honest words will have no way to reach the court,
and pure scholars will withdraw themselves and submit to punishment in the wilderness.
Court ministers are the means by which to maintain order,
but if many form cliques, there will be chaos;
worthy men are the means to support oneself,
but if they go into hiding in the wilderness, the ruler will be isolated,
and that such a ruler could survive
has never happened.
For this reason, when an enlightened ruler presides over the masses,
he makes it his business to seek words from below to illuminate the outside,
and respectfully accepts those of humble status to attract the worthy.
That he does not reject any words
is not because the words of every speaker are entirely useful,
but because he fears that by rejecting what is useless he will turn away what is useful;
that he does not treat the humble with contempt
is not because every such person is entirely worthy,
but because he fears that by slighting the unworthy he will cut off the hopes of the worthy.
Therefore, the Shèngwáng holds the minor accountable to encourage the great,
and rewards the lowly to recruit the worthy;
only then do fine scholars gather at the court,
and the sentiments of those below reach the ruler.
Thus above there are no policies that are overlooked,
and in office there are no ministers who subvert the law.
This is what benefits both ruler and people,
and is what the treacherous and sycophantic dread.
Formerly, Zhāng Lù had one audience and the Ráng Hóu was dismissed;
Yuán Sī stepped forward with a proposal and Zhōu Bó was demoted.
For this reason, those in power
always envy upright and honest scholars,
fearing they might get a single word to the ruler to correct their wickedness.
Therefore, above they adorn false words to make the ruler's mind manifest their own,
and below they establish authority to secure their hold over the scholars and people.
Zhào Gāo threw the government into chaos;
fearing his evils would be heard by the ruler,
he preemptively urged Qín Èrshì, saying:
"If you frequently see the various ministers and discuss government affairs with the multitude, you will appear common;
being common will reveal your shortcomings.
It is better to hide yourself and make decisions alone;
thus you will appear divine and majestic.
The Tiānzǐ calls himself Zhèn,
precisely so that people only hear his name."
Qín Èrshì then deeply secluded himself,
and only Zhào Gāo was allowed access.
Inside, Zhào Gāo offered pleasant words to delight the ruler;
outside, he relied on imperial edicts to aggrandize himself.
The world collapsed like a rotting fish,
and the people led one another to rebel against Qín.
Zhào Gāo was terrified
and shifted the blame to the ruler;
he then sent Yán Lè to reprimand and kill him.
The ruler wished for one meeting with Zhào Gāo but could not, and so he died.
Tián Cháng imprisoned Jiǎn Gōng
and Chuò Chǐ hung up Mǐn Wáng;
Qín Èrshì had already heard of these events.
Yet why did he still follow in their footsteps of ruin?
His fault was in not accepting the admonitions of his high officials,
and not listening to the songs and sayings of the common people,
believing himself to be worthier than Jiǎn Gōng and Mǐn Wáng,
and Zhào Gāo to be worthier than those two ministers.
Thus the state was already in chaos while the ruler was unaware,
and calamity had already arisen while those below did not come to the rescue.
This was not because the masses collectively abandoned the ruler,
but rather the ruler entrusted the lives of the masses to Zhào Gāo;
it was the malady of cutting himself off from the people.
How can the rulers of later, decadent ages know of their peril?
Shùn said:
"If I err,
you must assist me.
Do not follow me to my face,
and then have words to say once you have withdrawn."
Thus the way to govern a state
is to encourage others to offer admonition
and to spread the word to make them speak;
only then will the ruler be perceptive and the circumstances of governance be clearly understood.
Furthermore, all arrogant ministers like to hide worthy men;
they both fear that their righteousness will be used to restrain them,
and they feel ashamed that while occupying high positions their wisdom does not equal those below,
or that while holding their offices policies do not originate from them.
Therefore, Xì Wǎn won the hearts of the masses and Zǐcháng killed him;
Qū Yuán won the ruler’s favor and Jiāo and Lán fabricated slanders;
Gěng Shòu established the Ever-Level Granaries and Yán Yán envied his counsel;
Chén Tāng killed Zhìzhī and Kuāng Héng disputed his merit.
Looking at it from this perspective,
if one occupies a humble position and wishes to perform good service for the ruler,
then one must first become an enemy of the favored ones.
They rely on long-standing favor to obstruct one from within,
while the humble one tries to prove their sincerity from without;
this is why a ruler who thinks of the good
and a scholar who wishes to be loyal,
even though they live together in the same age
and their anxious hearts are clear to one another,
they ultimately never manage to meet.
Of all the great tasks of a ruler,
none is more urgent than knowing the worthy;
and of the short path to knowing the worthy,
none is more urgent than examining their achievements.
If achievements are truly examined, then order and chaos will be clearly revealed;
if good and evil are verified, then the upright and worthy will not be obstructed,
and the sycophantic and clever will not be able to conceal their wickedness.
If a sword is not tested, its sharpness or dullness remains hidden;
if a bow is not tested, its strength or weakness remains misrepresented;
if a hawk is not tested, its skill or clumsiness remains confusing;
if a horse is not tested, its quality or mediocrity remains in doubt.
That these four things can be confused
is because they have not been tested and examined.
Now, if the various ministers are not tested,
the disaster will not merely end in misrepresentation, hiddenness, doubt, and confusion,
but will certainly lead to habits of negligence and disrespect.
Suppose a family has five sons and ten grandsons,
and the parents do not distinguish between the diligent and the weak;
then those who are industrious will become lazy,
and those who are idle and disrespectful will persist in their faults;
this is the path to wasting assets and ruining the family.
If between fathers, sons, and brothers,
in the plans of a single household,
it is still like this,
then how much more so for the many ministers collectively managing public affairs?
The Chuán says:
"If good and evil are not made manifest,
how can one discourage or encourage?"
Therefore, if the head of a family does not examine achievements,
the descendants will be lazy and the family will be ruined and impoverished;
if the heads of offices do not examine achievements,
then officials will be negligent and arrogant, and wickedness and villainy will arise;
if emperors and kings do not examine achievements,
then the upright and worthy will be suppressed and the deceitful and false will prevail.
Thus the Shū says:
"Every three years, examine the results of their work,
demoting the incompetent and promoting the brilliant."
This is the means to illuminate the worthy and the foolish and to encourage the capable and the incapable.
When the Shèngwáng established the hundred officials,
it was all to follow Heaven and govern the Earth,
and to shepherd and nourish the myriad people.
Therefore, those with titles must conform to the canonical records,
and those named for their principles must be verified by reality;
thus no office will have its duties neglected,
and no position will be held by the wrong person.
As for Shǒuxiàng and Lìngzhǎng,
their effectiveness lies in governing the people;
as for Zhōumù and Cìshǐ,
their effectiveness lies in being perceptive in oversight;
the Jiǔqīng divide their duties
to assist the Sāngōng;
the Sāngōng oversee everything
and are in charge of harmonizing the Yīn and Yáng;
all should have their governance examined to verify the reality of their service as an excellence for the king.
Shìzhōng, Dàfū, Bóshì, and Yìláng
take speech as their duty
and remonstrance as their office;
as for those selected as Màocái, Xiàolián, Xiánliáng Fāngzhèng, Dūnpǔ, Yǒudào, Míngjīng, Kuānbó, Wǔměng, and Zhìjù,
these all have names that designate them and titles that define them,
and they are what all ministers should devote their true feelings and exhaust their thoughts to in order to fulfill the ruler's commands.
Now, however, it is not so.
Magistrates and regional governors do not think of establishing merit;
they are greedy, cruel, and arbitrary;
they do not follow laws and decrees;
and they oppress and wrong the common people.
Provincial authorities do not rectify this,
causing people to travel from afar to the capital to submit petitions and complaints.
The *Shàngshū* does not hold the *Sāngōng* responsible;
the *Sāngōng* do not reprimand the provinces and commanderies;
and the provinces and commanderies do not punish the counties and towns.
Consequently, the wicked and cunning find it easy to wrong others.
Officials such as the *Shìzhōng*, *Bóshì*, and *Jiànyì*
sometimes remain in their positions for many years,
yet in the end, they never speak of promoting the worthy, detesting the evil, or rectifying omissions and flaws,
nor do they have the worry of being demoted or dismissed.
Among the officials who recommend candidates for office,
some recommend the stubborn and obtuse for *Mòucái*,
the rebellious for *Zhìxiào*,
the gluttonous for *Liánlì*,
the cunning for *Fāngzhèng*,
the flattering for *Zhíyán*,
the frivolous for *Dūnhòu*,
the empty for *Yǒudào*,
the ignorant for *Míngjīng*,
the cruel for *Kuānbó*,
the weak for *Wǔměng*,
and the foolish for *Zhìjù*.
Names and realities do not correspond;
the requested candidates do not match the requirements.
The wealthy rely on their resources and strength;
the noble obstruct with their influence and power.
Having much money is considered being worthy,
and being headstrong is considered being superior.
Generally, the reason those in office are mostly the wrong people
and official governance is frequently chaotic and neglected is this.
In ancient times, when the feudal lords presented candidates,
if one was suitable, it was called "loving virtue";
if a second was suitable, it was called "valuing the worthy";
if three were suitable, it was called "having merit,"
and they were granted rewards.
If they failed to present candidates,
for one failure, their rank was reduced;
for a second, their land was reduced;
after three reductions, both rank and land were completely taken away.
Those who colluded with subordinates to deceive superiors were put to death;
those who colluded with superiors to deceive subordinates were punished.
Those who participated in state governance but were of no benefit to the people were dismissed;
those in high positions who could not promote the worthy were expelled.
Their receiving of tasks and emphasis on selection,
and their scrutiny of names and realities to determine rewards and punishments were like this.
Therefore, they could distinguish the worthy from the foolish and obtain many talented men,
establish education and transformation, and pacify the common people.
During the *Sāndài*,
all achieved *Tàipíng*.
Since the Sage *Hàn* ascended the throne,
it has been thirty-two years,
yet this has not been achieved because
education is not applied, merit is not examined,
rewards and punishments are delayed, and amnesties and ransoms are frequent.
A proverb says:
"Crooked wood hates the straight plumb-line;
heavy punishment hates clear evidence."
This is why the various ministers enjoy general confusion and hate the examination of merit.
The Sage is the mouth of Heaven;
the worthy are the interpreters for the Sage.
Therefore, the words of the Sage
are the heart of Heaven.
What the worthy explain
is the intent of the Sage.
The former master Lord *Jīng*
categorized and scrutinized the examination of merit
to leave it to the talented and eminent.
The foundation of *Tàipíng*
must start from this;
the transformation through *Wúwéi*
must come from this.
Therefore, for a worldly ruler to ignore the examination of merit yet long for *Tàipíng*
is like wanting to discard the compass and square yet make circles and squares,
or wanting to cross a great water without a boat or oars.
Although one might say they are unrestrained,
they do not realize that following these measures is easy and fast.
The various officials and leaders
all have their respective offices;
each resides in their position
to be held accountable for their results.
The hundreds of commanderies and thousands of counties
each follow their predecessors
to plan for their successors.
Verbal responses
each follow their written text
to verify their reality.
Then, service in office will not be lax,
and those who state their opinions cannot deceive.
The *Shū* says:
"Assess their intake by their words,
test them clearly by their merit,
and award chariots and robes according to their services."
"Who could not yield?
Who could not respectfully respond?"
This is how *Yáo* and *Shùn* nurtured the common people and achieved *Shíyōng*.
That by which a state exists is order;
that by which it perishes is chaos.
No ruler does not love order and hate chaos,
or enjoy existence and fear perish.
However, constantly observing ancient records,
since recent antiquity,
there have been three perished dynasties
and countless defiled states.
Why is this?
Examining their failure,
it is always because the rulers constantly loved that which caused chaos
and hated that which caused order;
they loathed that which caused existence
and cherished that which caused perish.
Therefore, though separated by a hundred generations,
though years apart by a cycle,
though bounded by the *Jiǔzhōu*,
and with different customs a thousand *lǐ* away,
yet the signs of their perish and the traces of their failure
are like overlapping compasses and matching squares,
like tally-marks fitting together.
Therefore it is said:
Though one has the beauty of *Yáo* and *Shùn*,
one must be tested against the *Zhōusòng*;
though one has the evil of *Jié* and *Zhòu*,
one will surely be criticized in the *Bǎn* and *Dàng*.
"The mirror of *Yīn* is not far;
it is in the generation of the sovereign of *Xià*."
One who shares the same illness as the dead
cannot live;
one who follows the same path as a perished state
cannot exist.
Is this empty talk?
How does one know a person is about to be ill?
By their lack of appetite for food.
How does one know a state is about to be in chaos?
By its lack of appetite for the worthy.
Therefore, in the kitchen of a sick family,
it is not that there are no fine delicacies;
rather, it is that the person cannot eat them,
thus they proceed toward death.
In the officialdom of a chaotic state,
it is not that there are no worthy people;
rather, it is that the ruler cannot employ them,
thus it proceeds toward ruin.
Fresh rice and fine grains,
delicious wine and sweet spirits,
are that which nurtures life,
but the sick person loathes them,
thinking them not as good as the beans, wheat, chaff, and dregs they desire to purge;
this is the sign of their impending death.
Honoring the worthy and employing the capable,
trusting the loyal and accepting remonstrance,
are that which brings peace,
but a dark ruler loathes them,
thinking them not as good as the words of the treacherous, flattering, lowly, and slanderous;
this is the sign of their impending ruin.
*Lǎozǐ* said:
"Only by being distressed by distress
does one avoid being distressed."
The *Yì* says, "'It is perishing! It is perishing!'
Tie it to a cluster of mulberry trees."
Therefore, the gentleman who nurtures longevity
takes medicine before falling ill;
the ruler who nurtures his age
employs the worthy before chaos ensues.
In this way, his person is always at peace and the state lasts forever.
Upper doctors heal the state;
next, lower doctors heal illnesses.
Governance of a state
is truly a reflection of the governance of the body.
Illness is the disease of the body;
disorder is the disease of the state.
A body's illness awaits a doctor to be cured;
a state's disorder awaits the virtuous to be governed.
To govern the body, there are the arts of *Huángdì*;
to govern the world, there are the classics of *Kǒngzǐ*.
However, when illness is not cured and disorder is not governed,
it is not because the methods of acupuncture and stone-needling are mistaken
or that the words of the *Wǔjīng* are false,
but rather because those who employ them are not the right people.
If it is not the right person,
then the compass will not make circles and the square will not make rectangles,
the marking line will not be straight and the level will not be flat,
drilling for fire will yield no flame,
smelting stone will yield no metal,
a metal horse cannot pursue speed,
and an earthen boat cannot cross water.
All these eight things
are the manifest Way of Heaven,
visible and tangible objects.
If the person is not right,
even they will achieve nothing,
so how much more so for one who harbors the Way and its arts to soothe the populace,
and rides the six dragons to steer the heart of Heaven?
Governing the world without obtaining the truly virtuous
is like treating an illness without obtaining a good doctor.
To treat an illness, one should get genuine *rénshēn*,
but instead gets *zhīluófú*;
one should get *màiméndōng*,
but instead gets *zhēng kuàngmài*.
Not recognizing the genuine oneself,
one compounds and takes them;
the illness grows increasingly severe,
yet one does not realize they have been deceived by others.
One then conversely claims the prescription is not honest and that medicines are of no benefit in treating illness,
thus discarding subsequent medicine and not daring to drink it,
and instead seeks shamans and sorcerers.
Even if they die, it is expected.
A lord seeks the virtuous,
but those below respond with the vulgar,
and present the crooked instead of the straight.
If he does not draw in the genuine himself
and accepts the common to appoint them to office,
the state will fall into increasing disorder,
and he will not realize he has been deceived by those below.
He then conversely claims the classics are not to be trusted and that the virtuous are of no benefit in saving the state from disorder,
thus casting aside the truly virtuous and no longer seeking their advancement,
instead employing vulgar clerks.
Even if the state is destroyed, it is expected.
Since the *Sāndài*,
everyone has been compounding medicine with *zhīluófú* and *zhēng kuàngmài*;
the illness grows more feverish daily until death ensues.
The *Shū* says:
"If people have ability,
let them follow their conduct,
and the state will thus flourish."
Therefore, the former kings selected people for office
and were certain to obtain those with talent.
Their achievements were bestowed upon the people,
and their virtue matched their positions.
Consulted by humans and consulted by spirits,
the common people approved of their ability,
and they worked in harmony to move Heaven and Earth in this manner.
This is how the *Sāndài* founded states and established marquises,
and why they were able to pass their succession through a hundred generations,
lasting for thousands of years.
Since after the *Chūnqiū* period,
by the systems of the *Zhànguó*,
generals, ministers, and powerful officials
must come from the families of relatives.
Brothers of the empress,
sons-in-law of the lord, and maternal grandsons—
though their age is still that of children
and they have not yet shed their shackles,
they take up these official posts based on such ties.
Their achievements are not bestowed on the people,
and their bounty does not reach those below, yet they take the rank of marquises
and receive much land.
Furthermore, they cannot govern the people or demonstrate ability to repay the commoners;
they eat heavy stipends in vain,
eating without working and occupying offices like corpses.
They only engage in excess and extravagance,
sitting and acting with pride and luxury,
and they are ruined before they can pass their status to the next generation.
*Zǐchǎn* had a saying:
"If one cannot yet handle a knife but is made to cut,
the injuries will indeed be many."
Therefore, when the lords of the age deal with their noble relatives,
they love the beauty of their favorites and flatterers
and grant them office without weighing their talent.
They do not make them establish merit to entrust themselves to the people,
but carelessly strive to raise their ranks and positions
and heap honors and gifts upon them.
This causes them to incur the resentment of the common people
and fall into the guilt of evil.
Once their accumulated faults are complete,
how could they not collapse and fall?
This is what is called:
"Your love for the person
only ends up harming them!"
In the systems of the former kings,
in appointing people to office, they were certain to assess their talent.
Only after the assessment was fixed did they grant them rank;
only after the position was fixed did they grant them a stipend.
If the lord of men does not examine this
and carelessly allows relatives or those favored for their looks to take charge of offices,
it is like replacing a driver or servant with a beloved child,
or exchanging bright pearls for broken tiles and gravel.
Though there may be feelings of love and fondness,
they will certainly overturn the great carriage and kill the sick person.
The *Shū* says, "The work is Heaven's; it is for man to act in its stead."
The *Chuán* says:
"Those who complete the power of Heaven and Earth
have never failed to be numerous and flourishing."
From this perspective,
if the lords of the age desire to make people without merit powerful and wealthy,
then this is to struggle against Heaven.
To make people without virtue or gifts struggle against August Heaven
and yet hope to stand for long—
since ancient times,
such a thing has never existed.
In all governance by a lord of men,
nothing is greater than harmonizing *yīnyáng*.
*Yīnyáng* takes Heaven as its root.
If the heart of Heaven is followed, then *yīnyáng* are harmonized;
if the heart of Heaven is opposed, then *yīnyáng* are discordant.
Heaven takes the people as its heart;
if the people are peaceful and happy, the heart of Heaven is followed;
if the people are sorrowful and suffering, the heart of Heaven is opposed.
The people take the lord as their unifying guide;
if the lord’s government is good, the people are harmoniously governed;
if the lord’s government is bad, the people are resentful and disordered.
The lord takes caring for the people as his root;
if the ministers are loyal and good, the lord’s government is good;
if the ministers are treacherous and crooked, the lord’s government is bad.
Selection is the root;
if the selection and recommendation are substantive, the loyal and virtuous advance;
if the selection is false and deceptive, the wicked and partisan are presented.
Selection takes laws and orders as its root;
if the laws and orders are upright, the selection and recommendation are substantive;
if the laws and orders are deceptive, the selection is false and deceptive.
The law takes the lord as its master;
if the lord trusts the law, the law is followed and implemented;
if the lord cheats the law, the law is abandoned.
The efficacy of the lord, ministers, laws, and orders
is certainly demonstrated among the people.
Therefore, if the lord, ministers, laws, and orders are good, the people are peaceful and happy;
if the people are peaceful and happy, the heart of Heaven is comforted;
if the heart of Heaven is comforted, *yīnyáng* are harmonized;
if *yīnyáng* are harmonized, the *wǔgǔ* are abundant;
if the *wǔgǔ* are abundant, the people enjoy long lives;
if the people enjoy long lives, they will flourish in righteousness;
if they flourish in righteousness, there will be no treacherous conduct;
if there is no treacherous conduct, the age will be at peace;
the state will be tranquil, the *shèjì* will be secure,
and the lord will be honored and glorified.
Therefore, the heart of Heaven, *yīnyáng*, lord and ministers, the common populace, good and evil—these assist one another in arriving and serve as evidence for one another.
Heaven is the foundation of the state;
the lord is the unifying guide of the people;
ministers are the materials of governance.
"If a craftsman wishes to do his work well,
he must first sharpen his tools."
Therefore, one who is about to bring about *Dàpíng*
must first tune *yīnyáng*;
one who tunes *yīnyáng*
must first follow the heart of Heaven;
one who follows the heart of Heaven
must first bring peace to his people;
one who brings peace to his people
must first carefully select his men.
Therefore, the root of the state's survival or ruin
and the pivot of order or disorder
lie only in the clarity of selection.
The Sages knew this;
therefore, they made it the primary concern of demotion and promotion.
The *Shū* says:
"If you would bring peace to the common people,
how could the selection be of any but the right men?"
This is why the former kings brought about *Tàipíng* and gave rise to the sounds of praise.
Prosperity and decline wax and wane;
Yin and Yang do not coexist.
By observing where they gather,
the portents of rise and fall can be seen.
Jì, Xiè, and Gāo Yáo gathered together and brought about peace and prosperity;
Huángfǔ, Juě, and Jǔ gathered together and brought about calamities and anomalies.
Verily, the signs of good and evil
match like a tally across a thousand lǐ,
and accumulate their traces over a hundred generations;
natures are similar, but habits lead them apart.
For this reason, wisdom and folly reside in the heart,
not in noble or humble status;
trustworthiness and deceit reside in the nature,
not in closeness or distance of relation.
Those with whom Èrshì together lost the empire
were the Chéngxiàng and the Yùshǐ.
Those with whom Gāozǔ together seized the empire
were from the shops of silk-sellers and the stalls of dog-butchers;
the laborers of Líshān
and the bandits of Jùyě
all became famous generals.
From this perspective,
if one obtains the right person,
one need not worry about poverty or humble status;
if one obtains the right talent,
one should not dislike their reputation or past tracks.
Tracing back the traces since the time of Hàn Yuán onward,
arrogant and noble ministers
often received punishment and death;
when their partisans were in office
and were punished for their crimes,
it was commonly two or three out of ten.
From this perspective,
noble and favored ministers
have never failed to plant their private favorites and advance wicked partisans.
Therefore, Wáng Mǎng together with the Hàn Gōngqīng and Mùshǒu seized Hàn;
Guāngwǔ together with the abandoned people and discarded scholars of Hàn executed them.
If noble people were necessarily worthy and loyal,
and humble people were necessarily foolish and deceitful,
then how could it be like this?
From the time of Chéngdì onward
until Wáng Mǎng,
the Gōngqīng and Lièhóu,
down to the Lìngwèi,
officials great and small,
numbering nearly a hundred thousand men,
were all what Hàn called worthy, brilliant, loyal, upright, noble, and favored scholars.
When Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
only the Ānzhònghóu Liú Chóng and the Dōngjùn Tàishǒu Zhái Yì thought of the ritual of serving their lord;
with courage and righteousness bursting forth,
they wished to execute Wáng Mǎng.
Although their success was not achieved,
their will and integrity are worthy of record.
Out of a count of a hundred thousand,
those who could uphold and repay the favor
were but two men.
From this perspective,
in a declining age, the crowd of ministers truly has few worthies;
the greater their office, the heavier their crime,
and the higher their position, the deeper their sin.
Therefore it is said:
The virtue of a well-governed age
and the evil of a declining age
always correspond to their rank and position.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"When the state possesses the Way,
to be poor and humble
is a shame;
when the state lacks the Way,
to be wealthy and noble
is a shame."
The Shī laments the "gleaming white colt,
in that empty valley,"
and "Artful words flow like a stream,
letting one dwell in leisure."
This speaks of the scholars of a declining age:
the purer their will, the humbler their person;
the more skillful their flattery, the more honorable their office.
"Directions are gathered by category;
things are divided by group."
Those with the same clarity see each other;
those with the same hearing hear each other.
Only a sage knows a sage;
only a worthy knows a worthy.
Now, those in power today
are neither able to clearly distinguish the worthy from the base,
and yet they yield to the whims and hints of noblemen
and are intimidated by the entreaties of the powerful.
Petitioners crowd their gates,
and ritual gifts converge like wheel spokes.
Pursued by immediate urgencies,
they give precedence to these.
This is exactly why upright scholars are uniquely obscured,
while crowds of the wicked are advanced by their partisans.
When Zhōugōng served as the Zǎifǔ,
he humbled himself before scholars,
and thus was able to obtain true worthies.
When Qí Xī served as a Dàfū,
he recommended his enemy and promoted his son,
and thus was able to obtain upright men.
The lot who hold office in the present age
rely on the favor of sisters and concubines to be arrogant toward scholars,
and use the power of the "exalted dragon" to insult the worthy.
They wish to make scholars of will and righteousness
crawl and bow their bodies to serve them,
and mar their faces with flattery to seek closeness.
Only then do they maintain them.
Consequently, upright scholars gather vetch while starving and shivering,
dying in the depths of mountain caves;
how could they be willing to tread upon their gates and associate with such people?
Among the lords who possess a state,
there is none who does not desire good government,
yet good government is not seen in many generations
because those they appoint are not worthy.
The world is never without worthies,
yet worthies do not get to be employed
because the crowd of ministers is jealous of them.
The ruler has the heart to seek the worthy
but lacks the method to obtain the worthy;
the ministers have the reputation of advancing the worthy
but lack the reality of advancing the worthy.
This is why the ruler is isolated and endangered above,
while the Way is uniquely suppressed below.
That by which a ruler achieves good government is public spirit;
when public laws are implemented, chaos and disorder are severed.
That by which a flattering minister benefits himself is selfishness;
when private techniques are used, public laws are usurped.
That by which an eminent scholar establishes integrity is righteousness;
when upright integrity is established, the base sort are replaced.
This is why treacherous ministers, chaotic officials, and lawless individuals
are said to block the path between a worthy ruler and a righteous scholar day and night,
causing them both not to find one another.
When a worthy person serves as a minister,
he does not harm his lord to serve flattery,
he does not fawn upon the masses to seek acceptance,
he does not neglect the public interest to listen to private matters,
and he does not bend the law to reject the firm.
His brilliance can illuminate treachery,
and his righteousness does not join with partisans.
For this reason, when Fàn Wǔ returned to Jìn, the treacherous of the state fled;
when Huá Yuán returned to the court, the Yú Shì perished.
Thus, righteous scholars and wicked, crooked people cannot stand together.
When a ruler selects scholars,
if he cannot consult the common people
and judge with his own intelligence,
but instead merely believes the talk of chaotic ministers
and exclusively uses the words of corrupt officials,
this is what is called choosing an envoy together with an enemy,
or letting a prisoner select his official.
The Shū says:
"Consult with your own heart;
consult with the common people."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"When the crowd likes someone,
one must examine them;
when the crowd hates someone,
one must examine them."
Therefore, when a sage employs or dismisses someone,
he does not necessarily rely on the crowd,
nor does he necessarily rely solely on himself.
He must examine the conduct of both others and himself
and measure them by righteousness.
Sometimes he sets aside others' views and follows his own;
thus his appointments are without oversight and his government is without ruin.
A confused ruler is not so;
if he has someone he loves,
he then uses that to determine what is right,
without consulting the crowd
or deliberating in his heart.
Blindly dazzled by his affection,
he follows whatever words they say.
This is why government falls into ruin
and why scholars are cast out and lost.
In the past, Zhòu was fond of feminine beauty.
When Jiǔ Hóu heard of this,
he presented his daughter.
Zhòu was greatly pleased
and believed that there was no beauty in the world like her.
When he asked Dájǐ about her,
Dájǐ feared that if the girl were admitted to the royal chambers, she would steal his favor,
so she falsely lowered her head and wept, saying:
"Is Your Majesty already reaching old age?
Is your eyesight already failing?
How could such an ugly appearance be called beautiful?"
Thereupon, Zhòu changed his mind and considered her ugly.
Dájǐ feared that people in the world would present even more beautiful women,
so she spoke of Jiǔ Hóu's unprincipled behavior,
saying that he intended to use this to delude the King.
"If Your Majesty does not execute him,
how will you reform those who come after?"
Zhòu then became enraged,
subsequently making meat jerky of the daughter and boiling Jiǔ Hóu.
From this time onward,
those in the world who had beautiful daughters
all kept them in inner chambers and closed their doors by day,
fearing only that Zhòu might hear of them.
Zhào Gāo monopolized power in Qín.
Intending to kill Èrshì,
he first demonstrated his authority to the multitude
by presenting a deer to the ruler
and claiming it was a fine horse.
Èrshì looked at it and said:
"It is a deer."
Gāo said:
"It is a horse."
Èrshì rubbed his eyes and stared at it, saying:
"Is the Prime Minister mistaken?
This is a deer."
Gāo continued to respond that it was a horse.
When the court officials were asked,
some of the court officials assisted Èrshì and said Gāo was wrong.
Gāo then said to Èrshì:
"These people are all flattering their lord and deluding their superior;
there is no greater disloyalty."
He then killed them all.
From this time onward,
no one dared to offer upright remonstrance,
and Gāo eventually killed Èrshì at Wàngyí,
which ultimately led to the dynasty's downfall.
Now, liking and disliking are evident to the eyes,
and the difference between a deer and a horse is manifest in their form;
these matters are already fixed.
Yet when it comes to slander,
such as the deceptive words and fabricated speeches of concubines and ministers,
then the ruler loses his own heart,
and people and things lose their reality to him.
How much more so when encountering those hidden in obscurity or prisoners,
where one must wait to verify their sincerity?
That is not like observing the focused intent of a seductive woman;
the discernment between the worthy and the unworthy
is not like the scrutiny and certainty of distinguishing a deer from a horse.
These two things
were both presented in the court
and their true nature exposed to the inner ministers.
When the ruler is deluded by affection, fawning, sycophancy, and clever rhetoric,
it is like dazzling the ruler's eyes
and subverting the ruler's heart,
so that he easily takes the beautiful for the ugly
and a deer for a horse.
How much more so for the worthy in the countryside
and the scholars outside the palace gates,
whom he has never even seen?
That those in power like to obscure the worthy and strive to promote their own factions
has been so since ancient times.
In the past, Táng Yáo was a great sage,
and his intelligence was widely proclaimed;
Yú Shùn was a great sage,
and the sound of his virtue was heard far and wide.
When Yáo was the Son of Heaven
and sought worthy men,
he consulted the various lords.
The lords were unwilling to recommend Shùn and instead praised the likes of Gòng and Gǔn.
Relying on Yáo's sagacity,
