he later raised up Shùn and exiled the four criminals.
Now, considering the character of the ancient sages,
the clarity of Yáo's hearing and vision,
and the brilliance of Shùn's virtue,
a wise ruler cannot be deceived,
and manifest virtue cannot be obscured.
Few people are sycophants by nature,
and those in power were as upright as that.
Nowadays, the conduct of the scholars
falls far short of Yáo and Shùn,
yet the customs are chaotic
and the laws of the age are increasingly manifest.
Consequently, for a ruler who seeks the worthy
and a scholar who pities the people
to meet each other
is surely unlikely.
When Wén Wáng was out hunting,
he met Jiāng Shàng by the banks of the Wèi River.
He examined his words and observed his will
and saw into his heart.
He did not consult his attendants
nor did he deliberate with his ministers.
He subsequently carried him back in his carriage,
entrusted him with the government,
and was thus able to establish the Zhōu dynasty.
Therefore, Yáo examined the local communities to find Shùn,
and Wén Wáng examined for himself to find Lǚ Shàng.
How could they be like Yīn Xīn and Qín Zhèng,
who, even if they obtained worthy men,
instead left the resolution of matters to their enemies,
executed the upright,
and promoted and employed the factions of treacherous ministers?
For this reason, an enlightened and sagely ruler follows the correct path.
He does not exclusively follow those of high rank and favor,
nor is he deluded by favorites and flatterers.
He does not discard those who are distant
or slight the young or lowly,
but examines and employs them.
Thus, in the systems of the Zhōu,
when the Son of Heaven listened to governance,
he had the Three Ducal Ministers down to the scholars present the codes,
the good historians present books,
the teachers give admonitions,
the blind musicians recite poems,
the sightless musicians chant,
the various craftsmen offer remonstrance,
the common people transmit words,
the close ministers offer full regulations,
the relatives make up for deficiencies and observe,
the blind historians provide instruction,
and the elders cultivate these matters.
Only then did the King deliberate upon them,
and therefore his affairs were carried out without failure.
In decadent ages, it is not so.
They only believe the arrogant and jealous discussions of the noble,
and exclusively use the sycophantic and deluding words of favorites.
Those who perform abundant rituals suffer blame and misfortune;
those who discuss virtue and righteousness are met with special hatred.
Then, flattering ministers follow up with laws of slander
and impose punishments for criticizing superiors.
This is the beginning of the worthy scholars' distress.
The laws of slander
are the axes that strike down the worthy,
and those who are arrogant and jealous
are the dogs that bite the worthy.
When a ruler inwardly wields the axe that strikes the worthy
and controls the dog that bites the worthy,
yet outwardly seeks the worthy,
wanting them to arrive,
is it not tragic?
In this world, there is no greater blessing,
yet there is also no more painful disaster.
One who occupies the highest position
cannot be without the greatest of merit.
Those who steal the extreme nobility of the "arrogant dragon"
have never failed to be destroyed and lost.
Those who achieve the great merit of Heaven and Earth
have never failed to flourish.
That which emperors and kings respect and which Heaven loves most
is the people.
Now, when a minister receives a high position from his ruler
to shepherd what Heaven loves most,
how can he not bring peace and benefit to them, and nourish and save them?
Therefore, when a gentleman holds office, he thinks of benefiting the people;
when he reaches high status, he thinks of promoting the worthy.
What merit is greater than this?
Therefore, when he is in a high position, those below do not feel burdened;
when he is in front, those behind do not feel left out.
The Shū says:
"The work is Heaven's; it is man who acts in its stead."
A king models himself after Heaven and establishes officials;
from the Ducal Ministers on down
to the minor officials,
which of them is not a Heavenly official?
For this reason, an enlightened ruler does not dare use private affection,
and a loyal minister does not dare falsely claim ability.
To steal another person's property
is still called theft;
how much more so to steal a Heavenly office for one's own private ends?
If a crime against a person
must be punished,
how much more so when one offends Heaven—
can there be no misfortune?
In the Wǔdài, marquises were established,
founding states and setting up houses;
their succession was passed down for a hundred generations,
and they lasted for thousands of years.
This was all because they were able to fulfill their Tiānguān and
extend their merits to the common people.
When Zhōugōng went on his eastern expedition,
later generations remembered him with longing;
as for Shàogōng and the sweet pear tree,
people could not bear to cut it down.
When one is loved like this,
how could anyone wish to privately harm them?
Of the enfeoffed lords of later times, there are many;
some do not last their whole lives,
and some do not even last a full month
before falling into ruin.
Of those whose lineages ended,
their duration did not exceed a hundred years.
Why is this so?
The ministers of the Wǔdài
served their rulers with the Way
and comforted the world with benevolence;
their grace reached even the plants and trees,
and they benefited both the external and internal realms.
Under the vast heaven and throughout the land,
none were not covered by their virtue.
That which they kept safe and sound
was truly the work of Heaven.
Therefore, their blessings and prosperity flowed down,
and their branches and roots lasted for a hundred generations.
The ministers of a declining age
do not think of following Heaven,
but only flatter the current ruler.
They call those who defeat enemies "loyal"
and those who kill many "worthy."
Bái Qǐ and Méng Tián
were regarded as meritorious by Qín,
but regarded as villains by Heaven.
Xīfū and Dǒng Xián
were regarded as loyal by their ruler,
but regarded as thieves by Heaven.
The likes of these,
though honored by the rulers of their time,
did not follow the heart of Heaven above
and did not gain the will of the people below.
Thus in the end they wept blood and wailed,
ending in disgrace.
The Yì says:
"When virtue is thin but position is noble,
when wisdom is small but plans are great,
when strength is little but responsibility is heavy,
seldom do they escape calamity."
Therefore, if virtue does not match the responsibility,
the disaster will certainly be harsh;
if ability does not match the position,
the calamity will certainly be great.
Furthermore, as for those who usurp their positions,
Heaven takes away their discernment,
and the spirits delude their hearts.
Therefore, in times of poverty and low status,
though they may have the talent of clear discernment and the will of benevolence and righteousness,
once they attain wealth and honor,
they turn their backs on relatives and abandon old friends,
losing their original heart.
They all distance themselves from kith and kin and draw near to sycophants,
neglect wise friends and favor dogs and horses.
Wealth and goods fill the quarters of servants and concubines,
while stipends and gifts are exhausted on cunning slaves.
They would rather see millions of coins rot on their strings
than endure giving one coin to another;
they would rather accumulate grain until it rots in the granary
than endure lending one decaliter to another.
These people are mostly arrogant and reckless,
and they do not repay their debts.
Their relatives harbor resentment at home,
and the common people slander them on the roads.
Their predecessors have already failed,
yet successors scramble to follow their lead;
it is truly lamentable.
Observing the intentions of the noblemen of previous generations,
they are like infants.
Infants have common illnesses,
noble ministers have common disasters,
parents have common failings,
and rulers have common errors.
The infants' common illness
is being harmed by overfeeding;
the noble ministers' common disaster
is being harmed by over-favor.
The parents' common failing
lies in being unable to stop doting on a favored child;
the ruler's common error
lies in being unable to stop indulging an arrogant minister.
If breastfeeding is too much,
then one will certainly suffer from convulsions and fits;
if wealth and honor are too extreme,
then one will certainly become arrogant and idle and commit errors.
Therefore, those whose doted-upon children ruin themselves
are not just from one family;
those arrogant ministers who cause their families' destruction
are not just from one generation.
Some fail through rebellion, perversion, and lack of the Way;
some because their thin virtue did not match their high status.
Wénchāng establishes merit,
and Sīmìng points out errors;
they observe the depth of the evil
and mete out punishment according to the crime.
Some are captured and beheaded,
some have their shoulders broken and chests torn open,
are thrown to their deaths in deep pits,
carry a blade in the capital market,
leave stiff corpses and broken homes,
or have their lineages overturned and clans exterminated—
these are all those who had no merit for the common people.
Yet later generations are greedy for power and covetous of favor,
accumulating wealth without limit;
they think of climbing the tower of downfall
and take pleasure in following the tracks of the overturned cart,
wishing to augment their blessings
to act as seat-fillers until the measure is full—
in what age are they not present?
In the time of the Lǚshì prominence,
the Empress Dowager reigned and monopolized the government,
and Lù and Chǎn managed affairs and held power.
They arbitrarily installed four kings,
enfeoffed many of their sons and brothers,
and held both generalships and chancellorships,
entrenching themselves both inside and outside the court.
They thought that even if Tāng or Wǔ were to rise
or the Wǔbà were to appear,
they could not be endangered.
Thus they discarded benevolence and righteousness and valued majesty and cruelty,
and they destroyed ritual and trust and pursued trickery and deceit.
The whole world was resentful and pained,
and the people desired their downfall,
so in a single morning they were wiped out and no one mourned them.
In the time of the Huòshì prominence,
they exclusively assisted the young ruler,
executed their colleagues,
and deposed and installed emperors;
none dared to oppose them.
Yǔ succeeded to his father's position,
Shān and Yún managed affairs,
the various sons-in-law exclusively commanded the imperial guards,
and they married within their own clan.
In the time of the Wángshì prominence,
there were nine marquises and five generals,
and twenty-three red-wheeled carriages.
The Empress Dowager monopolized the government,
and they held power for three generations.
Mǎng became the State Regulator
and was enfeoffed as the Ānhàngōng;
he acted as regent under a false title,
personally facing south as ruler,
and finally usurped the throne
for over ten years.
He thought that having held the position for so long,
with majesty established and grace extended,
there would never be disaster or failure.
Thus he let his heart be reckless and his will arbitrary,
favoring those close to him and forgetting those far away.
He gathered and exalted petty people,
heavily taxed and exhausted the people
to provide for those without merit,
and acted with villainy and deceit.
He claimed his actions were based on the Classics
to delude the common people
and deceive Heaven and Earth.
He thought himself secret
and that no one knew,
but August Heaven from above observed his villainy,
and the Divine Brightness from the shadows illuminated his true state—
how could there be any mistake!
Now, birds consider the mountains too low and build their nests high upon them,
and fish consider the deep pools too shallow and bore holes within them;
yet the reason they are finally caught is the bait.
Noble relatives fear their families' lack of good fortune and gather various fine reputations;
they fear their gates are not strong and make iron pivots for them.
Yet the reason they finally fail
is not because they suffered from a lack of taboos or because the door pivots rotted,
but always because they suffered from exalting wealth and goods and practicing arrogance and usurpation,
oppressing the common people and losing the hearts of the populace.
Kǒngzǐ said:
“Do not worry about having no position;
worry about whether you have established yourself.”
Therefore, if ministers do not honor and follow the ritual laws,
exhaust their spirit in thinking of their duties,
provide sincere assistance to the sovereign,
and demonstrate merit to the common people;
if they do not personally attach themselves to the commoners below,
nor follow the will of Heaven above,
but instead desire to follow their private knowledge,
usurp the sovereign's majesty and virtue
to oppress the common people,
go against Heaven and Earth,
deceive the spiritual beings,
advance through improper means,
and enrich themselves;
then they reside in the peril of piled-up eggs
while planning for the security of Tài Shān.
They engage in conduct as fleeting as morning dew
yet think of achievements lasting generations.
This is like Shǐhuáng abandoning virtue and relying on punishment,
wishing to calculate his line from the first generation to ten thousand.
Is this not delusional!
A King treats the four seas as one family
and counts the millions of people as a single whole.
If one man does not plow,
the world will surely suffer hunger for it;
if one woman does not weave,
the world will surely suffer cold for it.
Now the whole world abandons farming and sericulture
to pursue commerce.
Oxen, horses, carts, and carriages
fill and block the roads.
Idle hands engage in clever crafts
and fill the cities and towns.
Those who cultivate the roots are few,
while those who eat as idlers are many.
“The city of Shāng is bustling;
it is the standard for the four quarters.”
Now observing Luòyáng,
those in secondary pursuits are ten times more numerous than farmers,
and those who are false and idle are ten times more numerous than those in secondary pursuits.
Thus, one man plows,
and a hundred people eat;
one woman tends the silkworms,
and a hundred people wear the cloth.
With one person supporting a hundred,
who can sustain it?
Across the hundred commanderies and thousand counties of the world,
and the tens of thousands of market towns,
they are all like this.
How can the roots and branches possibly sustain each other?
How then can the people not be hungry and cold?
When hunger and cold arrive together,
how can they not commit wrongs?
When they commit wrongs, there is treachery and disorder;
when treachery and disorder abound,
how can the officials not be severe and cruel?
When severity and cruelty are repeatedly applied,
how can those below not feel sorrow and resentment?
When those with sorrow and resentment are many,
then signs of misfortune arrive together.
The common people have no means of livelihood,
and High Heaven sends down calamities;
then the state is in peril.
Indeed, poverty is born from wealth,
weakness is born from strength,
disorder is born from order,
and peril is born from security.
Therefore, when a wise King nurtures the people,
he worries for them and labors for them,
he teaches them and instructs them,
he is cautious of the subtle and guards against the budding,
to cut off their evil.
Thus the Yì praises “limiting with institutions,
not wasting wealth,
and not harming the people”;
the poem Qī Yuè,
teaches the great and the small,
ending and then beginning again.
Viewed from this perspective,
the people certainly cannot be allowed to be indulgent.
Now the people are extravagant in their clothing
and lavish in their food and drink;
they devote themselves to rhetoric and practice deception
to cheat one another;
they are shoulder to shoulder.
Some take plotting treachery and forming cliques as their profession,
while others take wandering and gambling as their business.
Some able-bodied men do not touch the plow or hoe for generations,
but carry pellets and slingshots,
wandering hand in hand.
Some take fine earth to make pellets and sell them;
externally, these cannot be used to resist invaders,
and internally, they are not enough to stop rats.
Jìn Líng liked them and thereby increased his wickedness;
one has never heard of a man of ambition and righteousness who enjoyed carrying them for wandering.
Only thoughtless people
and crowds of boys
take and hold them,
recklessly shooting at birds and sparrows,
failing to hit one in a hundred shots,
but instead hitting people in the face or eyes;
this is most useless and harmful.
Some sit and make bamboo mouth organs,
sharpening their tips
in the appearance of something that causes injury;
they coat them with wax and honey
as if they are of the kind that sweetens the tongue;
all of these are not auspicious or good omens.
Some make mud carts, clay dogs, horse riders, and puppets—
various toys to amuse children through clever deception.
The Shī criticizes: “She does not spin her hemp;
the girl dances and swirls.”
Now many do not cultivate their household duties
but “cease their silkworm weaving”
to start learning to be shamans and hags,
drumming and dancing to serve the spirits,
to deceive the simple people
and bewilder the common women.
In families of the weak and the sick,
filled with worry and confusion,
all are easily frightened,
to the point that they are made to rush about at supposedly favorable times,
leaving their proper residences
to stay in rugged places by the roadside,
leaking above and damp below,
harmed by wind and cold,
exploited by evil people,
and struck by thieves and robbers,
increasing their misfortunes and calamities
until the severe cases are beyond counting.
Some abandon medicine
to go and serve the spirits;
thus, when they arrive at death,
they do not know they were deceived and misled by shamans,
but instead regret serving the shamans too late.
This is the peak of bewildering the simple people.
Some cut fine silk
to make hair coverings,
having artisans paint them
and hiring people to write prayers on them,
using empty adornments and clever words,
wanting to invite many blessings.
Some tear apart colorful silk,
cutting it several inches wide
and five inches long,
then sewing and painting it to wear.
Some spin colorful silk and make cords,
cutting them to wrap around their arms.
These are forever of no benefit to good or bad fortune,
but vainly ruin fine silk
and agitate the common people.
Some carve and cut patterned silks,
stealthily using eight colors within an inch,
to make patterns of elm leaves, infinity, and water ripples,
finely stitching and sewing
to make bags, skirts, jackets, clothes, and quilts,
wasting a hundred bolts of silk
and using ten times the labor.
Those of this kind
neither assist the growth of farming, industry, or weaving,
nor do they benefit the world;
yet they sit and eat the fine grain,
waste the daylight,
destroy successful work,
breaking what is whole,
making the sturdy perishable,
turning the large into small,
and the easy into difficult;
all of these should be prohibited.
Mountains and forests cannot supply a wildfire,
and rivers and seas cannot fill a leaking goblet.
Xiàowén Huángdì personally wore robes of coarse black silk,
wore leather shoes on his feet,
used a leather belt for his sword,
and used the bags of collected petitions to make curtains for the palace.
During the intense heat of midsummer,
he wished to build a terrace,
but calculated the cost at one million;
considering it an extravagant waste, he did not build it.
Today, the noble relatives in the capital
have clothing, food and drink, carriages and palanquins, ornaments, and dwellings
that all exceed the royal regulations;
their arrogance and overstepping are extreme.
Even their slaves and concubines
all wear fine Gédǐ and Shēngyuè linens,
Tóngzhōng female-woven cloth,
delicate silks and gauzes,
and ice-white fine silks and embroideries.
They possess rhinoceros horn, ivory, pearls, and jade,
amber and tortoiseshell,
hidden ornaments of mountain stones,
and gold and silver inlays and engravings.
They wear shoes made of roe deer and muntjac leather
and sashes of patterned silk.
In their arrogance and extravagance, they overstep their masters,
and boast to one another;
what Jìzǐ once sighed over
is now found among slaves and concubines.
When the wealthy and noble marry,
they use ten covered carriages each,
with mounted slaves and servant boys
flanking the wheels and leading the way.
The rich compete to surpass one another,
while the poor feel ashamed of not keeping up.
Therefore, the cost of a single banquet
ruins the livelihood of a lifetime.
In ancient times, one had to be a mìngmín
before being allowed to wear patterned silks and ride in carriages.
Since today we cannot entirely return to antiquity,
though the common people truly ought not to require it,
they actually surpass the Xiàowén of old:
their clothes must be delicate,
their shoes must be of roe deer and muntjac,
their sashes must be patterned,
and their decorated socks must be made of Yúcǐ silk;
they ornament their horses and carriages
and keep many male and female slaves.
All those who are able to live like this
neither grow grain
nor do they do anything but sit as parasitic pests.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"In the burials of antiquity,
people covered the body thickly with firewood
and buried it in the middle of the wilds,
with neither mound nor trees,
and no fixed period of mourning;
later sages replaced this with the inner and outer coffins."
Using paulownia wood for the inner coffin
and kudzu fibers for the bindings,
it does not reach the springs below,
nor does it release odors above.
Later generations used catalpa, pagoda tree, cypress, and other woods,
each taken from what the local land produced.
Glues and lacquers were applied to the seams,
fine nails were used for the joints,
and surfaces were planed and polished
so that no joints could be seen.
Its strength was sufficient to rely on,
and its utility was sufficient for the task;
this was enough.
After that, the noble relatives in the capital
insisted on using nèn-catalpa and Yùzhāng camphor and phoebe wood;
even in the remote borders and lower lands,
people competed to imitate them.
As for the nèn-catalpa and Yùzhāng camphor,
their origin is extremely distant,
and they grow in deep mountains and remote valleys.
Passing through mountain peaks,
standing a thousand paces high
above hundred-fathom ravines,
leaning over dangerous obstacles,
the terrain is rugged and inconvenient.
They are found only after searching for many days,
and the felling and hacking are completed only after many months.
Only by gathering a multitude can they be moved or carried;
only by lining up oxen can they be brought to the water.
They float along to reach the sea,
then travel along the Huái and against the current of the Hé,
journeying several thousand lǐ
before arriving at Luò.
Artisans carve and treat them,
accumulating days and months;
calculating the completion of a single coffin,
the labor amounts to ten million.
When it is finally used,
it weighs as much as ten thousand jin,
and cannot be lifted without a great crowd,
nor pulled without a great wagon.
From Lèlàng in the east
to Dùnhuáng in the west,
within ten thousand lǐ,
people compete to use them.
This waste of labor and harm to agriculture
is truly heartbreaking!
In ancient times, tombs were not elevated.
When Zhòngní lost his mother,
the mound was four feet high,
but it collapsed when it rained;
his disciples asked to repair it.
The Master wept and said:
"In ritual, one does not repair tombs."
"When Lǐ died,
there was an inner coffin but no outer coffin."
Xiàowén Huángdì was buried at Zhǐyáng,
and Míng Dì was buried south of Luò;
neither hid jewels or pearls
nor built temples
nor raised mountain-like mounds.
Though their tombs were low, their sagacity was high.
Today, the noble relatives in the capital
and the powerful families of the commanderies and counties
do not give their best in nurturing the living
but instead make burials extravagant upon death.
Some go so far as to carve gold and engrave jade,
use nèn-catalpa, camphor, and phoebe,
use fertile fields for gravesites,
and place hoards within the yellow earth.
They bury many precious treasures, figurines, carriages, and horses,
build great mounds,
plant pines and cypresses extensively,
and erect dwellings and ancestral halls,
being excessively extravagant and overstepping their status.
Favored ministers and noble relatives,
and the great families of the provinces and commanderies—
whenever there is a funeral or burial,
the capital officials and subordinate counties
each must send officials with offerings,
carriages, horses, and curtains,
and lend items for hosting guests,
competing to create a magnificent spectacle.
This provides no benefit to honoring the deceased,
adds nothing to filial conduct,
and only creates trouble and disturbance,
harming the officials and the people.
Now, consider the suburbs of Hào and Bì,
the tombs of Wén and Wǔ,
the ramparts of Nánchéng,
and the tomb of Zéng Xī.
It was not that Zhōugōng was unfaithful,
nor that Zéngzǐ was unfilial,
but they believed that praising a ruler or honoring a father
did not consist of accumulating wealth,
and that making a name or honoring ancestors
did not consist of carriages and horses.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Much wealth and goods harm virtue;
when they are exhausted, ritual is lost."
Jìn Líng imposed heavy taxes to decorate his walls;
the Chūnqiū considered him no ruler.
Huà Yuán and Lè Lǚ gave Wén Gōng an extravagant burial;
the Chūnqiū considered them no ministers.
How much more so for the various officials and commoners
to overstep and rival the sovereign in extravagance
and exceed the Way of Heaven?
In the time of Jǐng Dì,
Wèì Bùhài, the Wǔyuán Hóu, was found guilty of a burial that exceeded the laws and was stripped of his state.
In the time of Míng Dì,
the Chuāngyáng Hóu in Sāngmín was found guilty of a tomb that exceeded the regulations and was punished with head-shaving and reduction of status.
Today, the superficiality and extravagance of the world have departed from the root,
and the overstepping of the superiors
has already become extreme!
All these things that are criticized
are not the nature of the people,
but those who strive for them
are made to do so by chaotic government and thin moral transformation.
When a King unifies the world,
he observes the people and establishes teachings;
only then can he change the winds and transform the customs
to achieve great peace.
Generally, the height of mountain peaks
is not something that suddenly rises from being carved out;
it must be increased step by step and gradually rise.
The depth of river valleys
is not something that suddenly sinks from being cut off;
it must be sloping and pooling and gradually descend.
Therefore, if the accumulation of height does not stop,
it must reach the height of Sōng Shān;
if the accumulation of depth does not cease,
it must reach the ultimate depth of Huángquán.
It is not only the mountains and rivers;
human conduct is also like this.
If a commoner accumulates good deeds without slackening,
they will surely reach the worthiness of Yán and Mǐn;
if they accumulate evil without ceasing,
they will surely reach the reputation of Jié and Zhí.
It is not only commoners;
ministers are also like this.
If they accumulate uprightness without weariness,
they will surely give rise to a will of integrity and righteousness;
if they accumulate wickedness without stopping,
they will surely give rise to a heart of violence and regicide.
It is not only ministers;
rulers of states are also like this.
If their administration and instruction accumulate virtue,
they will surely achieve the blessing of peace and tranquility;
if their actions and measures repeatedly fail,
they will surely bring about the calamity of peril and ruin.
Therefore, Zhòngní said:
Tāng and Wǔ did not become kings through a single good deed,
and Jié and Zhòu did not perish through a single evil deed.
The fall and rise of the Three Dynasties
depended on what they accumulated.
For those who accumulate much good,
even if they have one evil act,
it is called a mistake,
and is not enough to cause ruin.
For those who accumulate much evil,
even if they have one good act,
it is called an accidental hit,
and is not enough to ensure survival.
When a ruler hears this,
he may feel fear and awe.
When a commoner hears this,
he may change his expression.
For this reason, the superior man is "cautious and trembling,
becoming more prudent day by day,"
restraining himself and reflecting three times daily,
"seeking only what is right."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"If good is not accumulated, it is not enough to establish a reputation;
if evil is not accumulated, it is not enough to destroy oneself."
When worthies and sages humble themselves and change,
they then ascend to their blessings.
Qìng Fēng and Bó Yǒu
were dissolute with wine,
indulging without restraint,
thus ruining their families.
Jìn Píng neglected the government,
was deluded and lost his will,
and good ministers could not correct him;
therefore, they all met with calamity.
Chǔ Zhuāng and Qí Wēi
initially had dissolute behavior
and the defeat of weakening,
nearly reaching chaos and ruin;
but in the end, they were able to realize and awaken,
diligently cared for the people's affairs,
labored their spirits and thought deeply,
working untiringly.
They sent out Chén Yìng,
conferred rank upon Guǎn Sù,
summoned the magistrate of Jímò,
and boiled the Grandee of Ā.
Therefore, they were able to achieve a restoration,
became powerful hegemons among the feudal lords,
were honored and prominent at the time,
were remembered by later generations,
passed down a fine reputation,
and were recorded in charts and books.
Speaking from this,
for those who aspire to be rulers,
their conduct is the same:
knowing oneself is called enlightenment,
and overcoming oneself is called strength.
If there is anything not good, one never fails to know it;
once known, one never does it again.
This is why Yán Zǐ was called "nearly there."
The *Shī* says:
"Heaven protects and establishes you,
most securely indeed.
To make you truly thick in virtue,
what blessing is not dispensed?"
This is enough to destroy oneself.
"The petty man thinks a small good is of no benefit and does not do it;
he thinks a small evil is of no harm and does not discard it.
Thus, evil accumulates until it cannot be hidden,
and guilt becomes great and cannot be resolved."
This is why Jué and Jǔ confused the state and did not return,
and why the ends of the three dynasties went to ruin and did not recover.
Indeed, accumulating the minute leads to the manifest;
accumulating the conspicuous leads to results;
startling fame, startling fame;
startling results lead to survival or ruin;
the sage is always cautious about the minute.
Wén Wáng was careful and reverent;
Chéng Wáng was respectful day and night,
thinking of being cautious with the tiny,
guarding early against what has not yet sprouted.
Therefore, they could achieve great peace and pass it to their descendants.
Moreover, wickedness and uprightness
are like water and fire, coming from different sources;
they cannot flourish together.
If the upright nature prevails,
then one values oneself and cannot bear to diminish it;
thus Bó Yí died of hunger without resentment.
If the wicked nature prevails,
then one is habituated to fear and cannot bear to let go;
thus Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne without shame.
This is caused by the habit of accumulating evil.
The habit of accumulating evil does not take long,
and leading to death and ruin is not for one reason alone.
Generations of people follow this.
"Making you increase much,
so that everything is abundant."
These are good words;
they say that Heaven protects and assists the king,
establishing his nature and life
very firmly indeed.
Making you faithful and sincere—
what would not be governed?
And increasing it much,
so very numerous and manifold.
If one does not follow the Five Constants
and nourish nature and life accordingly,
how can one preserve the longevity of Nán Shān and the luxuriance of the pines and cypresses?
"Virtue is as light as a feather,"
and practicing benevolence depends on oneself.
"Do not join with the hornets,
lest you seek out their painful stings for yourself."
Calamity and blessing have no gate;
they are only summoned by people.
What Heaven assists is obedience;
what people value is trustworthiness.
To walk in trustworthiness and think of obedience,
and also to honor the worthy,
therefore, there is good fortune and nothing unfavorable.
How bright are these words!
Can one not reflect upon them?
Generally, the height of mountains and hills
is not formed by being carved out and rising abruptly;
it must be by gradual increments and rising slowly.
The depth of rivers and valleys
is not by being cut off and sinking down;
it must be by sloping pools and descending slowly.
Therefore, if the accumulation upward does not stop,
it will surely reach the height of Sōng Shān;
if the accumulation downward does not cease,
it will surely reach the depth of Huángquán.
It is not only the mountains and rivers;
human conduct is also like this.
If a commoner accumulates good deeds without slackening,
they will surely reach the worthiness of Yán and Mǐn;
if they accumulate evil without ceasing,
they will surely reach the reputation of Jié and Zhí.
It is not only commoners;
ministers are also like this.
If they accumulate uprightness without weariness,
they will surely give rise to a will of integrity and righteousness;
if they accumulate wickedness without stopping,
they will surely give rise to a heart of violence and regicide.
It is not only ministers;
rulers of states are also like this.
If their administration and instruction accumulate virtue,
they will surely achieve the blessing of peace and tranquility;
if their actions and measures repeatedly fail,
they will surely bring about the calamity of peril and ruin.
Therefore, Zhòngní said:
Tāng and Wǔ did not become kings through a single good deed,
and Jié and Zhòu did not perish through a single evil deed.
The fall and rise of the Three Dynasties
depended on what they accumulated.
For those who accumulate much good,
even if they have one evil act,
it is a mistake,
and is not enough to cause ruin.
For those who accumulate much evil,
even if they have one good act,
it is an accidental hit,
and is not enough to ensure survival.
When a ruler hears this,
he may feel fear and awe.
When a commoner hears this,
he may change his expression.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ is cautious and fearful,
becoming more prudent day by day,
restraining himself and reflecting three times a day,
and considering what is not yet visible.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"If virtue is not accumulated, it is insufficient to establish a name;
if evil is not accumulated, it is insufficient to destroy one's self.
The Xiǎorén thinks small virtues are of no benefit and thus does not practice them;
he thinks small evils do no harm and thus does not abandon them.
Consequently, evil accumulates until it cannot be hidden,
and crimes grow large until they cannot be resolved."
This is why Jué and Jǔ went astray in governing the state and never returned,
and why the rulers of the Sānjì persisted in their ways and could not recover.
Indeed, the accumulation of the subtle becomes manifest;
the accumulation of the prominent becomes renown;
renown and reputation;
these lead to survival or ruin,
so the Sage is always cautious about small beginnings.
Wén Wáng was careful and reverent;
Wǔ Wáng was respectful day and night,
thinking prudently of subtle matters
and guarding against what had not yet sprouted.
Thus they were able to achieve Tàipíng and pass it to their descendants.
Furthermore, evil and righteousness
are like water and fire—they do not have the same source
and cannot both flourish together.
When the righteous nature prevails,
one values oneself and cannot bear to diminish it;
thus Bó Yí died of hunger without resentment.
When the evil nature prevails,
one becomes habituated and cannot bear to let go;
thus Wáng Mǎng stole the throne without shame.
This is caused by the accumulation of evil habits.
The accumulation of evil habits does not happen overnight,
but the resulting death does not come from a single cause.
Generations of people follow such paths.
When sages and worthies practice humility and reform,
they ascend to good fortune.
Qìng Fēng and Bó Yǒu
were dissipated in wine,
indulging without limit,
thereby ruining their houses.
Jìn Píng Gōng neglected government,
was deluded and lost his will;
his good ministers did not correct him,
so they all met with disaster.
Chǔ Zhuāng Wáng and Qí Wēi Wáng
initially behaved with dissipation
and suffered the defeat of weakening,
nearing chaos and ruin.
But in the middle of their reigns, they were able to awaken,
worked diligently for the people's affairs,
exerted their spirits and agonized in thought,
and were diligent without laziness.
They sent out Chén Yìng,
granted titles to Guǎn Sū,
summoned the Governor of Jímò,
and boiled the Grandee of Ā.
Thus they were able to achieve a restoration,
became strong hegemons over the feudal lords,
were honored and prominent at the time,
were remembered by later generations,
their fine names were passed down,
and they were recorded in books and registers.
Speaking from this,
for those who aspire to be lords of men,
their path is the same:
knowing oneself is called enlightenment,
and overcoming oneself is called strength.
If there is something unvirtuous, one never fails to know it;
knowing it, one never does it again.
This is why Yán Zǐ was praised as being "nearly there."
The Shī says:
"Heaven protects and establishes you,
with great firmness.
It makes you truly substantial,
so why should blessings be removed?
It gives you much increase,
so that nothing is not abundant."
This is what these words mean.
They say that Heaven protects and assists the King,
establishing his nature and life,
very firmly.
If it makes you sincere and substantial,
what would not be well-governed?
And it increases it greatly,
making things very numerous.
Should one not follow and practice the Wǔcháng,
nourish one's nature and life accordingly,
to preserve the longevity of Nán Shān and the lushness of pines and cypresses?
"Virtue is as light as a hair,"
practicing benevolence depends on oneself.
"Do not join with bees,
lest you seek your own sting."
Fortune and misfortune have no gate;
they are only what people summon.
That which Heaven assists is compliance;
that which people value is trustworthiness.
Practice trustworthiness and think of compliance,
and also honor the worthy;
therefore, there is good fortune and nothing that is not favorable.
How brilliant are these words!
How can one not contemplate them?
A state rises through the worthy
and declines through flattery;
a ruler is secure through loyalty
and endangered through jealousy.
This is a constant discourse of ancient and modern times,
known by all in the world.
Yet the succession of declining states and endangered rulers is unending.
Is it because the world lacks loyal, trustworthy, upright, and honest scholars?
It is truly because the way of loyalty, trustworthiness, uprightness, and honesty cannot be practiced.
Within ten paces,
there must be lush grass;
in a town of ten households,
there must be talented scholars.
The birth of worthy talents
continues day after day and month after month,
never ceasing.
Therefore, the chaotic Yīn had Three Benevolent Men,
and the small state of Wèi had many Jūnzǐ.
With the vastness of Hàn,
its numerous scholars and people,
the clarity of the court,
and the order between high and low,
yet it is said that the offices have no upright officials
and the positions have no good ministers.
This is not because the present age lacks worthy men,
but because the worthy are discarded and imprisoned, unable to reach the court of the Sage Sovereign.
Those who set their will on the Dào have few friends;
those who follow the customs of the world have many companions.
Thus, the whole world forms factions and acts for private gain,
competing in hollow qualities and practicing superficiality.
Those who recommend scholars
no longer rely on their essential substance
or measure their talent and conduct;
they simply fabricate empty beauty
and speak with groundless eloquence.
They select those deemed capable and record them;
among the Excellencies, Ministers, Regional Inspectors, and Attendants,
the Màocái and Xiàolián candidates number nearly two hundred.
But if one examines their records,
their virtue is likened to Yán Yuān, Bǔ, and Rǎn,
yet when their conduct and ability are evaluated,
most do not even reach the average level.
If they were truly like what is written in their records,
then each year would yield two hundred great worthies.
Then why would there still be disasters, anomalies, and famine?
This shows these are not the effects of reality.
Descriptions of fine grains and meat
may look good on the surface,
but they are not as edible as coarse grain and steamed greens.
Pictures of Xī Shī or Máo Qiáng
may please the heart,
but they are not as useful as a plain wife or an ugly concubine.
Spreading empty and high reputations
and forcefully hiding flaws
to deceive and show off to one another
may please the ear,
but it is not as good as choosing loyal and practical conduct that can be employed in office.
Zhōu Xiǎn was constrained by the times,
and thus employed Sū Qín;
Yàn Kuài was fond of empty reputation,
and thus abdicated to Zǐzhī.
Both abandoned reality and listened to sound;
such is the error of empty flattery.
The Sage is pure,
while the worthy man is mixed.
Zhōu Gōng did not seek perfection in one man,
and the Sìyǒu did not possess all talents,
how much more so in these later ages?
Therefore, those who assisted Gāozǔ
and the generals and ministers of Guāngwǔ
did not follow false recommendations
and did not demand all-encompassing conduct.
Those discarded by the fallen Qín
and rejected by Wáng Mǎng
were employed by the two Ancestors to suppress violence and chaos
and achieve order and peace.
In this age of Great Peace,
to say there are no scholars,
and to frequently open special recruitments
without obtaining upright men—
this is truly infuriating!
The edicts of an enlightened ruler are like sounds,
and the harmony of a loyal minister should be like an echo;
whether long or short, large or small,
clear or turbid, swift or slow,
they must harmonize with one another.
For this reason, if one seeks a horse, one inquires about horses;
if one seeks a donkey, one inquires about donkeys;
if one seeks a hawk, one inquires about hawks;
if one seeks a Máng, one inquires about Mángs.
From such teaching and commands,
then rewards and punishments will be certain.
Grandiose discourse that involves mutual deception
is not as good as loyal discourse that is sincere and truthful.
Furthermore, one polishes jade with stone,
refines gold with salt,
washes brocade with fish,
and launders cloth with ash.
Among things, there are inherently those where the lowly is used to manage the noble,
and the ugly is used to manage the beautiful.
The wise person discards their shortcomings and adopts their strengths
to achieve success;
an enlightened ruler’s use of scholars is also like this.
If objects have their proper uses
and their talents are not discarded,
how much more so for people?
Cultivating the person and being cautious in conduct,
being earnest, upright, and honest,
pure, incorruptible, and stainless,
and being tranquil and practicing non-action—
these are the foundations of transformation.
To worry for the ruler and grieve for the people,
to see the source of disorder alone,
to love good and hate evil,
and to make rewards and punishments strict and clear—
these are the materials of governance.
An enlightened ruler encompasses both virtues and accepts both types of men;
those who are like tools of wicked conduct
are used as the iron and steel for the gold and jade of precious administration.
Without these two treasures,
if one merely strives to act differently to seek fame
or feigns stillness to delude the masses,
then it ruins customs and harms transformation.
Those in the present age who admire the vacuous
call this Jiān Bái.
The conduct of Jiān Bái
is hated by enlightened rulers
and not adopted by the Wángzhì.
For this reason, when selecting the worthy and recommending scholars,
one must examine their simple and pure character,
and speak according to the reality.
If they have small flaws,
do not force them into fine clothes
to bolster a hollow reputation.
For scholars with a single ability,
let each recommend what they are best at;
whether in office or retirement, in silence or in speech,
do not force them to combine all qualities.
If so, then how could the discourses of Xiāo, Cáo, Zhōu, and Hán
be sufficient?
Men such as those of the Wú, Dèng, Liáng, and Dòu clans
could be obtained tenfold.
According to what is appropriate for each,
and assigning responsibilities based on measuring talent,
then the various offices will not be neglected,
great deeds can be accomplished,
Tàipíng can be achieved,
and the Qílín will arrive.
Furthermore, Yān was small
and its position was low,
yet Zhāo Wáng was still able to summon and gather the talents of other states,
to rise up and punish the violent and chaotic,
and to achieve a state of being well-governed and strong.
Now, the land of Hàn is vast and wide,
and the Tiānzǐ is venerable and enlightened,
yet there is not even one good minister.
This is truly because there is no pity for the sorrow and suffering of the millions of people,
and no urgency to have worthy people assist in governance.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"It is not that he does not think of it;
what distance is there?"
Loyal and good officials are truly easy to obtain;
it is just that the sage king does not desire them so.
In the times of remote antiquity,
when the people were first born,
there was no high or low,
and yet they were naturally orderly.
Heaven had not yet acted upon them,
and rulers had not yet been established.
Later, people gradually became deceptive and disrespectful,
or oppressed and maltreated one another.
Exploitation did not stop,
creating great harm for the common people.
Thereupon, Heaven commanded sages to serve as their overseers and shepherds,
to ensure they did not lose their nature.
All within the four seas received the benefits,
and none were not covered by their virtue.
Together they all supported and honored them,
calling them the Tiānzǐ.
Therefore, Heaven’s establishment of a ruler
was not for the private benefit of this person
to use the people as servants;
it was to punish the violent, remove harm, and benefit the common people.
Thus, through the plans of men and the plans of spirits,
the capable occupy the position.
The Shī says:
"Great is Shàngdì!
Looking down in majesty.
He surveyed the four quarters,
seeking the sufferings of the people.
Observing these two states,
their governance was not successful.
Observing these four states,
where should He investigate and measure?
Shàngdì pointed to it,
hating their wickedness.
Then He turned His gaze to the west,
and gave this place to be measured."
These words
mean that the governance of the two states of Xià and Yīn was not successful,
but instead used extravagance and boastful expansion.
Shàngdì hated them,
and looked again for a sage who cared for the people's sufferings,
investigating and measuring with the four states of the world to make him dwell there.
Previously, when summoning good men,
there was a hatred for the limitless extravagance and boastful expansion without order.
Thus one only measured models and laws,
clearly manifesting the order of rituals,
creating superior laws and arts,
and hanging them up for eternity.
Therefore, the Zhuàn says:
"In establishing rituals,
the upper limit of objects does not exceed twelve;
this is the Way of Heaven."
Consequently, the former sages had regulations for the imperial fields,
measures for offerings to the spirits,
limits for personal use,
and set numbers for honoring the worthy.
High and low, large and small,
noble and base, close and distant—
all had their grades of dignity.
The levels were tiered and reduced
so that each was sufficient to provide income for their rank and position,
and the public and private followed their respective grades,
while rituals were performed with virtue and righteousness.
At this time,
within the Jiǔzhōu,
spanning a total of three thousand lǐ,
there were eight hundred states.
In the distribution of stipends,
the output of a top-tier farmer was taken as the standard,
beginning with the commoners in official service,
whose stipends were sufficient to substitute for farming,
generally enough to feed nine people.
The lower officers of the feudal lords were the same.
Middle officers received double the amount of lower officers,
feeding eighteen people.
Upper officers received double the amount of middle officers,
feeding thirty-six people.
Great officers received double that,
feeding seventy-two people.
The ministers of a small state
received twice the amount of a great officer.
The ministers of a medium state
received three times the amount of a great officer.
The ministers of a large state
received four times the amount of a great officer,
feeding two hundred and eighty-eight people.
Each ruler received ten times the amount of his ministers.
The Sāngōng of the Tiānzǐ held fiefs equivalent to those of dukes and marquises,
roughly one hundred lǐ square.
Ministers held fiefs equivalent to earls,
seventy lǐ square.
Great officers were equivalent to viscounts and barons,
fifty lǐ square.
Primordial officers were equivalent to dependencies,
thirty lǐ square.
Those who achieved success were enfeoffed.
For this reason, official administration was dedicated to the public interest
and did not concern itself with private households;
sons and younger brothers applied themselves to learning
and did not interfere in wealth or profit;
they kept to themselves behind closed doors
and did not compete with the common people.
Thus, there was no path of hunger or cold,
and they did not fall into ruin;
officials were nurtured generously and were not constrained;
functionaries cherished their offices and were not greedy;
the people were peaceful and exerted their strength;
thus the foundation of Tàipíng was established.
Only then were tributes and selections carefully handled,
and dismissals and promotions were clearly defined;
offices obtained the right people,
and people performed their duties;
"Respectfully following Hàotiān,
reverently granting the seasons to the people,"
"Together with my wife and children,
I carry food to the southern fields";
superiors strove for temperance in ritual,
rectifying themselves to set an example for inferiors;
inferiors delighted in the administration,
each taking pleasure in exhausting themselves to support their superiors.
Consequently, Heaven and Earth interacted in harmony,
the yīn and yáng were balanced and peaceful,
the people had no deceit or concealment,
the celestial instruments did not tilt,
virtuous Qi spread abroad, and songs of praise arose.
Later, the nurturing of the worthy was suddenly neglected, and the "Lùmíng" expressed longing;
clans were turned away from, and the "Cǎifán" expressed resentment;
taxes were levied based on acreage, and the "Shuòshǔ" was written;
taxes and levies were heavy, as reported by successive interpreters;
the distribution of stipends was biased, and the "Qīngfǔ" satirized it;
travelers were settled, and the "Miánmán" criticized it;
thus, exhaustion, chaos, decline, and weakness ensued.
When the Zhōu house weakened, the Wǔbà arose;
when the Liùguó were worn out, the cruel Qín arose.
They turned their backs on righteousness and principle, favoring power and force;
they destroyed ritual and practiced greed and gluttony.
They increased taxes and levies to enrich themselves
and strengthened the ministers to weaken the branches;
those of refined virtue did not receive titles of nobility,
and the ranked marquises did not obtain them.
Therefore, worthy men could not practice ritual to follow the Dào,
and ranked officials could not avoid being crooked to pursue profit.
Rulers, moreover, frequently granted amnesties to release criminals;
the people had no sense of shame and many committed thefts.
Why was this?
The atmosphere of the masses is influenced by the customs of those above;
when troubles and harms press closely and are forced by hunger and cold,
this is why Zāng Hé could not stop his thieves.
The Shī says:
"The great wind has its path;
the greedy man ruins his kind."
"It is your teaching
that the people follow."
Therefore, when the former kings were about to issue commands and orders,
they were earnest and sincere,
fearing only that they might not be appropriate and lead toward evil.
Thus they created canons to serve as the ultimate standard for the people,
shared by both high and low,
without private bias;
the three high offices formulated laws,
and one never heard of pardoning those who were guilty
or that prison bribes were considered treasures.
Therefore, a bright ruler presiding over the masses
must use the correct path;
having no dissatisfaction with what he has,
he strives for temperance in ritual and is generous to inferiors;
he restores virtue and exalts transformation,
causing everyone to be abundant in their livelihood and to compete in integrity and shame.
Thus, the heads of office are upright and the common people are transformed;
evil hearts are cast out and deceitful concealment is ended;
then they can harmonize the Qi and achieve Tàipíng.
The Yì says:
"The Sage nurtures the worthy so as to reach the myriad people."
Taking the people as the root,
a ruler takes his ministers as the foundation,
and only then can his high position be exalted;
when the horse is fat,
only then can a distant journey be achieved.
If a ruler does not strive for this but wishes to achieve Tàipíng,
it is like having a thin foundation and expecting a high wall,
or having an emaciated steed and demanding a long road;
it is certain that it cannot be obtained.
Generally, one who treats a disease
must first know the emptiness or fullness of the pulse
and where the Qi is blocked,
and only then can they create a prescription;
thus the illness can be cured and life can be long.
One who governs a state
must first know the suffering of the people
and the origin of disasters,
and only then can they establish prohibitions;
thus villainy can be blocked and the state can be at peace.
Among those who severely harm good people today,
none is greater than frequent amnesties.
If amnesties and redemptions are frequent,
then evil people will flourish and good people will be harmed.
How is this made clear?
It is said:
Families of filial piety and fraternal duty
cultivate themselves and act cautiously,
not violating the prohibitions of superiors.
From birth until death,
they do not have even a tiny amount of guilt;
yet there are frequent amnesties and redemptions,
from which they have never received grace,
and it often turns into misfortune for them instead.
Why?
Upright scholars who serve as officials
do not avoid the powerful and resistant,
nor do they yield to superior officers.
When engaged in supervision and inspection,
they are often resented,
and the cliques of the treacherous and slippery
further add slanderous words.
Knowing that an amnesty will not be long in coming,
they then together commit injustices and encroachments,
falsely reporting crimes and laws.
Now the sovereign recklessly executes punishments,
as high as death or exile,
and below them are those sunk in injustice.
The families of the wronged
are only just starting to petition for investigations and report the facts to prove their integrity,
yet it is of no benefit to those who have already died.
As for the reclusive scholars of conduct
and the virtuous gentlemen,
they are covered and oppressed by the slanderous and sharp-tongued;
of the wronged people of the lower lands
who are able to reach the palace gates,
there is not one in ten thousand.
Of those who obtain an inquiry,
it is no more than one in a hundred.
After facing the Shàngshū,
those who are sent away empty-handed
are another sixty or seventy percent.
Even if they receive a re-examination,
the zhōu and jùn look to one another,
delaying the true facts.
Spring and summer wait for autumn and winter,
and autumn and winter again cross into spring and summer.
In this way, those who encounter amnesties on their journey
are too many to count.
Furthermore, cautious people
use the way of Heaven,
share the benefits of the Earth,
and choose not to violate the soil.
They are careful of their persons and temperate in their expenses,
accumulating little by little
so as to reach even small achievements.
These are the simple, good, and covering people,
who are truly the foundation of the state.
Frivolous and wicked youths,
unprincipled and malevolent people,
who contemplate villainy and evil
and rise up to become bandits and thieves,
killing people's parents for wealth or lust,
slaughtering people's children,
exterminating people's families,
and taking people's property;
as well as those who are greedy, cruel, and lawless,
and the evil and corrupt officials
who plunder and kill the innocent
and oppress and victimize the common people—
all hope that the Sage Emperor will execute the wicked and rectify injustices
to resolve their accumulated grievances.
Instead, an amnesty is granted to them all,
causing the wicked to hold grand gatherings and boast,
and career thieves to wear their hidden loot as they pass by the victims' doors;
filial sons see their enemies but cannot seek vengeance,
and owners of stolen goods see their property but cannot reclaim it;
nothing is more painful than this.
Therefore, when an amnesty is about to be granted and there is a sudden onset of bitter cold,
it is because there are many people with deep-seated grievances and sorrowful resentment.
For cultivating weeds harms the grain crops,
and showing kindness to villains harms the good citizens.
The *Shū* says:
"Wén Wáng established punishments,
applying penalties to these criminals without pardon."
Thus, when the former kings established the penal laws,
it was not because they enjoyed wounding people's flesh
or cutting short people's lives,
but rather to intimidate villains, punish evil, and remove harm from the people.
The world exists because the people cannot govern themselves,
and so a king was established to rule over them.
The world relies on upholding Heaven's majestic mandate
and together carrying out rewards and punishments.
Thus the Classics state: "Heaven mandates the virtuous,
with five degrees of official robes and five insignia;
Heaven punishes the guilty,
with five punishments and five applications."
The *Shī* criticizes: "That person deserves to be guilty,
but you instead let them escape."
In ancient times, only the sovereign who first received the mandate,
inheriting the peak of great disorder
and suffering from the evils of the previous king,
when the people were all acting as enemies,
when none were not bandits, righteousness had vanished, and villains were plundering and seizing—
having changed the mandate and received the throne
to act as their parents,
could they grant a single amnesty.
From the successors onward,
there should be no deviation from the law.
Why is this?
The lord of men matches Qián in benevolence,
nurturing the myriad people to achieve great merit;
he must not consider nurturing villainy and sparing the guilty as benevolence,
nor consider being indulgent toward those who harm Heaven as being wise.
Now, those of a wicked nature
are neither filial nor fraternal at home,
are neither respectful nor reverent in public,
are frivolous, insolent, and arrogant,
and are fierce, violent, and undiscerning;
they clearly make intimidation, insult, and personal gain their conduct
and consider banditry and cruelty as virtues,
thus repeatedly falling foul of the King's law—
these are the thieves of the people,
the lowest of the foolish and the most extremely wicked people.
Though they are released from shackles
and emerge from prison,
they ultimately have no heart for repentance;
they rely on their defiance and hold their heads high,
and how could those who leave prison with a restless spirit not violate the law again?
In Luòyáng, there are even those who master the coordination of murders,
known as the "Houses of Gathering and Responsibility."
They receive a hundred thousand coins from people
and pay out several thousand to their agents.
They also give heavy bribes to local officials,
with whom they collude in villainy;
the profits are immense,
their factions are intertwined like tangled teeth,
requesting favors even from noble relatives and favored ministers,
their persuasion is heard by those above,
and their petitions are carried out by those below.
Therefore, even with a strict Prefect or Intendant,
they ultimately cannot break or eradicate this system.
Why is this?
Generally, those who dare to commit great villainies
must have talents exceeding the common crowd
and be able to ingratiate themselves with those above.
They scatter much of their ill-gotten wealth
and offer flattering words
to manipulate others in turn;
unless one has the integrity and uprightness of Dìwǔ Gōng,
who could fail to look after them?
Looking now at those masterminds of murder in Luòyáng,
the highest counts reach dozens,
and the lowest are four or five;
if they themselves do not die, the killings do not stop,
all of which is caused by the frequent amnesties.
Viewed from this perspective,
the nature of the extremely wicked
ultimately cannot be transformed;
though years pass,
it only serves to encourage villainy.
It is confusing that
when the Three Luminaries show certain omens
and the heavenly ether suggests an amnesty,
the sovereign follows this to bestow grace.
This is not necessarily the case.
The King is the most noble
and communicates in spirit with Heaven;
when his heart has a thought
and his mind has a concern,
before it is expressed in voice or appearance,
Heaven changes in response.
Perhaps like the various signs of fortune or calamity,
or the moon following the stars,
these things ought to happen naturally.
Thus, when auspicious or strange signs are seen,
they may be warnings to the sovereign.
If he neglects and fails to examine them,
these are what he himself has induced,
yet he conversely thinks it is Heaven's intent that it be so;
this is not correct.
Common people also say:
"In former generations, when an amnesty was desired,
they would first send horses to travel through the markets and neighborhoods,
listening at street corners;
if everyone said an amnesty should be granted,
it was taken as the teaching of Heaven,
and grace was bestowed accordingly."
If such words were to be believed,
it would be a grave error.
For the nature of the people
is indeed to enjoy making conjectures;
seeing long periods of overcast weather, they say a flood is coming;
seeing long periods of sunshine, they say a drought is coming;
seeing a slight rise in prices, they say a famine is coming;
seeing a slight drop in prices, they say a bountiful harvest is coming;
yet sometimes they are right and sometimes wrong.
Viewed from this perspective,
what the people say
does not necessarily reflect the state of the world.
In former generations, amnesties and ransoms were rare and infrequent,
so the people had no greedy expectations.
In recent times,
amnesties and ransoms have become frequent and numerous;
therefore, every spring and summer,
they always hope for another amnesty;
those families with members who have committed crimes
hope for the luck of receiving grace,
and therefore spread such rumors
to please themselves.
If a benevolent ruler truly hears this
and thinks it is Heaven's teaching and immediately follows it,
no mistake could be greater.
Many commentators say:
"If an amnesty is not granted for a long time, then villainy blazes
and officials cannot control it,
so amnesties and ransoms are used to resolve it."
This is the very root of inviting chaos
and the words of one who does not examine where disaster and fortune originate.
The reason why the people lightly become bandits and thieves,
and the reason why officials easily commit villainy and concealment,
is because amnesties and ransoms are frequent, giving them lucky expectations.
If those who commit crimes were bound by their sentences for their whole lives
and were certainly punished when caught,
then the schemes of villainy would be broken
and the heart that contemplates evil would be cut off.
For if good things can be redeemed,
and children can be managed,
mediocre people
can still be led downwards.
Thus the proverb says:
"With an amnesty granted within a single year,
even slave boys sigh with joy."
This means that when the King's punishment is not carried out,
then even those who have suffered and been punished will lightly offend again,
how much more so for the cunning?
If one truly fears that bandits are many and villainy cannot be overcome and thus grants an amnesty,
then this is acting on behalf of the state to reward villains.
The Way of Heaven rewards the good and punishes the excessive;
"Heaven's work—let man carry it out on its behalf."
Therefore, whenever a king is established,
it is to execute the wicked and nurture the upright and good;
but to indulge the wicked and rebellious—
no absurdity could be greater.
Moreover, a state has no permanent order,
nor does it have permanent disorder.
When laws and decrees are implemented, the state is ordered;
when laws and decrees are lax, the state is in disorder.
Laws are not permanently implemented,
nor are they permanently lax;
if the ruler respects the law, the law is implemented;
if the ruler neglects the law, the law is lax.
Long ago, in the time of Xiàomíng Dì,
a Màocái candidate was recommended.
When he passed through the palace gates to give thanks for the honor,
and after he had been granted a meal,
the Emperor asked him if there was any unusual news.
He replied:
"In Wū, there are nine formidable bandits.
The Cìshǐ has frequently reported that they were plundering the commandery,
but in the end, he has been unable to capture them."
The Emperor said:
"Are you not a Cóngshì official in the Nánjùn division?"
He replied:
"I am."
The Emperor then flared up in anger
and said:
"If bandits arise in your division and you cannot capture them,
then how can your talent be considered 'Flourishing' (Màocái)?"
He was beaten several hundred times
and immediately dismissed from office,
while the provincial and commandery authorities were sternly reprimanded.
Within ten days,
the bandits were executed.
From this perspective,
capturing and exterminating bandits
lies in making the laws clear,
not in frequent amnesties.
Nowadays, rewards and punishments are not clearly carried out to distinguish good from evil,
nor are the Mù (Governors) and Shǒu (Administrators) strictly supervised to capture the treacherous and cunning.
Instead, frequent amnesties are granted to encourage them.
The text of these usually says:
"Even those who have committed rebellion, great sedition, and unprincipled acts,
and offenses that should not receive pardon, are all cleared;
I shall purify the hearts of the Shìdàfū and make a fresh start with them."
Every year they are purified,
yet one has never seen treacherous people or redundant officials
who are willing to change their hearts, repent, submit, and praise the decree.
When officials report on matters,
it is also a common custom that minor offenses from before an amnesty
hinder a prominent promotion today.
In that case, the decree to reform the past and cultivate the future
and to make a fresh start
is also not trusted.
The Shī critiques: "The gentleman makes frequent covenants,
and disorder is thereby prolonged."
Therefore, it is better to make one's decrees rare
and ensure that one's words are certain.
If it is truly impossible to avoid amnesties altogether,
making them rare is better.
If we followed the ancient times of an amnesty once in a generation or many years,
then it is certain that treacherous and wicked acts would decrease by eighty or ninety percent.
Long ago, when the Dàsīmǎ Wú Hàn was old and ill and about to die,
Shìzǔ asked him for his final admonition.
He replied:
"I am foolish and unintelligent,
insufficient to know how to govern.
Simply be cautious not to grant amnesties, and that is all."
Indeed, "directions gather by category,
and things divide by group."
"The feelings of people are all revealed in their words."
Therefore, all those who say there should not be amnesties
are either those who cultivate themselves and act cautiously,
or those who are anxious, sorrowful, and prudent, and who hate treacherous and evil people like poison.
All those who benefit from frequent amnesties
are either those who do not understand the administration of amnesties,
or they must harbor hidden worries and have things they wish to do.
When a ruler issues a decree,
he must consult with his ministers.
Among the treacherous and wicked ministers,
they naturally must have crimes to hide.
Even upright officials
still have public errors.
Unless they are like Yù Quán or Lǐ Lí,
who would be willing to punish their own bodies to correct the state?
Thus, they all rely on private calculations to discuss public policy.
Consulting with foxes about making a fur coat—
there will never be a time when it is possible!
The Zhuàn says:
"When the people have many strokes of good fortune,
it is the state's misfortune."
That those who have crimes should suffer their full punishment,
and that grievances should be redressed and principles trusted—
this is the correctness of Heaven
and the law of the King.
Therefore it is said:
"Do not indulge those who are deceptive and compliant,
so as to be cautious of the unprincipled."
If one wrongs good people to benefit the treacherous and evil,
this is called "accumulating resentment and considering it virtue."
The late Emperor established laws
regarding those who concealed daggers.
Why?
Because they harbored treacherous and evil hearts
and had the intent to kill or harm.
The Sage Ruler has the affection of a parent for a child,
yet this person has the intent to kill or harm,
so he is executed;
how much more so for a crime already committed?
The Shàngshū · Kāng Gào says:
"The King said:
'Alas!
Fēng,
be reverent and clear in your punishments.
If a person has a small crime but it is not an accident,
but rather is persistent,
and he himself commits what is unlawful;
I warn you,
even if his crime is small,
he must be killed.'"
This says that one fears people whose crimes, though small,
are not committed through error,
but rather they intend to do them for their whole lives;
therefore, though small,
they must be killed.
Why?
Because they fundamentally act out of stubborn villainy and evil thoughts.
"But if there is a great crime that is not persistent,
but rather an accident,
a mere chance occurrence,
though the crime is reached in its extreme,
then he also must not be killed."
This says that even if a killer has committed a great crime,
if he does not wish to do evil his whole life,
but it was just a mistake or error,
he is not killed.
In cases like this,
it is acceptable to say they should be pardoned.
Using gold for redemption from punishment
and amnesties to excuse crimes
all refer to good people and upright men
who occasionally have mistakes or errors
and unfortunately fall into transgressions.
The former kings deliberated on legal cases based on regulations,
tracing the circumstances and considering the intent
in order to save good people;
it was not their intention to allow for the collective indulgence of evil and rebellion so as to harm people.
For this reason, the Zhōu Guān distinguishes the punishments of the Bā Yì (Eight Deliberations);
this is how the former kings organized the ten thousand people and achieved a period of harmony.
The Yì thus observes the people to establish teaching,
the meaning of adapting and changing with the times.
To save the world today,
nothing is better than this idea.
Gāozǔ established Hàn
and made a covenant with his ministers:
"None but members of the Liú clan shall be Kings,
and none but those with military merit shall be Marquises."
Xiàowén Huángdì first enfeoffed his maternal grandfather,
and this became a standard pattern
that has been followed until today.
Xiàowǔ Huángdì granted titles of nobility to the Chéngxiàng
to praise the virtuous,
and later rulers also continued this,
until it was discontinued in the Jiànwǔ era.
As recorded in the chronicles,
Jì, Qiè, Bó Yí, Gāo Yáo, and Bó Yì
were all daily recipients of enfeoffed lands.
In the time of Zhōu Xuān Wáng,
the assisting ministers
who aided governance through virtue
also obtained states.
Therefore Yǐn Jífǔ composed two poems of enfeoffment praise;
the Shī says:
"Assiduous was Shēn Bó,
the King continued his service,
enfeoffing him with the city of Xiè,
to be a model for the southern states."
It also says:
"The four stallions go trot-trot,
the eight bells of the bits go jingle-jingle.
The King commanded Zhòng Shānfǔ
to build a wall in the east."
This says that the civil virtue of Shēn Bó and Shānfǔ brought about a period of peace,
so the King enfeoffed them with joyful lands
and granted them grand robes.
The *Yì* says:
"The cauldron breaks its legs,
upsetting the lord's stew;
its punishment is heavy.
Ominous."
This says that if a high official is not equal to his task,
then heavy punishment follows.
Therefore, after the *Sāngōng* have been in office for three years,
their performance should be clearly evaluated for promotion or dismissal,
and their talents should be carefully screened.
Those who show the governing effectiveness of *Jì*, *Qiè*, *Bóyí*, *Shēnbó*, or *Zhòng Shānfǔ*
should be enfeoffed as *Lièhóu*
and granted the tribute from the *Bāmán* of the southern lands.
Those who "eat the bread of idleness,"
having no achievements in governance and offering no words of loyalty or goodness,
should be subjected to heavy punishment.
This is what is called illuminating virtue and being cautious with punishment,
and the method of screening for competence.
If this were truly done,
the *Sāngōng* would compete to reflect on their duties,
and all officials would strive to exhaust their loyalty.
According to the system of the former kings,
successors were established as feudal lords
to emulate the worthy.
Although descendants have the right to benefit from the past virtues of their ancestors,
yet enfeoffing and establishing a state
as a feudal lord,
and organizing offices and appointing officials
as a Grand Master,
must require merit for the people
to retain one's position;
thus there is the principle of evaluating performance, promotion and dismissal, and the Nine Bestowals or Three Reductions.
The *Shī* says:
"That gentleman,
does not eat the bread of idleness."
Looking at it from this perspective,
there has never been anyone who could receive a salary without merit.
Nowadays, the *Lièhóu*
mostly inherit the titles of their ancestors
and rely on the positions of their forefathers;
they themselves have no merit for *Hàn*
and no virtue for the people.
They dominate their states facing south,
eating heavy salaries while lying idle,
exhausting the common people below
while the state is wealthy;
this is the height of eating the bread of idleness.
*Xiàowǔ Huángdì* was troubled by this
and thus ordered the dismissal of those with insufficient *zhòujīn*,
but this caused much resentment.
Now, among the *Lièhóu*, some have virtue and are fit to care for the people,
yet their Way cannot be implemented;
others are cruel, stubborn, and unseemly
and are not fit to have a state,
yet their wickedness is not reported to the throne.
Furthermore, it is human nature for everyone to consider themselves worthy and desire to demonstrate their ability;
*Zhōugōng*’s admonition was:
"Do not let the high ministers resent not being employed."
The *Shī* says:
"Driving those four stallions,
the four stallions have thick necks."
Let it be ordered that those *Lièhóu* over thirty years of age
should all be tested as chief officials with black sashes or above;
*Guānnèihóu* should serve with yellow sashes,
to prove their intent
and signal their ability.
Those who have the virtue of *Hánhóu* or *Shàohǔ*,
who have merit for the *Tiānzǐ* above
and provide benefit to the common people below,
should be gradually promoted in rank and granted more land
to highlight their virtue.
Those who harbor treachery and hide wickedness and are particularly unprincipled
should have their land reduced and their state taken away
to make clear what is liked and disliked.
Furthermore, the *Lièhóu* all receive split tallies and appointment documents;
they are great ministers of the state.
Although they are physically outside,
their hearts are with the royal house.
They should assist the sovereign's perception and wisdom in distinguishing the wise from the foolish
to aid the *Tiānzǐ*.
How can they sit and act with extravagance and usurpation,
pridefully nurturing debt,
deceiving and oppressing the common people,
and indulging in wine and lust,
"being the ladder of disorder,"
and merely harming public morals?
Edicts for broad selection
are nonetheless special promotions,
but they do not order *Lièhóu* to recommend people.
This would make the ruler's virtue flow widely
and the *Lièhóu* attain greatness;
not doing so is not the way to hold the arts of governance, oversee and rebuke, exercise absolute authority, or manage subordinates.
Even if they are not yet made to govern the people as a start,
since there are broad selections,
one should follow the royal system
and make them all recommend scholars;
this should not be omitted.
This would truly be enfeoffing the *Sāngōng* to highlight accumulated virtue
and testing the *Lièhóu* to eliminate the bread of idleness,
matching the principle of establishing marquises above
and the law of evaluation and dismissal below.
When worthy talents hold office,
then those above and below receive blessings.
When those who eat the bread of idleness leave the state,
positions will have no wicked men.
If this were truly done,
the feudal lords would surely reflect inwardly on their conduct and assist the state.
Now, however, it is not so:
merit is not rewarded,
and lack of virtue leads to no reduction of land.
This is very far from the method of encouraging good and punishing evil,
attracting the loyal and worthy,
and transforming customs.
In the past, when the former kings governed the world,
they selected and trained those of bright virtue
to lead and manage the people.
The establishment of legitimate enfeoffments did not exceed a hundred *lǐ*,
taking the model from the *Zhèn* hexagram,
considering that the perception and wisdom of a worthy person does not exceed this;
also desiring that their virtue and ability be superior while the area governed be small,
then duties would be cultivated and the people would receive grace.
Nowadays, *Shǒuxiàng*
control territories of a thousand *lǐ*,
their prestige and power
being greater than that of the *Lièhóu*.
Their talent, intelligence, virtue, and righteousness
do not necessarily exceed those of the ancients,
yet the area they govern exceeds a hundred *lǐ*;
this is why what they govern is often chaotic.
Therefore, the *Shǒuxiàng* must be examined carefully.
