Formerly, *Xuān Huángdì* rose from among the common people
and knew them deeply.
Thus he often sighed and said:
"The reason the myriad people are safe in their fields and villages without worry or hardship
is that governance is fair and litigation is well-managed.
Those who share this task with me
are only the good officials of *Èrqiān dàn*."
Thereupon he clearly selected *Shǒuxiàng*.
When they were first appointed,
he would surely see them in person,
observing their intentions
to reveal their ability,
clearly inspecting their governance
and giving weight to their punishments and rewards.
For those where treachery decreased and the population increased,
he rewarded them with gold and silk
and ranks up to enfeoffment as marquises.
Those who were wasteful and chaotic without reason
all held the knife and shed blood in the marketplace.
Rewards were heavy and certain,
punishments were painful and inevitable.
The various officials were awed and encouraged,
competing to reflect on their duties.
Thus he could achieve stable governance and an era of peace,
bringing down the phoenix and attracting the *qílín*.
Heaven and man were delighted,
and auspicious omens arrived together.
His merit and virtue were lush and abundant,
and he was established as *Zhōngzōng*.
From this perspective,
the shepherds, governors, and great ministers
are truly the root of prosperity or decline;
they must be selected and trained.
Laws and punishments or rewards
are truly the pivot of order or chaos;
they must be strictly enforced.
Long ago, *Zhòngní* said:
"If governance is lenient, the people will be slow;
if they are slow, correct them with severity.
If it is severe, the people will be harmed;
if they are harmed, treat them with leniency.
Use leniency to supplement severity
and severity to supplement leniency;
governance will thus be harmonious."
Nowadays, *Cìshǐ* and *Shǒuxiàng*
are mostly negligent and slow,
violating the laws
and neglecting the imperial edicts.
They follow their own whims and pursue profit,
not caring for public affairs.
The common people have grievances knotted within,
with nowhere to file complaints.
In the distant borderlands,
those who can reach the palace gates
are not even a few in ten thousand,
and those whose cases are reviewed and managed
are not even one in a hundred.
The commanderies and counties rely on this state of affairs;
thus they even dare to delay deadlines
while the people go daily to submit petitions.
This is all caused by excessive leniency.
Regarding the hexagram of *Shìkè*,
the lower part is movement and the upper is clarity.
Its *Xiàng* says:
"The ancient kings, by clarifying punishments, refined the laws."
Now, in a custom of accumulated indolence,
if rewards are not generous, then goodness is not encouraged;
if punishments are not heavy, then evil is not deterred.
Therefore, those who wish to transform the atmosphere and change customs
are those who execute rewards and punishments;
they must make them sufficient to startle the heart and shatter the soul,
only then will the people change their perspective.
If a sagely ruler is truly willing to clearly examine his officials,
and for those who exhaust their spirits, fulfill their duties, and have merits,
does not begrudge the expense of gold, silk, and enfeoffment;
and for those who harbor villainy, conceal evil, and are otherwise without merit,
seeks the judgment of the axe and the chopping block.
Then good officials such as the likes of Wáng Chéng, Huáng Bà, Gōng Suì, and Shào Xìnchén
could be found in every neighboring commandery;
divine omens and auspicious responses
could be brought about within a single year.
That by which a state is a state
is because it has people;
that by which the people are people
is because they have grain;
that by which grain is abundant and multiplying
is because of human labor;
that by which labor can be established
is because of the strength of the day.
In a well-governed state, the days are leisurely and long,
therefore the people have leisure and surplus strength;
in a chaotic state, the days are hurried and short,
therefore the people are burdened with affairs and have insufficient strength.
What is called the days of a well-governed state being leisurely and long
is not by petitioning Xīhé to make him travel slowly,
nor is it by being able to increase the degrees of measurement or add to the water-clock.
It is when the ruler is clear-sighted and the various officials are orderly,
the subordinates follow what is right and find their proper place,
then the people are peaceful and have surplus strength,
therefore the days appear long.
What is called the days of a chaotic state being hurried and short
is not by petitioning Xīhé to make him drive quickly,
nor is it by being able to reduce the degrees of measurement or shorten the water-clock.
It is when the ruler is not clear-sighted, so the various officials are in chaos and treachery arises,
laws and orders are sold and corvée and taxes are frequent,
then the common people are burdened by the administration of officials,
those in service are exhausted by protocol and ritual,
wronged people go to prison before they find justice,
upright men engage in private dealings to be protected,
treacherous ministers indulge their hearts above,
and chaotic influences flow below,
gentlemen carry their gifts of introduction and rush in their carriages,
the commoners carry their wealth and scurry about,
therefore the days appear short.
The *Shī* says:
"The King's business is never-ending,
I have no leisure to nourish my father."
This means that in ancient times there was leisure and one could practice filial piety,
but now one is hurried and cannot provide nourishment.
Kǒngzǐ said that once the people are numerous, enrich them;
once they are enriched, teach them.
Therefore, ritual and righteousness arise from abundance,
theft and robbery arise from poverty,
wealth and nobility arise from leisure,
and poverty arises from having no time.
The sages deeply knew that labor is the root of the people and the foundation of the state,
therefore they strove to reduce corvée and cherished the people's time.
This is why Yáo commanded Xīhé:
"Reverently follow the August Heaven,
and respectfully grant the people their seasons."
Shào Bó, in adjudicating lawsuits, could not bear to trouble the people,
and he listened and decided under a sweet pear tree,
being able to raise a time of harmony and bring about the abandonment of punishments.
Nowadays it is not so.
Ten thousand officials harass the people,
district magistrates and headmen boast of themselves,
and the common people abandon farming and sericulture to rush to the government courts;
unless it is dawn or dusk, they cannot get through,
and unless they have influence, they cannot be seen;
whether a lawsuit is filed or not, it drags on for months and days,
the whole household abandons work
to look after one another;
for the family of the litigant,
they always ask neighbors to help respond and send provisions;
by the time the matter is finished,
a whole year's labor has been lost,
then there are those in the world who alone suffer hunger because of it,
yet the mediocre and vulgar officials who manage the laws
do not even notice it.
Once the commanderies and counties have added injustice,
the provincial officials do not correct it,
forcing families to ruin their livelihoods
and travel far to the ducal offices.
The ducal offices are unable to clearly distinguish truth from falsehood,
and only wish to dismiss them through the means of prolonged hardship;
so they basely state a rule,
ordering them to register for one hundred days,
only then will they send a letter;
if they have not completed one hundred days,
they always change the count,
which greatly violates the principle of Shào Bó adjudicating under the pear tree.
This is what is meant by reciting the three hundred poems of the *Shī*,
but when given the task of government,
failing to achieve the goal,
though they be many, of what use are they?
Kǒngzǐ said:
"In hearing lawsuits,
I am like anyone else."
From this perspective,
those of middle talent or above
can all deliberate the distinction between right and wrong,
and the principles of penal law are accessible;
the officials of the villages, pavilions, and departments
are sufficient to make decisions
and ensure there are no grievances.
Yet the reason they do not,
is because there is a reason.
The *Zhuàn* says:
"They hate the upright and loathe the correct,
indeed, they are numerous and have many followers."
Now, the upright are loyal and correct and do not bend their will,
and they grant no favors to the officials.
The enemies and managing parties bind themselves with goods and wealth,
so the village and pavilion officials join them to exclude the upright family;
later, when the case is reviewed, the officials would be incriminated,
so they together pervert justice in the court.
When a weak commoner sues a powerful official,
their power is not equal.
For this reason, the county and the department unite;
later, if there is a review,
the chief official would be incriminated,
so the whole county excludes them from the commandery.
When one person sues a whole county,
their power is not equal.
Therefore, the commandery and the county unite;
later, if there is a review,
the Grand Administrator would be incriminated,
so the whole commandery excludes them from the province.
When one person sues a whole commandery,
their power is not equal.
Therefore, the province and the commandery unite,
and are unwilling to adjudicate,
thus they go far to the ducal offices.
The ducal offices are unable to investigate,
and merely wish to assess them through money and wealth;
then the poor and weak with little wealth will never reach the end of the ten-day periods or the full term requested.
The wealthy with abundant money hire retainers to go,
and can complete a thousand days,
not just a hundred.
Dealing with lawsuits like this
is to strive to help the powerful and crafty while suppressing the poor and weak;
what injustice can be resolved?
It is not only lawsuits in the villages and departments.
Even when military officers decide cases,
they are all first wronged by minor officials,
and finally suffer heavy injustice from high ministers.
Before the grievance is settled,
they always encounter an amnesty,
and the case cannot be tried again;
the upright man harbors his grievance and cannot be vindicated,
while the crafty official builds up his villainy and is not severely punished.
This is why commanderies and counties easily infringe upon the common people,
and why the world has so much hunger and poverty.
Aside from the Heavens being moved
to send down disasters that damage the grain,
speaking only of human labor and visible affairs,
nowadays, from the Three Offices downwards,
to the counties, districts, villages, and pavilions,
as well as the attendants and post-inspectors,
and the officials in charge of records,
the people abandon farming and sericulture to wait upon them.
In lawsuits and complaints,
and those responding to officials regarding government business,
if one person is involved in each,
one hundred thousand people's labor is wasted daily;
if we calculate further down,
for one person involved in a matter,
two people provide provisions;
this means three hundred thousand people daily abandon their work.
Based on the rate of middle-level farming,
then in a year, three million mouths suffer hunger from it.
In that case, how can bandits and thieves be eliminated,
and how can Great Peace be established?
Emperor Xiàomíng once asked:
"Why are there no petitions submitted this morning?"
His attendants replied:
"Because of the Fǎnzhī day."
The Emperor said:
"The common people have already abandoned their farming and come from afar to reach the palace gates,
and yet they are made to avoid the Fǎnzhī day.
This is further depriving them of their time and doing them an injustice."
He then ordered the Gōngchē to receive the memorials,
without avoiding the Fǎnzhī day.
The wise and sagely ruler above cherished the people's time in this way,
yet the officials below light-heartedly deprived the people of their time in that manner.
This is what is called having a ruler but no ministers,
having a master but no assistants;
the head is intelligent,
while the limbs are lazy.
The Shī says:
"The state is already being cut to pieces;
why is there no inspection?"
This laments that the Sāngōng occupy honorable positions
and enjoy heavy salaries,
yet they are unwilling to observe the people's total exhaustion.
Kǒngzǐ was distressed by those who, "before they have attained something,
worry about not attaining it;
and once they have attained it,
worry about losing it."
Today, the high officials rise from provincial and commandery levels to become prime ministers;
their intelligence and wisdom
are not necessarily dim;
the problem is that they improperly prioritize private interests over public righteousness.
The Shī says:
"No one is willing to think about the disorder;
who does not have parents?"
If the people's labor is given no respite,
how can the grain grow?
"If the common people do not have enough,
with whom can the ruler have enough?"
Alas!
How can one not reflect on this?
The five dynasties had different rituals,
and the three eras had different teachings;
it is not that they were intentionally contradictory,
but that as the ages changed, the customs and transformations differed.
When customs and transformations differ, the origins of disorder are distinct;
thus the three eras matched their times
and all reformed the established laws.
Gāozǔ established the Three-Chapter Covenant,
and Xiàowén abolished the punishments that mutilated the skin.
Therefore, except for cases of killing, injury, robbery, or bribery,
the laws for literary crimes
are not fixed in severity;
each follows what is appropriate for the time,
essentially aiming only to be sufficient to encourage good and eliminate evil.
The intention of establishing laws
is like building fences, hedges, moats, and ditches to provide a defense;
one selects the beasts most likely to frequently intrude
and makes the defenses deeper and thicker there.
Now, although the wicked and treacherous are many,
their origins are few;
although the affairs of the ruler are numerous,
their fundamental principles are simple.
Knowing that the origins are few makes it easy to block the wicked;
seeing that the principles are simple makes it easy to maintain the administration.
Block their origins, and wickedness will be cut off;
implement these methods, and both the near and far will be governed.
Nowadays, the cases adjudicated in a year,
though numbered in the tens of thousands,
yet the arguments in lawsuits,
the occurrence of brawls and thefts,
the management by local departments,
and the management by prison officials
are all of the same character.
Fundamentally, they all arise from the people's lack of sincerity and trust,
and their frequent mutual deception.
"Shùn ordered Lóng because 'slanderous speech and ruinous conduct
startle and alarm my people,'"
so this has been a concern since ancient times.
Therefore, one must first be cautious with one's own speech
to set a primary example for the people.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Where disorder arises,
speech serves as the stairs."
"The petty man feels no shame at being unkind
and feels no fear of being unrighteous."
Gazing intently and schemingly,
they always harbor treacherous thoughts;
they blindly pursue immediate gain
without regard for integrity or shame.
Acting carelessly in the moment,
they later end up in ruin and servitude,
causing calamities and changes;
such people can be found in every house.
It is not only the common people who are like this;
from enfeoffed lords, kings, and marquises to noble relatives and the wealthy,
there are even more among them.
They make false pretenses of arrogance and extravagance
to indulge in excess;
they owe debts as high as ten million
yet are unwilling to repay their obligations.
The common people wail and cry out at their gates,
but they have not a hint of alarm, shame, or pity.
They only value gathering drunkards and people without moral conduct,
passing around empty cups and drawing them full,
chattering and cursing,
arguing day and night,
loving only idle pleasure.
Some even beat their creditors,
leading to death;
this is no different from bands of robbers attacking and plundering
or kidnapping people.
Although they may encounter an amnesty or pay a fine,
they should not again be included in the categories for selection and appointment;
yet the provincial authorities and ducal offices instead compete to recruit them.
Furthermore, looking at those who dare to be recklessly extravagant and incur great debts,
it is certainly not to relieve hunger and cold or resolve urgent hardships,
nor to aid the poor or practice ritual and righteousness;
it is entirely to promote arrogance and luxury and to serve their dissipation.
According to the principles of the Chūnqiū,
those who know are held accountable, and the leaders are punished.
Emperor Xiàowén was extremely reserved,
wishing to rely on virtue;
yet Chén Xìn, the Marquis of Héyáng, was stripped of his state because he was found guilty of owing a debt for six months.
Emperor Xiàowǔ was benevolent and wise;
Tián Péngzǔ, the Marquis of Zhōuyáng, was stripped of his state because he was found guilty of occupying the residence of the Marquis of Zhǐ and not returning it.
Shào Yán, the Marquis of Líyáng, was found guilty of not coming out to hold the horse;
his body was executed and his state abolished.
Did these two emperors enjoy harming high ministers because of money or property?
They wished to cut off the beginnings of fraud and deception,
to ensure the laws of the state were upheld,
to prevent the source of disaster and disorder,
and thereby benefit the people.
Therefore, if one person submits to a just punishment and ten thousand households receive blessings,
a sagely ruler carries it out without hesitation.
During the Yǒngpíng era,
whenever the marquises owed debts,
they were immediately punished with reduction of rank or dismissal.
After this, they all did not dare to owe the people;
society became naturally frugal,
and lawsuits naturally dissipated.
Today, among the marquises and noble relatives,
some tell the people to be cautious in conduct,
not to violate virtue and righteousness,
and to practice restraint and follow rules,
while they themselves have never owed debts,
keep their persons pure and avoid wrongdoing,
and set their sights on the lofty clouds.
Yet others, having already cheated and burdened the common people,
submit petitions to use their enfeoffed taxes
to temporarily repay their debts;
this is ravaging and plundering the officials and people
and then returning to rely on the local magistrate.
Their deception and negligence
constitute no greater crime.
The Xiàojīng says:
"Explain to them with virtue and righteousness, and the people will be inspired to practice them;
show them what is liked and disliked, and the people will know what is forbidden."
If one now wishes to transform artifice and falsehood to promote beautiful transformation,
and to stop lawsuits to lighten official business,
there is nothing better than publicly commending those with good conduct
and severely punishing those without merit.
Guide them with the laws of civil and military affairs,
and clarify the reliability regarding deception.
Now, the marquises, kings, and noble relatives are not constrained,
and thus wickedness and treachery have become numerous.
Can it be said that every brawl or lawsuit
must be caused by women?
It is also seen in the commentaries.
If all these roots of calamity are not cut off early,
they will turn and spread like creeping vines;
people are like this.
Therefore, the reason why original officials and investigators are diligent in their reflections,
and the reason why ministers and the ruler are worried and toil,
is that fundamentally, what is governed in the townships and hamlets
is more than half born from fraud and deception.
Therefore it is said:
knowing that the origins are few makes it easy to block wickedness;
seeing that the principles are simple makes it easy to maintain the administration.
Regarding the conduct of a woman,
purity and cleanliness are esteemed.
Now that she has been married,
she has no face to return to the Jiǎ gates.
The county officials pardoned her,
and thus ordered that she remain in the household she had already entered.
They surely did not understand the root of disorder
and did not consider the words of those born of chastity and purity.
A chaste woman does not have a divided heart despite numerous changes,
hence there is the poem of "Fěi Shí."
She does not act crookedly to leave behind sorrow,
hence the intent of Guī Níng is praised.
Once promised, she does not change;
this is how chastity is fostered and the minds of fathers and brothers are put at ease.
For those who do not follow this and behave with inconsistent virtue,
these are households that fundamentally lack a sense of shame
and are not places of chastity and devotion.
For such people,
why should there be any further shame or reluctance?
Belittling fathers and brothers,
women who are lewd and depraved,
disregarding moral principles,
if they are negligent in even one virtue,
they borrow capital to make a living,
flee to avoid debts,
and eventually meet with the disaster of having their bellies cut open and necks severed or the extermination of their clan—
what is there that would not happen?
The former kings, regarding those human emotions of joy and anger that cannot be restrained,
established the ritual system for them and exalted virtue and yielding;
for what people can restrain,
they established legal prohibitions and clarified rewards and punishments.
Now, that there should be no mutual cheating in market sales
and no mutual deception in marriage
is not something impossible for human emotions.
Therefore, it is better to establish righteousness and follow the law
to cut off the source of evil.
Although there is initially shame or reluctance for one person,
in the end,
it is of long-term benefit for ten thousand generations.
"Small punishment serves as a great warning,"
this is the means by which the small are kept whole and the stubborn and wicked are saved.
The grand essence of establishing laws
must make good people be encouraged in their virtue and take joy in the administration,
and cause wicked people to suffer from their calamities and regret their actions.
If a single woman is promised to several families,
even if she has borne ten sons
and undergoes a hundred amnesties,
do not allow her to enjoy the favor of returning to her private family even once;
then this wickedness will be severed.
Otherwise, shave the heads of the husband and wife
and exile them to a harsh county over a thousand lǐ away;
only then can their hearts be pained and their lineage be cut off.
When wickedness and disorder are severed, then Tàipíng will arise.
Furthermore, there are chaste widows,
some with both sons and daughters,
with abundant wealth and goods,
who wish to maintain the ritual of a single marriage toast
and fulfill the righteousness of sharing the same grave,
holding their integrity firmly,
with their hearts set on death
and never a thought of remarrying.
But they encounter unkind uncles
or unrighteous brothers,
who either desire the betrothal gifts,
or covet their wealth and bribes,
or treat their sons as their own private property;
thus they use force and deception to marry them off,
and through coercion and threats, they are sent away.
Some people hang themselves in their rooms
or take poison in their carriages,
ending their lives and losing their bodies,
abandoning their young children.
This is equivalent to coercing someone to commit suicide.
Or the subsequent husband gathers many guests
to threaten and carry her away with force,
while guards hold her tight,
and only after many days is she finally bound;
this is no different from forcibly kidnapping someone to be a wife.
Women are soft and weak,
and when they are suddenly supported and coerced by many strong men,
and confined for many days,
even if they later wish to restore their original intent,
they are already entangled in the silk or have swallowed the poison.
Those who ruled the world without slackening the system
were the Sān Huáng;
those who transformed the four directions by drawing symbols
were the Wǔ Dì;
those who clarified legal prohibitions and harmonized the realm within the seas
were the Sān Wáng.
Those who applied rewards and punishments and regulated the myriad people
were the rulers of a governed state;
when a ruler establishes laws but those below do not follow them,
it is a chaotic state;
when ministers create policies and the ruler does not control them,
it is a perished state.
Therefore, the reason why the people are not in disorder
is that there are officials above them;
the reason why officials have no wickedness
is that the government has laws;
the reason why laws are followed smoothly
is that the state has a ruler;
the reason why the ruler's position is honorable
is that he himself possesses righteousness.
Righteousness is the ruler's administration;
law is the ruler's command.
When the ruler thinks correctly to issue orders,
and neither the noble nor the base, the wise nor the foolish, can defy them,
then the ruler sits in the position above,
and the common people are governed below.
If a ruler issues orders but arrogant ministers and officials do not comply,
then the ruler is close to being assassinated,
and the people are close to disorder.
Laws and orders
are what the ruler uses to govern his state.
If the ruler issues orders but they are not followed,
it is the same as having no ruler.
If the lord's orders are not followed, then the ministers' orders will prevail,
and the state is in danger.
Laws and orders
are the bit, reins, whip, and crop of the ruler,
and the people
are the ruler's carriage and horses.
If an official is allowed to discard the ruler's laws and prohibitions to implement his own administrative orders,
then it is as if he has snatched the ruler's reins and whip
and is driving alone.
The foolish ruler or darkened lord sits uselessly on the left,
while the treacherous minister who goes against the Way holds the reins on the right.
This is how Zōu Mǎ Shù of Qí was able to drown Hú Gōng in the Jù River,
and why Yáng Shū Zāng of Sòng was able to defeat Huá Yuán in the Zhèng army,
and no one could resist them.
This is why Chén Héng seized Jiǎn Gōng in Xúzhōu,
and Lǐ Duì harmed Zhǔ Fù in Shā Qiū;
they all used their poisonous schemes to snatch the ruler's reins and whip.
Therefore, the Wén Yán says:
"A minister assassinating his ruler
or a son killing his father
is not the result of a single morning or evening.
Its origin is gradual,
arising from not recognizing the changes early on."
Therefore, officials who recklessly violate the law
and ministers who recklessly create orders
cannot but be executed.
Commentators will surely think that execution and killing should not be used,
and that moral transformation alone can be relied upon.
This is not the argument of those who understand how to adapt to changes,
nor is it the speech of those in a troubled age.
Even the highest sages did not surpass Yáo and Shùn,
yet they banished the four wicked ones;
even the greatest virtue did not surpass Wén and Wǔ,
yet they showed their great anger.
The Shī says:
"If the gentleman is angry,
disorder will quickly be suppressed;
if the gentleman is happy,
disorder will quickly cease."
Thus, the joy and anger of a gentleman
are used to stop disorder.
Therefore, there is using execution to stop killing
and using punishment to resist cruelty.
Furthermore, governing the world is like climbing a hill;
one must first tread on the low parts
before one can step on the heights.
Therefore, first achieve a governed state,
and then the administration of the Sān Wáng can be applied;
let the Way be equal to the Sān Wáng,
and then the transformation of the Wǔ Dì can be implemented;
let the Way be equal to the Wǔ Dì,
and then the Way of the Sān Huáng can be followed.
Moreover, laws
are the administration of the former kings;
orders
are one's own commands.
The administration of the former kings is shared with the multitude;
one's own commands are used to govern people alone.
If a ruler can truly uphold the law and occasionally grant leniency,
and issue orders that must be carried out,
then none of the ministers and officials will dare not to follow his orders with all their heart.
When one's own orders are not violated,
then the laws and prohibitions will surely be implemented.
Therefore, when administration and orders are carried out,
and the laws and prohibitions are followed,
there has never been a case where a state was not well-governed.
This is a matter of tightening and relaxing,
using the present to implement the ancient,
and the technique of balancing the light and heavy, the honorable and the base.
The people of remote antiquity
were pure, honest, simple, and sincere.
The supreme sages governed them
with tranquility, detachment, and non-action,
embodying the Dào and practicing virtue.
They simplified punishments and lightened their majesty;
they did not kill or execute,
and the people transformed of their own accord.
This is the height of virtue.
As virtue gradually declined and thinned,
evil intentions proliferated.
Lesser sages followed,
observing the people to establish teachings.
They created executions and rewards
to encourage them through majesty.
Having created the five weapons,
they also established laws
to correct and discipline them.
The *Shī* says:
"Repair your chariots and horses,
your bows, arrows, spears, and halberds,
to serve as a warning and a rule,
and to keep the barbarian regions far away."
Therefore it is said:
"The establishment of weapons has existed for a long time."
Passing through the five generations
until the present day,
a state has never failed to prosper through virtue and become strong through weapons.
Nowadays, clever military equipment
fills the storehouses,
and the words of Sūn and Wú
ring in the ears of the generals.
However, when the various generals employ them,
advancing to battle results in defeat,
and retreating to defend results in the loss of cities.
Why is this?
It is said:
The conditions of both sides
are not heard by the Sovereign,
and the calculations of victory and defeat
are not clear in the hearts of the generals.
The soldiers see no benefit in advancing and feel no fear in retreating;
this is why it is so.
To carry a heavy load up a slope
or to gallop a thousand lǐ
is a calamity for a horse.
Yet a restrained horse enjoys it
because Wáng Liáng is sufficient to make it exert its full strength.
To be the first to climb the walls or break the enemy ranks,
and to face death against a stern foe,
is a calamity for the people.
Yet an upright soldier enjoys it
because an enlightened ruler is someone for whom he can sacrifice his life.
Generally, the reason why people are willing to face death without hesitation
is either to pursue profit
or to avoid harm.
This is true for the worthy and the base, the foolish and the wise alike;
it is only that what they consider profit and harm differs.
If they do not value a distinguished name,
then they value generous rewards;
if they do not avoid shame and disgrace,
then they avoid disaster and turmoil.
Other than these four things,
even a sage king cannot constrain his ministers,
and a compassionate father cannot command his son.
An enlightened master knows this deeply;
therefore, he honors profit and clarifies harm to bargain with those below,
ensuring that the kin and the distant, the noble and the base, the worthy and the vulgar, the foolish and the wise,
must all follow his orders to obtain their desires.
Consequently, as soon as the war drums thunder
and the banners are raised together,
the soldiers are all roused and excited,
competing to fight to the death against the enemy.
Is it because they are tired of living long
and take pleasure in harm and death?
It is rather that the righteous man seeks to gain his reputation,
and the greedy man seeks to obtain his reward.
Nowadays, the officials who follow the army to defeat and die in public service
are numbered in the hundreds of thousands.
Above, they do not hear the honored name of condolences and sighs;
below, there is no substantial reality of stipends and rewards.
The upright soldiers have nothing to admire or emulate,
and the common men have no profit to covet.
This is why people harbor discouragement and laziness
and are unwilling to face death again.
Since the start of the military operations,
the army has been exposed for five years.
The officials in charge of the troops
are numbered in the thousands.
Large and small battles
occur dozens or hundreds of times a year,
yet rarely is there success.
If one examines their failures,
there is no other reason:
they all stem from the generals being ignorant of changing circumstances
and the soldiers not being encouraged to fight to the death against the enemy.
That the soldiers cannot die
is because the generals cannot set an example.
When rewards are mentioned, they are not given;
when punishments are mentioned, they are not carried out.
For a soldier, advancing brings the calamity of dying alone,
while retreating brings the blessing of collective survival.
This is why they flee from battle
and compete to think of running away.
Sūnzǐ said:
"A general is one who possesses wisdom,
benevolence,
respect,
trustworthiness,
courage,
and strictness."
Therefore, wisdom is used to break the enemy,
benevolence to attach the masses,
respect to attract the worthy,
trustworthiness to ensure rewards,
courage to increase spirit,
and strictness to unify orders.
Thus, by breaking the enemy, one can adapt to changes;
when the masses are attached through love, they think of fighting with all their strength;
when the worthy and wise gather, secret plans succeed;
when rewards and punishments are certain, the soldiers exert their full strength;
when courage and spirit increase, the military momentum naturally doubles;
when majesty and orders are unified, they follow only the general's command.
One must possess these six qualities
to break through and capture the enemy,
to assist the ruler and pacify the people.
When the Qiāng first rebelled,
the generals took command of established and orderly groups,
relied on abundant reserves,
occupied a line of cities with advantageous positions,
held authority over a hundred thousand troops,
and led brave and outstanding soldiers
to punish the newly risen, newly rebelled, scattered and disorganized weak captives.
They attacked small bandits who had come of their own accord,
yet could not capture or destroy them,
and were constantly defeated by them.
Consequently, they rose up like steam,
forming alliances horizontally and vertically.
They swept through Bìng and Liáng,
invaded Sīlì internally,
raided Zhào and Wèi to the east,
and plundered Shǔ and Hàn to the west.
Five provinces were ruined,
and the traces of six commanderies were nearly erased.
This was not a calamity from Heaven,
but the fault of the senior officials.
Sūnzǐ said:
"The general
is the arbiter of the people's fate
and the master of the state's safety or peril."
Therefore, in all commanderies where there are bandits,
the Grand Protectors and Chiefs must not be ignorant of military matters.
Looking at the various generals today,
they neither have the ingenuity to cut off the enemy and adapt to changes,
nor do they have the trustworthiness to clarify rewards and ensure punishments.
Furthermore, their soldiers and people are extremely poor and destitute;
their equipment is not selected or practiced;
and the general's kindness has not been established beforehand.
Suddenly, when there is an emergency,
the officials use sudden violence to mistreat their soldiers,
and the soldiers use their clumsiness to face the enemy's skill.
This is a case of generals and officials driving resentment to resist an enemy,
and soldiers leading themselves with bound hands to await the bandits.
If a general cannot encourage his soldiers,
and the soldiers cannot use their weapons,
these two situations are the same as having no army.
Without soldiers and without weapons,
yet wishing to engage in battle,
their defeat
is a matter of logical necessity.
Therefore it is said:
their failure
is not a calamity from Heaven,
but the fault of the general.
For a man of abundant talent living in this world,
his only worry is not having a position.
Therefore, if one has land,
the common people can be made wealthy;
if there are marketplaces,
merchants can be made to come;
if there are soldiers and people,
the state can be made strong;
if there are laws and orders,
evil and wickedness can be prohibited.
A state cannot be governed from the outside,
and an army cannot be directed from the center.
If the senior officials of commanderies and counties
are fortunate enough to have the authority to decide these matters for themselves,
yet cannot live up to the enlightened decrees to pacify the common people,
this is because they are mediocre and insignificant people,
having no inner worth.
In this world, there are extraordinary people,
and only then can extraordinary matters be settled;
there must be a path through extraordinary failures,
and only then will they appear.
Therefore, when selecting high officials who command troops,
they should be outstanding and magnanimous,
and one should go beyond the ordinary to choose the obscure and marvelous,
those whose talents are clear and who can adapt to changes,
to serve as generals and commanders.
One must not carelessly rely only on seniority and rank,
or show favoritism to relatives,
when appointing officials in charge of the military.
This is what is called giving one's state to the enemy.
The governance of a Sage King
covers all universally and loves all equally,
showing no partiality to those close or intimate,
nor neglecting those distant and remote.
Auspiciousness, calamity, disaster, and fortune
are shared with the people,
and the emotions of sorrow and joy
are extended to others through empathy.
He looks upon the people as newborn infants,
and rescues them from disaster as if pulling a hand from fire.
Therefore, all within the four seas are joyful
and work together in harmony.
In the past, when the Qiāng barbarians rebelled,
it began in Liángzhōu and Bìngzhōu,
extended to Sīlì,
brought disaster east to Zhào and Wèi,
and plundered west to Shǔ and Hàn.
Five provinces were devastated,
and six commanderies were depopulated;
for a thousand lǐ around,
nothing remained in the wilds.
The calamities of raiding and plundering
ceased neither day nor night;
the common people were annihilated,
and their days and months were exhausted in suffering.
Yet those scholars of the inner commanderies who were not afflicted
all said they should let things take their course for now
to wait for the timing of Heaven.
With intentions like this,
how can it be the heart of a human!
When the Qiāng first rebelled,
the high ministers and chief officials all wished to abandon Liángzhōu
and retreat to defend the Sānfǔ region,
but the imperial court did not listen.
Later, when the Qiāng finally invaded,
many commentators regretted not following that deluded proposal.
I secretly laugh at them;
it is what is called regretting the peace
and also regretting the lack of peace,
never having understood the logic of change.
The land has no fixed border;
to have no border is to lose the state.
Therefore, if Liángzhōu is lost,
then Sānfǔ becomes the border;
if Sānfǔ is pulled inward,
then Hóngnóng becomes the border;
if Hóngnóng is pulled inward,
then Luòyáng becomes the border.
Inferring from this by analogy,
even if we reached the Eastern Sea, there would still be a border.
Now, instead of sharpening our military might to punish the barbarians
and selecting talented men to secure our territory,
they say the border cannot be defended
and wish to first cut it off themselves,
showing weakness to the enemy;
is this not a delusion!
In the past, Yuè Yì, with the tiny state of Yān,
destroyed the powerful Qí,
his prestige shaking the world;
he truly could be called a fine general.
Yet the Grandee of Jímò defended a lone city,
not falling for six years,
and eventually saved his people.
Tián Dān was at his wit's end,
but leading five thousand cavalry,
he attacked and drove them back,
recovering more than seventy cities for Qí;
he can be said to have been skillful in using troops.
The sieges of Liáo and Jǔ lasted for years,
yet they could not be taken.
All these instances were the strongest attacking the weakest,
the most intelligent plotting against the simple,
yet they still could not conquer—why is that?
I say:
Attacking is usually insufficient,
while defending always has a surplus.
In recent days, the various commanderies
all occupied walled cities and possessed large numbers of people.
The intelligence of the Qiāng barbarians
is not that of Yuè Yì or Tián Dān;
the peril of the commanderies and counties
was not like that of Liáo, Jǔ, and Jímò.
Yet they were all unwilling to focus on a firm defense,
and instead forcibly drove and coerced the people,
abandoned the granaries and storehouses,
and fled the walled towns.
From this perspective,
it is not the hardship of a city lacking grain,
but simply the hardship of a general who will not stay.
Breaking the enemy's charge and pacifying the people
depends essentially on employing the worthy,
not on shrinking the borders.
Qí and Wèi retreated to defend,
but their states were not secured by it.
Zǐyīng diminished himself,
but Qín did not survive by it.
Emperor Wǔ repelled the barbarians and expanded the borders,
extending several thousand lǐ;
to the east he opened Lèlàng,
to the west he established Dùnhuáng,
to the south he crossed Jiāozhǐ,
and to the north he built Shuòfāng.
He eventually pacified Nányuè
and struck down Dàyuān.
Wherever his martial armies went,
everything was destroyed.
Now the barbarians cause trouble near the capital's territory,
yet we cannot capture them;
this is truly painful,
and is not the fault of having a border.
When the lips are gone, the teeth are cold;
when the body is wounded, the heart feels pain.
These are matters of necessity;
what doubt is there?
A gentleman sees the signs;
how much more so when they are already manifest?
Recently,
the border disasters have shaken like thunder
and flared like the sun and moon,
yet speakers all avoid the topic,
calling them mere whirlwind petty thefts.
Superficial talk claims all is well and peaceful,
causing gentlemen to be negligent,
wishing to make the court think the bandits are small
and thus not worry early on.
The harm has come to this,
yet they still do not wish to save it.
A proverb says:
“When pain does not touch one’s own body, one says it can be endured;
when money does not leave one’s own home, one says it can be given.”
If the sons and brothers of the high ministers were afflicted by the Qiāng disaster,
feeling the urgency day and night like the border people,
then they would compete to say the Qiāng must be destroyed.
Now, just because they themselves have no sorrow or painful resentment,
they sit properly and follow one another's lead,
not clearly repairing the preparations for defense,
but remaining carefree and indifferent,
lying down and leaving everything to the will of Heaven.
The Qiāng come and go as they please,
penetrating deep and killing many,
while they themselves are mediocre,
leading each other to the palace gates,
making pleasant speeches and ceremonial thanks,
and withdrawing to report the situation.
When meeting in the audience hall,
they have no sincere concern for the state or pity for the people,
but merely look at one another,
none willing to speak out against or stop it.
The day grows late and time passes,
the discussion settles nothing,
and they just wait for later.
When a little peace is later obtained,
they calmly discard and forget it.
In the space of a month or so,
the barbarians cause harm again,
military reports fly back and forth,
and urgent dispatches arrive in succession,
and they return to being panicked as before.
Since it has been like this
for nine years,
hoping things would improve,
only for evil to break out again,
confused and disordered,
where will it end!
The Chūnqiū criticizes “Zhèng abandoning its army”,
how much more so to abandon the people?
If one person sighs in distress,
the Kingly Way is diminished;
how much more so when a million people,
crying out and weeping, move the heart of Heaven?
Furthermore, the state takes the people as its foundation,
and the noble take the lowly as their root.
Therefore, the Sage King nurtures the people,
loving them like children
and worrying for them as for his own family;
he brings peace to those in danger
and preserves those who are perishing,
rescuing them from disasters and suffering,
and eliminating calamities and chaos.
For this reason, the campaign against Guǐfāng
was not because of a fondness for martial arts;
the expulsion of the Xiǎnyǔn
was not out of greed for land.
It was "to stir the people and cultivate virtue"
and to pacify the borders.
"In ancient times,
the Son of Heaven maintained his defense among the four Yí tribes";
"from those Dī and Qiāng,
none failed to come and present offerings,"
for all under heaven thought of submission,
and even the "Reeds" (Xíngwěi) relied on his virtue.
How much more so when our own people suffer such calamities as these—
can we not rescue them?
Generally, the reason the people serve their superiors
is that they cherish righteousness and kindness.
When in pain, they lose their sense of shame;
when in disaster, they lose their benevolence.
Resentment, defiance, and bitterness
are born from the lack of a sense of shame.
Now the Qiāng have been in rebellion for a long time!
The harm they have done is great!
The common people are in desperate straits!
Their worry and calamity are deep!
Superiors and inferiors follow one another in this state,
and no end is in sight.
If we do not immediately commission a Great General to sweep away the ugly rebels,
and instead the provinces gradually raise corvée labor
in a continuous and unending stream,
it is like using a screen to block the wind
or digging through sand to dam a river—
it can defend nothing
and only exhausts oneself.
Now several provinces have stationed over a hundred thousand troops;
they all receive their provisions from the local officials,
totaling several million hǔ annually,
in addition to monthly salaries.
This consumption of resources
cannot be sustained,
yet we conversely dread the temporary expense of sending an expedition;
this is truly not a good plan.
Furthermore, those in danger are easily toppled,
and those in doubt are easily transformed.
Now that the rebels have newly seized the borderlands,
they do not yet dare feel secure;
they are easily shaken.
The common people have newly departed from their old loyalties,
but their longing has not yet faded;
they are easily encouraged.
We truly ought to take advantage of this to dispatch a Great General to punish and suppress them,
to pressure, disperse, and destroy them.
If we grant them time and leisure,
allowing them to accumulate wealth and status
until each cherishes a sense of security and stability,
then they will be difficult to move.
The *Zhōu Shū* says:
"Every sage must hasten to catch the opportune moment."
Therefore, the strategy for war and defense
must be settled early.
One who is clear about the reality of calamity and fortune
cannot be confused by empty theories;
one who observes the conditions of order and chaos
cannot be swayed by flowery decorations.
Therefore, regarding matters that are not in doubt,
the Sage does not deliberate;
regarding floating rumors,
the Sage does not listen.
Why?
A plan should not turn its back on reality to engage in further arguments.
Hence, a brilliant ruler first fully understands human nature;
he does not solely rely on a good general.
He cultivates his own preparations
and does not depend on others.
Thus, he can attack and certainly defeat the enemy,
and defend and certainly protect himself.
When the Qiāng first rebelled,
their planning was not good,
their alliances were not yet formed,
their masses had not yet gathered,
and their weapons were not prepared.
Some held bamboo or wooden branches,
and some joined with empty hands.
They ate wild grass and were disorganized,
without a commander;
they were very easy to break.
However, the Grand Protectors and Prefects
were all cowardly and fearful, not daring to strike.
Thus they allowed the rebels to take advantage of victory and grow stronger,
destroying provinces and eliminating commanderies.
Day by day their flames grew,
devastating the Sānfǔ region
and "reaching even to the Guǐfāng."
This has already continued for ten years.
The common people have been victimized,
and it has not stopped until now.
Yet foolish children and ignorant youths
still say we should not rescue them
and should wait for the timing of heaven.
With intentions like these,
are they even human?!
For the benevolent man extends his own feelings to others,
and the wise man speaks of achievements and manages affairs.
Now the ministers do not internally feel the pain of the soldiers and people being wiped out,
and externally they do not consider the calamity of a long-drawn-out war.
Each cares only for the moment,
escaping what is in front of them.
They blindly say that troops should not be moved,
and they no longer know how to uphold the principles of kings
or trace the ultimate outcome of these calamities.
The *Yì* discusses controlling rebels;
the *Shī* praises minor campaigns.
Since ancient times there has been war;
it is not only today.
The *Zhuàn* says:
"Heaven produced the five materials,
and the people use them together.
Not one can be discarded.
Who can do away with weapons?
Weapons are used to overawe the lawless and to manifest civil virtue.
They are the means by which the Sage rises
and the chaotic man is discarded."
Qí Huán, Jìn Wén, and Sòng Xiāng—
even as lords of a declining age,
they still felt ashamed when states in the world were destroying each other and they could not rescue them.
How much more so for the master of the four seas appointed by Imperial Heaven?
The grandees of Jìn and Chǔ,
who were ministers of small states,
still felt ashamed if their own persons were subjected to aggression.
How much more so for the Son of Heaven and the Three Excellencies who hold the responsibilities of the age?
Gōng Liú's benevolence and virtue
widely covered even the "Reeds" (Xíngwěi);
how much more so for living beings
who are of our own kind?
If one person sighs,
the Kingly Way is diminished;
how much more so when a million people are wiped out?
The *Shū* says:
"The Son of Heaven acts as the father and mother of the people."
As for a parent toward a child,
how can they sit and watch them be slaughtered and skinned by rebels and thieves,
or stand by and see them eaten by dogs and pigs?
Putting aside benevolence and kindness,
let us speak in terms of calculating profit.
The state takes the people as its foundation,
and the noble take the lowly as their root.
I ask that you examine since the beginning of the world:
Who has there been whose people were in danger while the state was secure?
Who has there been whose inferiors were poor while the superior was wealthy?
Therefore it is said:
"One who rules a state
is supported by the people.
If the people are truly emaciated,
how can the ruler become fat?"
Since the common people receive the eternal mandate of Heaven,
I secretly wish the Sagely Lord would deeply consider the injuries and illnesses of the state's foundation
and far-sightedly consider the source of calamity and fortune.
Furthermore, all things have periods of prosperity and decline,
time shifts and passes,
events have points of intensification and meeting,
and people undergo changes.
Wise men gauge the signs;
is it not appropriate?!
Mèng Míng redeemed his faults in Héxī,
and Fàn Lǐ collected debts at Gūxū.
Thus their great achievements were established in their generation,
and their fine names were passed down for eternity.
Now the borders are disturbed,
and clan-ending calamities occur daily.
The common people hope day and night for the imperial court to rescue them,
whereas the ministers and officials think the expense is too burdensome and impossible.
I merely laugh at this in private;
how is it any different from Àn Zǐ making light of the stores in the granaries while begrudging the cost of a drill for a single cup?
Now they only know to love the visible, meager money and grain,
but they do not know that what is not seen—the people—should come first;
they know the difficulty of mobilizing labor, but they do not know that the central land depends on the peace of the borders.
The *Shī* laments, "Some know not how to cry out,
while some suffer in bitter toil."
Now the high officials, as long as they themselves are not harmed,
compete to carve off the nation's territory to give to the enemy
and slaughter the Sovereign's people to feed the Qiāng.
When planning like this,
it cannot be called wisdom;
when serving as ministers like this,
it cannot be called loyalty.
Their talent and intelligence are not sufficient to be allowed into deliberations.
Furthermore, all that is within the Four Seas
is what the Sages left to their descendants;
official positions and duties
are where the various ministers entrust their persons.
Those who pass things to descendants
think of peace for ten thousand generations;
those who entrust their persons
each take only what is needed for a single interval.
Therefore, their words are often not practiced for long,
and their legacy cannot be long sustained.
Indeed, this is truly what a brilliant monarch should subtly observe
and a sagacious ruler should decide alone.
Now, if it is said that one does not wish to disturb or trouble the people, that is acceptable.
If so,
then the preparations for defense must be cultivated.
In current planning,
one must make the captives dare not come,
so they gain nothing;
and make the people not suffer from bandits,
so they lose nothing.
Now, however, it is not so;
they merely dread the exhaustion of the people's strength,
yet lightly allow them to suffer the great calamity of destruction.
This is not the way of a lord over men,
nor a general of the people,
nor an assistant to the lord,
nor a master of victory.
Furthermore, deliberation
is the manifestation of clarity;
words
are the expression of the heart.
"Because it is present within,
it appears as such without."
A proverb says:
"How can one subdue the stubborn?
There is nothing better than listening to them."
Now, as for those who say the frontiers can be safe without being rescued,
they should truly be sent in person, along with their sons and younger brothers, to fill the posts of frontier Tàishǒu, Lìng, Zhǎng, Chéng, and Wèi;
only then will the reality of right and wrong be settled,
and the rescue of the frontier will be without trouble.
When the frontiers have no trouble,
Zhōngguó will then attain peace and tranquility.
One who governs a state
must illuminate and examine the truth and falsehood of matters near and far
and anticipate where misfortune and fortune originate;
only then can they fully utilize the strength of their ministers
and preserve and prosper their nation.
When the Qiāng first rebelled,
the uprising was new and crude,
and their equipment was not ready;
some of the captives held bronze mirrors to imitate weapons,
while others carried wooden boards to serve as shields;
they were terrified and in turmoil,
unable to hold their ground.
A single city could have easily controlled them,
yet the commanderies and counties all became ablaze with trouble.
By the time the common people were suddenly struck by calamity
and lost their property and goods,
the people grieved and were roused to anger,
each wishing for revenge;
but the generals and commanders were all cowardly and weak,
not daring to attack,
merely sitting and drafting documents
to deceive the Imperial Court.
If a hundred people were actually killed, they would say one;
if one captive was killed, they would say a hundred.
Sometimes the captives were many, yet they called them few;
sometimes they were few, yet they called them many.
They used devious and clever wording
to seek personal convenience and benefit,
rather than being solely concerned with the great plans of the nation
or grieving over the deaths of the people.
Furthermore, they squandered money and grain,
exhausting the treasuries and granaries,
and then proceeded to take loans from the people,
forcibly seizing property and goods.
Families of great wealth
were stripped until nothing remained;
the myriad people were exhausted,
and those who subsequently died
were all starved to death by the officials.
The bitterness and pain of this
was worse than encountering the captives.
Bandits and plundering captives
pass by suddenly,
and one might not necessarily be killed or wounded.
But when it comes to the searches and looting of officials,
their tracks cover the ground;
sometimes entire clans and families are exterminated,
leaving no survivors;
some women are left widowed or orphaned,
becoming slaves to others,
sold off to distant places,
even to the point of being unable to survive;
they are beyond counting.
This provokes Heaven and brings about disasters,
being especially contrary to Yīnyáng.
Furthermore, people value staying put
and cherish the graves of their ancestors;
this is the same for the worthy and the unworthy alike.
For the people, being forced to migrate
is worse than facing execution.
Facing execution is no more than one person in the family dying.
But those who lose their property and goods,
have their land taken and are moved far away,
are not accustomed to the local customs
and find the environment unsuitable;
most such families are wiped out,
and few are able to return.
A horse from Dài looks toward the north,
and a dying fox turns its head toward its home hill;
the frontier people are simple and sincere,
and they especially loathe remaining in the interior.
Though they know the calamity is great,
they still wish to guard their inherited livelihoods
and die in their native places;
truly, their desire not to leave is extreme.
The Tàishǒu, Lìng, and Zhǎng
fear and loathe military affairs;
since they are originally not people of that land,
the pain does not touch their own bodies
and the disaster does not reach their own families,
so they compete to move the commanderies and counties inland.
They go so far as to send officials and soldiers
to seize the people's crops,
tear down their houses,
level their camps and walls,
and destroy their livelihoods;
they forcibly plunder and drive them,
bringing them into the interior,
while abandoning the weak and infirm
to die where they were.
At this time,
the myriad people were filled with resentment and pain,
weeping tears of blood and crying out;
it truly grieved the ghosts and gods and moved the heart of Heaven.
However, the common people are simple and weak,
unable to reach the Imperial Palace gates themselves;
dependent on the families of officials,
and pressured by their authority and dignity,
they dare not show any resistance.
Having had their land seized and their livelihoods lost,
the people then encountered locusts, droughts, and famine;
they fled eastward along the roads,
drifting and scattering
through Yōu, Jì, Yǎn, and Yù,
and through Jīng, Yáng, Shǔ, and Hàn;
from hunger and exhaustion,
they further lost more than half their number.
The frontier lands subsequently became mounds of ruins and overgrown wastes,
and to this day remain uninhabited.
If one traces the origin of the calamity,
it was entirely the fault of the officials.
Land
is the foundation of the people;
it truly should not be left desolate for long but should be cultivated.
Furthermore, when Biǎn Què treated diseases,
he examined blockages and cleared stagnation,
supplemented what was deficient,
and purged what was excessive;
thus the illness was cured and his name became famous.
When Yī Yǐn assisted Tāng,
he established the balance of weights and facilitated trade between those who had and those who had not,
reducing surpluses to supplement deficiencies;
thus the Yīn dynasty was well-governed and the monarch was honored.
Jiǎ Yì lamented the diseases of partial paralysis and lameness.
Now the frontier commanderies stretch for a thousand lǐ,
with each area having only two counties,
and the households numbering only a few hundred;
yet the Tàishǒu travels ten thousand lǐ
through a void without people,
where beautiful fields are abandoned and none are cultivated.
Meanwhile, in the central provinces and interior commanderies,
the land is planned and borders expanded,
yet they cannot revitalize the frontiers;
with populations of a million
and every acre of field occupied,
the people are numerous while the land is scarce,
leaving no room even to place one's foot;
this is also a kind of partial paralysis and lameness.
The *Zhōu Shū* says:
"Where land is abundant and people are few,
its resources are not produced;
this is called 'void land,'
which can be raided and attacked.
Where land is scarce and people are numerous,
the people are not truly their ruler's people;
they can be exhausted and abandoned."
Therefore, land and people must correspond to each other.
Now, the border commanderies suffer many harms and labor service is intense,
every move leading into the gateway of calamity.
If we do not promote benefits and remove harms,
and have means to encourage them,
then for a long time there will be no way to recover them,
and at our gates, there will be the intentions of bandits and invaders.
The western Qiāng and northern barbarians
will surely give birth to covetous desires;
this is truly a great concern.
The various craftsmen manufacture tools,
all to fill the borders,
distributing them in double the amount;
how could this be for private gain?
It is simply to secure the interior.
The former sages established laws,
also striving to populate the borders,
primarily to bring peace to Zhōngguó.
It is like a family encountering bandits;
they must place the old, young, weak, and frail in the center,
while the strong and martial guard the exterior.
Those inside provide sustenance,
those outside ward off danger;
like the Qióngqióng and the Jùxū,
relying on one another,
only then can both survive in peace.
According to edicts and laws:
for every two hundred thousand people,
or one hundred thousand in border commanderies,
one xiàolián is recommended each year;
within the quota, one liánlì is also recommended for hereditary service.
Since the Qiāng rebellion,
the population has decreased,
and the Grand Protectors have been changed frequently,
to the point that for ten years no recommendations could be made.
Those performing their duties with diligence are not recorded,
the worthy and talented accumulate but are not fully utilized,
the gentry have nothing to hope for,
and the farmers have no profit to seek;
thus they meet with disaster while pursuing their crops,
and none are willing to go to the frontier.
In ancient times, to benefit the people,
they enticed them with profit
and did not threaten them with punishment.
The *Yì* says:
"The former kings inspected the regions, observed the people, and established instruction."
Therefore, at the beginning of the Jiànwǔ era,
when the border commanderies were regained,
though there were only a few hundred households,
it was ordered that a xiàolián be recommended every year
to attract newcomers.
Now it would be truly appropriate to temporarily order border commanderies to recommend one Filial candidate,
one liánlì for hereditary service,
and additionally establish one scholar of the Classics with a hundred-dan salary;
if people from the inner commanderies bring their wives and children to settle there
for five years or more,
they should be treated equally with the residents
and all be eligible for recommendation and election.
Also recruit people to transport and farm the borders and contribute grain:
one thousand hú for distant commanderies,
two thousand hú for nearby commanderies,
and bestow the rank of wǔdàfū.
For those who do not desire rank,
let them receive double the price for grain compared to the inner commanderies.
In this way,
gentlemen and commoners will each have something to gain,
then even if one wished to order them not to go,
one could not stop them.
This is the essential method to balance hardship and joy, equalize labor service, fill the borders, and secure Zhōngguó.
Since the opening of heaven and earth, there have been spirits and people;
though people and spirits have different tasks, their refined essence communicates.
Actions have their summons,
destiny has its encounters and followings;
as for the timing of good and bad fortune,
Heaven is difficult to rely upon.
Even though the sages and worthies were perceptive, they did not rely solely on themselves;
so they established divination to consult the spirits.
Kǒngzǐ praised it, saying: "The virtue of the milfoil stalks is round and spiritual,
the virtue of the hexagrams is square and wise."
He also said:
"When a gentleman is about to take action,
he asks of them and they speak,
receiving his mandate and providing direction."
This is how Yǔ obtained Gāo Yáo
and how Wén Wáng recruited Lǚ Shàng;
the omens revealed their images
and divination confirmed their thoughts,
to bring about their good fortune.
When a gentleman hears of good, he is encouraged and joyfully advances;
when he hears of evil, he reflects and corrects his faults;
thus he is tranquil and enjoys much blessing.
When a commoner hears of good,
but when he hears of evil he becomes terrified and acts recklessly;
thus he is frantic and meets much calamity.
Therefore, all those who practice divination
primarily inquire into the nature of good and bad fortune,
and speak of the timing of rise and fall,
causing people to cultivate themselves and act cautiously to welcome blessing.
Furthermore, when the sage kings established divination,
they did not consider it auspicious to go against the people,
nor did they rely on it exclusively to decide matters.
Therefore, in the divination of the *Hóngfàn*,
great consensus is what is valued.
The *Shū* also says:
"I consult you, Great Tortoise,
but dare not know the fortune."
The *Shī* says:
"My tortoise is already weary
and does not tell me the plans."
From this perspective,
the nature of the milfoil and tortoise
perhaps changes according to the times or is simple and easy;
is it not based on sincerity?
Or is it that the world lacks the talent of Shǐ Sū,
and those who understand the spirits are few?
As for the Zhōu Scribe's divination for Jìng Zhòng
and Zhuāng Shū's divination for Mù Zǐ,
it can be said they were able to "explore the profound and search out the hidden,
to hook the deep and reach the distant."
Had Xiàn Gōng early accepted the words of Shǐ Sū
and had Mù Zǐ beforehand prepared for the warnings of Zhuāng Shū,
then the slanders of Lí Jī and Shù Niú
would also have had no way to enter,
and there would have been no calamity of destroying the state and endangering themselves.
The sages placed great importance on divination;
yet for matters without doubt,
they did not ask.
They were very reverent toward sacrifices;
yet for prayers not in accordance with ritual,
they did not perform them.
Therefore it is said:
"The sage does not trouble divination,"
and "revere the ghosts and spirits but keep them at a distance."
Ghosts and spirits have different qi and different concerns from humans;
unless there is a reason,
what can they do to us?
Therefore, Kǒngzǐ praised Chǔ Zhāo for not sacrificing to the River,
but detested the Jì clan for performing the lǚ sacrifice to Tài Shān.
Nowadays, common people are obsessed with divination
and sacrifice to spirits that are not their own;
is this not delusion!
There are also those who falsely link surnames to the Five Tones,
and establish the order of the five types of residences according to charms;
this is deceitful in the extreme!
In ancient times there was yīnyáng,
and after that the Five Elements.
The Five Emperors relied on the movement of qi
to give birth to the people;
after many long generations,
surnames and names were given to the people.
Names and styles
are simply to distinguish one from the masses and identify the person,
not to record the Five Tones or determine hardness and softness.
Now common people cannot trace their ancestral origins,
but instead want to use sounds and spoken words to determine the Five Elements;
no error is greater than this.
Now, fish dwell in water and live;
birds occupy nests and lay eggs.
Even if one does not trace back to their ultimate ancestors,
and only follows the harmony of phonetic categories,
if one calls a bird a "fish,"
can it be placed in the water?
If one calls a fish a "bird,"
can it roost in a tree?
This is an impossible thing.
If one names a foal a "calf,"
it will ultimately become a horse.
Therefore, for every surname that has a musical note,
it must follow what its original ancestor ruled.
Tàihào is the essence of Wood;
he ruled by succeeding Suì;
his descendants should all belong to the *jiǎo* note.
Shénnóng is the essence of Fire;
he ruled by succeeding Yínghuò;
his descendants should all belong to the *zhǐ* note.
Huángdì is the essence of Earth;
he ruled by succeeding Zhèn;
his descendants should all belong to the *gōng* note.
Shǎohào is the essence of Metal;
he ruled by succeeding Tàibái;
his descendants should all belong to the *shāng* note.
Zhuānxū is the essence of Water;
he ruled by succeeding Chén;
his descendants should all belong to the *yǔ* note.
Although titles change a hundred times,
the musical note and the Phase do not change.
Vulgar craftsmen also say:
"For the house of a family belonging to the *shāng* note,
it is suitable for the gate to face west."
This again is empty talk.
According to the Five Phases, one should go out riding upon what one overcomes,
and reside in its hidden depths to be peaceful and auspicious.
If a family of the *shāng* note faces east to enter,
entering from the east is conversely taken as Metal felling Wood,
and the spirits within the home will fight daily.
The Five Phases are all like this.
They also say:
"Houses have grades of *gōng* and *shāng*,
and years of the direct talismans."
Since this is so,
if one increases or decreases the number of gates upon it,
can one change its musical note and bypass the talisman?
Now, in a single residence,
people of the same surname clash,
some experiencing good luck and others bad;
in a single palace,
people of the same surname clash,
some being transferred and others dismissed;
in a single palace,
the days King Chéng and King Kāng resided there, it flourished,
but the days King Yōu and King Lì resided there, it declined.
Observing from this,
it is clear that good and bad luck, prosperity and decline, do not reside in the house.
As for the various gods and spirits like Tàisuì, Fēnglóng, Gōuchén, and the Tàiyīn Jiāngjūn,
these are the officials of Heaven;
they are not what common people should be concerned with.
Heaven has these spirits
to support the completion of *yīn* and *yáng* and to benefit all things,
just as human governance has governors, protectors, and magistrates.
If one faces them, why should they be angry?
If one turns away from them, why should they be resentful?
The way between the ruler and the people is close,
yet they should not blame each other;
how much more so for the spirits who are exceedingly noble
and follow different rituals from humans—
how can one expect anything from them?
Moreover, if you want people to avoid ghosts,
then roads would be untraversable
and homes would no longer be habitable.
This refers to worthy men and gentlemen who maintain upright hearts
and whose spirits are firm.
As for common petty people,
ugly concubines and maids,
the shallow, ignorant, and foolish,
once they are tainted by these ideas,
they frequently scatter their essence and lose their courage.
Now, if one does not follow where their sincerity leads,
but forces them into what they fear,
it only increases their illness.
How can we clarify that this is so?
That which makes a human a human
is not this eight-foot body,
but rather that they have a spirit.
When people die of terror,
it is not caused by an added disease,
nor by the consequence of human effort.
However, when it reaches the point of being irreparable,
it is because the essence and sincerity have left them.
Mèng Bèn could toy with a fierce tiger without being flustered,
but a baby-like person might be terrified by a mole cricket or an ant and cry out.
Now, if a learned man wants to force a weak and sick fool
to do what he cannot,
I fear that would not be entirely good.
The root of shifting customs and changing traditions
lies in opening their hearts and rectifying their spirits.
Nowadays, the people do not see the correct path in their lives,
but grow up amidst depravity, falsehood, and delusion;
their belief in these things
cannot be suddenly undone.
Only a true king can change them.
For all people, good or bad luck
is primarily determined by their conduct
and decided by fate.
Conduct is one's own quality;
fate is Heaven's regulation.
What lies within oneself
can certainly be worked upon;
what lies with Heaven
cannot be known.
Shamans, invocators, and prayers
are also aids,
but without virtue, they do not work.
Shamanic historians and invocators
are meant to interact with ghosts and gods to save one from minor matters;
but regarding the great mandate of life,
there is nothing they can do.
It is like common people petitioning an official;
it can resolve minor faults,
but cannot acquit one of a major crime.
Suppose there is a person here
who day and night neglects and insults the teachings of his ruler and father,
violates the prohibitions of the former kings,
does not restrain his own heart,
or think of correcting his faults for the better,
but instead hurriedly offers petitions to seek release and avoidance;
he will certainly not come close to success.
It is better to cultivate oneself,
be careful, fearful, and cautious,
and not violate the mandatory orders of superiors.
Therefore, Kǒngzǐ did not listen to Zǐlù,
but said, "Qiū's prayer has been for a long time."
The *Xiàojīng* says:
"In this way,
while alive, their parents are at peace with them;
and when sacrificed to, the ghosts enjoy it."
Observing from this,
if virtue and righteousness are not violated,
only then do the ghosts and gods enjoy the offerings;
when ghosts and gods receive enjoyment,
then blessings and prosperity flourish.
Therefore, the *Shī* says:
"Blessings descend in abundance,
blessings descend in great measure,
the majestic demeanor is orderly.
Having been drunk and satiated,
blessings and wealth return."
This says that when a person's virtue and righteousness are lush and beautiful,
the spirits find them sweet, enjoy them, and are satiated,
and thus repay them with blessings.
The Duke of Guó invited a spirit and quickly perished;
Zhào Yīng sacrificed to Heaven and was soon destroyed.
This is what is meant by the spirits not enjoying their sacrifices
and the people not attending to their duties.
Therefore, the History of Lǔ records:
"When a state is about to rise,
it listens to the people;
when it is about to perish,
it listens to the spirits."
King Zhāo of Chǔ did not perform a propitiation for the clouds,
Duke Jǐng of Sòng did not shift his fault,
Zǐchǎn kept Bì Zào at a distance,
Duke Wén of Zhū went against the divination of the historian;
these are all people who examined themselves and knew the Way,
cultivating themselves to wait for fate.
Yàn Píngzhòng had a saying:
"If prayers can bring benefit,
then curses can also bring harm."
Jì Liáng’s remonstrance to the Marquis of Suí,
and Gōng Zhī Qí’s persuasion of the Duke of Yú,
can be called understanding the way of Heaven and man,
and comprehending the distinction between spirits and the people.
Anomalies do not overcome virtue,
and evil does not conquer righteousness;
this is the constant law of Heaven.
Though there are occasional deviations,
a wise person upholds the correct path
and does not associate with wanton spirits.
What are called wanton spirits
are idle evil essences
and are not true divine spirits with official duties.
Spirits having these traits
are like humans who use deceitful words and feign fairness to make demands.
If one entices them,
they will come from afar without ceasing,
and in the end, there will surely be misfortune.
The same applies to ghosts and gods;
therefore Shēn Xū said:
"What people dread,
their energy flares up to attract it.
If a person has no flaw,
anomalies do not arise by themselves."
This means a person should not have many taboos;
many taboos lead to reckless fear,
which actually brings about anomalies and omens.
Moreover, humans have ranks and positions,
and ghosts and gods have high and low status.
Heaven, Earth, mountains, rivers, the Altars of Soil and Grain, the five sacrifices, and the various lords, ministers, and officials who have merit toward the people
are those whom the Son of Heaven and the feudal lords command to be sacrificed to.
As for what shamans and sorcerers call "solitary speech,"
which commoners hope for or fear—
the seven spirits such as Tǔgōng, Fēishī, Jiùmèi, Běijūn, Xiánjù, Dānglù, and Zhífú—
as well as the trivial and minor prohibitions regarding repairs among the populace,
these are fundamentally not things that the Heavenly King should dread.
In former times, the capital did not take precautions
regarding the prohibitions on construction and labor,
yet auspicious signs and omens still arrived,
and descendants flourished;
they could not surpass those who came before.
Furthermore, if a ruler fears his ministers,
or a superior seeks from an inferior,
then he will surely show weakness and invite contempt;
this is certainly not the way to invite blessings.
I have observed in the ancient records
that when a ruler cultivates himself and acts uprightly, and rewards and punishments are clear,
the state is well-governed and the people are at peace.
When the people are peaceful and happy,
Heaven is pleased and extends the ruler's years.
Thus the *Shū* says:
"The King, through the common people, receives the eternal mandate of Heaven."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"What Heaven assists is compliance;
what people assist is trustworthiness.
Practicing trustworthiness and being mindful of compliance,
and furthermore honoring the worthy—
because of this, Heaven blesses them,
and there is good fortune with no disadvantage."
This is the root of warding off calamities and bringing about blessings and goodness.
The *Shī* says: "Heaven produced the teeming masses;
where there are things, there are laws."
Therefore, a person's body, shape, and appearance all have their corresponding types;
bone structure, forehead, and flesh each have their assigned parts
to manifest the span of their life
and display the signs of nobility or lowliness.
In the body of a single person,
the qi of the Five Elements and the Eight Trigrams are complete.
Thus Shī Kuàng said, "A red complexion does not lead to longevity,"
for the family of Fire is easily extinguished.
The "Shuō Guà" of the *Yì* says:
"*Xùn* refers to people with many white eyes."
Those whose physiognomy shows "four whites" will die by the sword,
as this is like Metal striking Wood.
The *Jīng* says:
"Close at hand, take it from the body;
far away, take it from things."
"The sages saw the utmost profundities of the world,
