and modeled them upon shapes and forms,
symbolizing what is appropriate for things."
This is also what worthy men observe,
recording the past to know the future,
and establishing them as constitutional rules.
The method of physiognomy
is sometimes in the facial features,
sometimes in the hands and feet,
sometimes in the gait,
or sometimes in the voice.
The face should be broad, level, moist, and lustrous;
the hands and feet should be deep-lined, fine, clear, and straight;
the gait should be stable and steady, like the earth carrying things;
the voice should be gentle and centered like the *zhōnggōng* note.
The head, face, hands, and feet,
the body shape, bones, and joints
should all match and be proportional to each other.
These are the general essentials.
Bone structure is the outward sign of emolument and status;
complexion is the omen of good or bad fortune;
the placement of features represents the timing in years;
and virtuous conduct is what attracts all three.
Heaven bestows nature and fate decisively.
Signs have clarity or subtlety;
colors have depth or lightness;
conduct has thickness or thinness;
and fate has its departures and arrivals.
Therefore, the timing of auspicious or inauspicious events,
and the success or failure of rank and emolument,
are not always certain.
Unless one is keen, wise, and intelligent,
and applies the mind with precision,
who can hit the mark?
Formerly, when Nèishǐ Shūfú passed through Lǔ,
Gōngfù Áo heard that he was capable of physiognomy
and presented his two sons to him.
Shūfú said:
"Gǔ will provide for you;
Nán will bury you.
Gǔ has a full lower face;
he will surely have descendants in Lǔ."
When Mùbó grew old,
Wénbó provided for his needs;
when he died,
Huìshǔ presided over the mourning.
Lǔ eventually established Xiànzǐ
to continue the line of the Mèng clan.
When Wángsūn Shuō assessed Qiáo Rú,
Zǐshàng was wary of Shāng Chén,
Zǐwén worried over Yuè Jiāo,
Shūjī disliked Shí Wǒ,
Dān Xiāng Gōng observed Duke Lì of Jìn,
Zǐgòng observed Zhū and Lǔ,
Zāng Wén listened to Yù Shuō,
and Chén Xián saw Zhāng—
worthy men and accomplished scholars
observe with a virtuous heart,
and they never fail to hit the mark.
When Táng Jǔ read the features of Lǐ Duì and Cài Zé,
or Xǔ Fù read those of Dèng Tōng and the Marquis of Tiáo,
even if the Master of Fate distributed emoluments
and followed their recorded deeds,
it could not surpass their predictions.
Nevertheless,
that humans have bone structures
is like the myriad things having categories
and timber having its constant suitability.
Skilled craftsmen follow the forms,
and each has what they are assigned:
the curved are suitable for wheels,
the straight are suitable for carriage boxes,
sandalwood is suitable for spokes,
and elm is suitable for hubs.
This is the correct method and general principle.
If the material exists
but the craftsman does not treat it as timber,
what can be done?
Therefore, all physiognomists
can predict the ultimate potential,
but they cannot make it necessarily arrive.
Regarding the ten types of soil,
though rich loam is fertile,
if it is not plowed, there will be no harvest.
As for a horse of a thousand *lǐ*,
though its bone structure is complete,
if it is not whipped, it will not arrive.
If a ceremonial vessel is not carved,
it does not become a finished utensil;
if a scholar does not serve in office,
he does not achieve a position.
In cases like these,
Heaven and Earth cannot make them noble or lowly,
and ghosts and gods cannot make them poor or rich.
Some are descendants of kings and dukes,
serving in office until old age,
yet they do not reach prosperity.
Some are commoners or lowly servants,
who suddenly leap upward
and reach the heights of rank and position.
This is receiving nature and fate from Heaven,
which is as it must be.
The *Shī* says, "Heaven is hard to rely upon";
the quality of nature and fate
and the attraction of virtuous conduct
are given and received in complex interlocking ways,
and they are unchanging.
However, the essential points
take bone structure as primary
and complexion as the manifestation.
The appearance of the five colors
has its times of flourishing and declining.
The wise person sees auspicious omens
and cultivates goodness to welcome them;
when there are signs of worry,
they examine their conduct and correct their faults.
The foolish person is contrary and perverse
and does not reflect upon themselves;
even if auspicious signs and features appear,
blessings turn into disasters.
Alas, the gentleman!
Can he not be reverent?
Regarding dreams in general:
there are direct dreams,
symbolic dreams,
concentrated dreams,
associative dreams,
status-based dreams,
atmospheric dreams,
seasonal dreams,
inverse dreams,
illness-based dreams,
and dispositional dreams.
In the past, when Wǔ Wáng's
consort Yì Jiāng was pregnant with Tài Shū,
she dreamed that the Dì said to her:
"I name your son Yú,
and will give him Táng."
When he was born,
his palm had the character 'Yú',
so they used it as his name.
When Chéng Wáng destroyed Táng,
he subsequently enfeoffed him there.
This is called a direct-response dream.
The Shī says:
"Visions of brown bears and grizzly bears
are omens of sons;
visions of cobras and snakes
are omens of daughters."
"Seeing schools of fish
portends a bountiful year;
seeing banners and streamers
portends a thriving family."
This is called a symbolic dream.
Kǒng Zǐ was born in a chaotic age;
by day he thought of the virtue of Zhōu Gōng,
and by night he dreamed of him.
This is called a dream of concentrated intent.
When a person has something on their mind,
they dream of its arrival;
when they have worries, they dream of the matter.
This is called a dream of remembered thoughts.
In current affairs,
if a noble person dreams of it, it is an omen;
if a lowly person dreams of it, it is a strange portent;
if a gentleman dreams of it, it is an honor;
if a petty man dreams of it, it is a disgrace.
This is called a dream of human status.
Jìn Wén Gōng, at the Battle of Chéng Pú,
dreamed that Chǔ Zǐ pinned him down and sucked out his brains;
this was very ominous.
When they fought,
he achieved a great victory.
This is called an extreme-inverse dream.
Dreams of overcast rain
make one feel oppressed and deluded;
dreams of sun and drought
make one feel scattered and confused;
dreams of great cold
make one feel resentful and sorrowful;
dreams of great winds
make one feel drifting and unsettled.
This is called a dream of environmental influence.
Spring dreams relate to growth,
summer dreams relate to brightness,
and autumn and winter dreams relate to ripening and storage.
This is called a dream responding to the seasons.
Yīn illnesses lead to dreams of cold,
Yáng illnesses lead to dreams of heat,
internal illnesses lead to dreams of chaos,
and external illnesses lead to dreams of eruptions;
dreams of various diseases
either disperse or gather.
This is called a dream of physical qi.
The sentiments and hearts of people
have different likes and dislikes;
what is auspicious for one
may be inauspicious for another.
Each must observe for themselves,
regularly divining based on what they follow.
This is called a dream of individual disposition.
Thus, those where there is a prior discrepancy
are called concentrated;
when one thinks of something by day
and dreams of the matter by night,
sometimes auspicious and sometimes inauspicious,
with good and evil being unreliable,
these are called associative;
nobility and lowliness, wisdom and folly,
men and women, old and young,
these are called status-based;
wind, rain, cold, and heat are called atmospheric;
the flourishing and supporting phases of the Five Elements are called seasonal;
the peak of Yīn becoming auspicious
and the peak of Yáng becoming inauspicious
are called inverse;
observing what one suffers from
and examining what one dreams
are called illness-based;
the focus of the heart's likes and dislikes
being verified by events
is called dispositional.
Generally, these ten
are the broad outline for interpreting dreams.
But those who determine good or ill fortune often find things to be reversed;
what is the reason for this?
Is it perhaps because being awake is Yáng
and being asleep is Yīn,
and the functions of Yīn and Yáng are naturally opposite?
This also refers to cases that are not extreme.
Suppose one dreams of an auspicious event and feels great joy in one's heart,
arising from the focus of the heart,
then it is truly auspicious.
If one dreams of an inauspicious event and feels great fear or sorrow,
arising from the focus of the heart,
then it is truly evil.
As for dreaming of death or injury in autumn or winter,
it is auspicious because it accords with the season.
Nevertheless,
wealth can be a great harm,
and it is better not to have dreamed at all.
In observing the general nature of dreams:
images that are clean and beautiful,
strong and robust in appearance,
bamboo and trees lush and fine,
palaces and implements newly made,
square and open,
bright and warm,
and signs of rising and prospering are all auspicious and joyful,
plans will be followed and tasks completed.
All things foul and rotten,
withered and obscured by mist,
leaning and crooked,
mutilated and uneasy,
blocked and dark,
and signs of falling and declining are all ominous;
plans will not be followed,
and undertakings will not succeed.
Strange portents and bizarre events,
and hateful or loathsome things all lead to worry.
Drawings and sculpted forms,
carvings that are not real,
and empty earthenware vessels,
all represent being deceived.
Singers, actors, and dancers,
and signs of children's play,
all represent laughter and joy.
These are the main categories.
Dreams may be very clear but have no interpretation,
or very subtle but have a response;
why is this?
Answer:
What is originally called a dream
is a term for being unable to clearly observe,
and it is a name used when one is confused and muddled.
Therefore, one should not rely on them exclusively to decide matters.
When people plan matters face-to-face
and set out to do them,
there are still those that fail;
how much more so for fleeting and confused dreams,
can they be certain?
Only when there is a movement of deep sincerity and a resonance from spirits,
when there is something the divine spirits report,
only then is there an interpretation.
Therefore, the extraordinary dreams of a gentleman
are not merely delusions;
there must be a reason for them.
The extraordinary dreams of a petty man
are not merely coincidences;
sometimes they contain omens.
Thus, Wǔ Dīng dreamed of finding a sage and obtained Fù Yuè;
Èr Shì dreamed of a white tiger and lost his fief.
As for extraordinary dreams,
most have a cause and few are without meaning.
Now, in the dreams of a single sleep,
things may transform repeatedly
and a hundred objects appear in succession.
If the dreamer cannot thoroughly describe them,
then the diviner's predictions may not hit the mark.
This is not the fault of the divination,
but rather the error of the dreamer.
Or perhaps the dream is related clearly,
but the interpreter cannot connect similar categories or observe broadly,
so the outcomes of good or ill are not verified.
This is not the falseness of the books,
but the error of the interpreter.
Therefore, the difficulty in interpreting dreams
lies in the difficulty of reading the books.
To interpret a dream, one must be careful with its changes and causes,
examine its signs and omens,
internally investigate the emotions and intentions,
and externally examine the *wáng xiàng*,
then the tallies of good and bad fortune
and the effects of virtue and vice
can almost be seen.
Furthermore, in the way of humanity, those who see an auspicious sign and cultivate their virtue
will surely see their fortune fulfilled;
those who see an auspicious sign but become licentious and unrestrained
will find their fortune turned to calamity.
Those who see a baleful omen and are arrogant or contemptuous
will surely see the calamity fulfilled;
those who see a baleful omen and are cautious and fearful
will find the calamity turned to fortune.
Thus, when Dà Sì had an auspicious dream,
Wén Wáng did not dare to simply enjoy the good luck.
He offered sacrifices to the various spirits
and then divined in the Míng Táng,
bowing before the auspicious dream.
He practiced self-reflection and caution,
greeting joy as if it were sorrow,
and was therefore able to fulfill the good fortune and possess the world.
When Guó Gōng dreamed that Rù Shōu bestowed land upon him,
he considered it auspicious.
He imprisoned Shǐ Yín
and ordered the state to congratulate him on the dream.
He heard of a cause for worry but rejoiced,
and was therefore able to fulfill the misfortune and bring about the destruction of his fief.
The *Yì* says:
"Make them know fear,
and make them clear about troubles and their causes."
Whenever there is a strange dream that moves the heart,
or signs of fortune and misfortune in others,
or the appearance of their complexions,
regardless of whether it is good or bad,
one should always be fearful and practice self-reflection,
meeting it with virtue.
Then one will encounter good fortune,
and "Heaven's favor will last forever."
Gēng Zǐ asked Qiánfū:
"The virtues of Yáo and Shùn
cannot both be beautiful;
is it truly like Hán Zǐ’s story of the spear and the shield?"
Qiánfū said:
"This is to not understand the challenge and not understand categories.
Now, the shield is the *fá*;
its nature is to be beneficial.
The spear is the *gē*;
its nature is to be harmful.
Thus the spear is the transgressor
and the shield is the prohibition.
That they cannot both flourish
is indeed their nature.
As for Yáo and Shùn in relation to each other,
they are people,
not spears and shields.
Their Way is the same benevolence,
and they do not harm each other.
How could Shùn and the shield fail to both be firm?
How could Yáo and the shield fail to both be worthy?
Furthermore, the virtues of Yáo and Shùn
are like a pair of candles casting light into a dark room;
the first candle already illuminates it entirely,
and when the second candle enters, it becomes even brighter.
This is not because the first candle was dim and the second was bright,
but because the two followed each other to create a great light.
The two sages joined their virtues to achieve the merit of Great Peace.
Therefore, the movement of the Dà Péng
is not due to the lightness of a single feather;
the speed of the Qí Jì
is not due to the strength of a single foot.
Many excellences join their virtues
to accumulate and spread endlessly.
That Yáo and Shùn were both beautiful
is indeed the model."
Bó Shū said:
"You are mistaken.
Hán Fēi took the spear and shield as a metaphor
because he wished to borrow their mutual exclusivity
to challenge the impossibility of Yáo and Shùn both being praised.
To discuss their inherent nature as benevolent or transgressing—
does that not miss the point of the metaphor?"
Qiánfū said:
"Metaphors
arise because direct speech is not clear,
so one borrows the 'yes' or 'no' of objects to illuminate it.
That objects have a 'yes' or 'no'
is not because of their appearance,
but must be because of their truth.
Now you take the nature of the literal words as the metaphor
and wish for me to abandon the essence;
I am perplexed by this.
Moreover, I have heard that answering with Yáng when asked about Yīn
is called 'forced speech';
arguing West when challenged about East
is called 'forced difficulty.'
If you wish to be certain of yourself, you should reflect on it beforehand,
then seek the answer,
and not just be stubborn."
Gēng Zǐ said:
"Zhōu Gōng knew the evil of Guǎn and Cài,
yet he let them assist Wǔ Gēng
so they could spread their poison,
and then he executed them.
How is that benevolent?
If he did not know,
how is he a sage?
Between these two faults,
he must be in one of them."
Qiánfū said:
"The *Shū* says the two brothers supported Gēng Zǐ’s father in rebellion.
But do we know their kind?
Or were they contrary?
Furthermore, Heaven knew the evil of Jié yet made him the Sovereign of Xià;
it knew the evil of Zhòu yet made him the King of Yīn,
letting them oppress the two nations,
harm the people below,
spread much poison,
and destroy themselves.
Can Heaven also be called malevolent or ignorant?"
Gēng Zǐ said:
"That is not so.
Jié and Zhòu
had no kinship with Heaven,
so Heaven employed them without worry
and executed them without grief.
But Guǎn and Cài in relation to Zhōu Gōng
had the kinship of brothers
and the affection of flesh and blood.
To employ them without measuring their ability
and to charge them with tasks they could not handle—
therefore I say it is different from the relation between Jié, Zhòu, and Heaven."
Qiánfū said:
"August Heaven has no favorites.
Emperors and kings who succeed to the throne
serve Heaven as a father.
The King acts as the son,
therefore he serves Heaven as a father.
Among all the people within the borders,
'none are not the King’s subjects.'
If they must be executed,
the King's law is public.
There is no bias or partiality;
kin and stranger are treated the same.
'Sacrificing kinship for the greater righteousness'
is the duty to honor the King.
That Zhōu Gōng’s virtue reached the height of Heaven was because of this.
Beyond this point,
no one can know."
Qín Zǐ asked Qiánfū:
"Plowing and sowing are the root of life;
learning and inquiry are the branches of one's career.
Lǎo Dān had a saying:
'The great man stays with the solid
and does not dwell in the superficial.'
But Kǒng Zǐ said:
'In plowing,
hunger is found therein;
in learning,
emolument is found therein.'
I venture to ask: if we now made all the people in the world
abandon their hoes and plows to flock to schools together,
what would it be like?"
Qiánfū said:
"An excellent question!
The noble person labors with the mind,
and the small person labors with physical strength.
Therefore, what Kǒngzǐ praised
refers only to the noble person.
Now, from what the eyes see,
plowing is the root of food.
By tracing the Way with the mind,
learning is further the root of plowing.
The *Yì* says:
'The Way that establishes Heaven is called Yīn and Yáng;
the Way that establishes Earth is called soft and hard;
the Way that establishes Man is called benevolence and righteousness.'
To act contrary to virtue is to cause disaster."
Qiánfū said:
"Alas!
Have you not examined this?
Let me tell you.
As for the noble person,
their worthiness makes them fit to rule a state, and their virtue makes them fit to treat the people as their children.
Those fit to occupy such a position
are only people of benevolence and righteousness.
Therefore, those possessing benevolence and righteousness
are called noble persons.
In the past, Xúnzǐ said:
'Benevolence is to love others;
because one loves others,
one cannot bear to see them in danger.
Righteousness is to gather people;
because one gathers people,
one cannot bear to see them in chaos.'
For this reason, the noble person offers counsel and regulations day and night,
remaining upright and untiring,
because they worry about the danger and downfall of the ruler
and grieve over the chaos and displacement of the people.
Thus, worthy people and noble persons
extend their hearts of benevolence and righteousness;
they love their ruler as they would their parents,
and they love the people living in the world as they would their children and younger brothers.
When parents are about to face the peril of falling,
or when children and brothers are about to suffer the disaster of drowning,
how could one remain silent?
This is why 'the benevolent must possess courage,'
and a person of virtue must possess righteousness.
"Furthermore, when an entire country is in complete chaos,
no one can find a safe place for themselves.
The *Shī* says:
'None are willing to think of the chaos,
yet who does not have parents?'
This means that all will be harmed,
but those with parents will feel a deeper anxiety.
For this reason, worthy people and noble persons
not only worry about the people
but also act for their own sake.
When the roof covers the top,
the moisture spreads below.
If the ridgepole breaks and the rafters collapse,
there is fear of being crushed.
Therefore, when a great house is about to tilt and fall,
the people below do not wait for orders
but each compete to prop it up.
The benevolent person protects the homes of others
while also acting for themselves.
The *Yì* says:
'When the king is enlightened,
all together receive his blessings.'
This is why the woman in the side chamber leaned against the wall and sighed,
and the maiden of Chǔ raised a banner to stir the king.
Can the grace of benevolence and kindness,
or the feelings of loyalty and love,
ever be stopped?"
The saying goes:
"People should be old acquaintances,
but vessels should be new.
Brothers grow distant through the generations,
but friends grow closer through the generations."
This is the principle of social interaction
and the nature of human sentiment.
Today, however, it is not so;
many think of the distant and forget the near,
turning their backs on the old and turning toward the new.
Some grow more distant as years pass;
some abandon each other halfway.
They ignore the canons and warnings of former sages
and betray long-standing oaths.
What is the reason for this?
If one withdraws and examines it,
it can be known.
Circumstances have constant tendencies,
and principles have inherent certainties.
When there is wealth and rank, people compete to attach themselves to it;
this is the constant tendency of circumstances.
When there is poverty and low status, people compete to leave it;
this is the inherent certainty of principles.
As for those who associate with the wealthy and noble,
above, there is the utility of praise and reputation;
below, there is the benefit of goods and wealth.
As for those who associate with the poor and lowly,
at the most, there is the expense of providing relief and loans;
at the least, there is the loss from borrowing.
Now, even if an official combines the evils of Jié and Zhí,
if he passes by a scholar with a team of four horses,
the scholar still considers it an honor and turns to him;
how much more so if he actually provides benefits?
Even if a scholar in retirement possesses the worthiness of Yán and Mǐn,
if he wears coarse cloth and comes to one's gate,
people still consider it a disgrace and fear he will return;
how much more so if he actually causes loss?
Thus, the wealthy and noble easily find what is appropriate,
while the poor and lowly find it difficult to be suitable.
If they wear fine clothes, it is called extravagance and presumption;
if they wear bad clothes, it is called distress and hardship.
Walking slowly is called hunger and starvation;
walking quickly is called fleeing from responsibility.
Not waiting is called arrogance and rudeness;
coming frequently is called seeking food.
Arriving empty-handed is thought to show no sincerity;
bringing a gift is thought to be a desire for a loan.
Being respectful and humble is thought to be worthlessness;
being bold and expressive is thought to be frustration.
Such is the restraint and thinness of the scholar in retirement,
and the bitterness and cruelty of poverty and low status.
Occupying a lowly position,
harboring the deep sorrow of the "Běimén" poem,
one is blamed at home by wife and children
and mocked abroad by scholars and officials.
At auspicious gatherings, one cannot follow the rites;
at farewell banquets, one cannot keep up with the crowd.
One's goods and wealth are insufficient to cement friendships;
one's power and influence are insufficient to rely on in emergencies.
Despite long-standing joyous association,
when affection and friendship are neglected and not maintained,
people will naturally become distant for no reason.
As the distance grows, the lowly person feels more self-reproach and withdraws daily,
while the noble person becomes more occupied with his clique and forgets him.
For a lowly person who is increasingly distant
to lie low in the downstream
and look toward the noble person who daily forgets them—
this is what caused the inner devastation in the poem "Gǔfēng"
and why Jiè Tuī fled into the deep mountains.
Associations involving profit bring closeness;
associations involving harm bring distance.
Therefore, if long-standing oaths are abandoned,
it must be because one is of no use.
If an association gradually becomes close,
it must be because it is beneficial.
In the interactions of ordinary people,
profit gives rise to closeness;
accumulated closeness gives rise to affection;
accumulated affection gives rise to approval;
accumulated approval gives rise to the perception of worthiness.
If one's feelings deem another worthy,
then one unconsciously feels close to them in heart
and praises them with the mouth.
Lack of profit gives rise to distance;
accumulated distance gives rise to resentment;
accumulated resentment gives rise to disapproval;
accumulated disapproval gives rise to the perception of evil.
If one's feelings deem another evil,
then one unconsciously excludes them in heart
and slanders them with the mouth.
Therefore, even if wealth and rank are new,
the circumstances daily bring closeness;
even if poverty and low status are old,
the circumstances daily bring distance.
This is why the scholar in retirement cannot compete with the official.
The rulers of the world do not examine the origins of friendships and associations
but recklessly believe the words of noble ministers.
This is why pure scholars live alone in obscurity,
and treacherous heroes form cliques and soar high.
In the past, the retainers of the Lord of Wèiqí
flowed toward the Marquis of Wǔ'ān;
the officers of the Marquis of Chángpíng
moved to the Marquis of Guànjūn;
as for Lián Pō and Zhái Gōng,
their gates were sometimes filled and sometimes empty.
Now, even with the worthiness of these four gentlemen
and the long-standing favor of their former nobility,
their retainers still acted in this way;
how much more so then for those born into poverty and low status?
Only those with the spirit of ancient heroes
and scholars of will and righteousness
would not act thus.
When gratitude is bound,
it is never loosened throughout their lives;
when the heart values something,
it becomes even more sincere despite low status.
The *Shī* says:
"The virtuous gentleman,
his demeanor is consistent,
and his heart is as if bound."
Therefore, only when the year turns cold do we know that the pine and cypress are the last to wither;
only in times of distress do we know a person’s steadfastness.
Hóu Yíng and Yù Ràng
sacrificed themselves to repay favors;
Zhuān Zhū and Jīng Kē
risked their lives to be of service.
Thus, death can be embraced;
it is the way one handles it that is difficult.
Páng Xūn and Bó Diāo,
once they were accepted,
they immediately acted with righteous repayment;
how much more so for those with long-standing ties?
Thus, Zōu Yáng stated:
"The dog of Jié can be made to bark at Yáo;
the retainer of Zhí can be made to stab Xǔ Yóu."
How could these be empty words?
Vulgar men are shallow and short-sighted,
urgent for immediate gain;
seeing profit in going, they arrive first;
seeing no use, they lag behind.
Thus, those who seek quick advancement
compete to push themselves upward and have no time to attend to those below;
they struggle to chase those in front and have no leisure to care for those behind.
Therefore, Hán Ānguó could give Tián Fén five hundred pieces of gold,
yet could not relieve a single person in need;
Zhái Fāngjìn praised Chúnyú Zhǎng,
yet could not recommend a single scholar.
Now, Ānguó and Fāngjìn
were loyal and good men of former times,
and yet they were like this;
how much more so for the low-level officials at the end of their paths?
This is why treacherous heroes pursue factional advancement,
and why reclusive scholars become increasingly obscured.
If not for an enlightened and sagely ruler,
who could observe and examine this?
Furthermore, the birth of resentment and hatred
is like two people meeting.
If they face each other
with mutual affection,
pushing their intentions to the limit,
with absolute sincerity reflecting each other,
piercing the heart and reaching the marrow,
and their love and joy are at their peak,
they would lightly die for one another;
thus, Hóu Shēng and Yù Zǐ slit their throats without regret.
If they turn their backs on each other,
their feelings becoming contradictory,
pushing their intentions to the limit,
they separate and gallop away,
reaching the far east and the far west,
their hearts still unresolved;
thus, Chén Yú and Zhāng Ěr in their old age completely destroyed each other without feeling pain.
From this perspective,
the principle of social interaction
is a matter of great emotion.
It is not only so for friends;
it is also like this for ruler and subject, or husband and wife.
When they are in joy,
even father and son cannot come between them;
when they are at odds,
even enemies cannot surpass their resentment.
Therefore, the sage is always cautious of small beginnings to solidify the end.
Riches and honor are not necessarily to be valued;
poverty and low status are not necessarily to be despised.
Human hearts have different likes;
their capacities differ by ten thousand or a hundred million.
Xǔ Yóu declined the imperial throne,
while vulgar men fight over a county office;
Mèng Kē refused a salary of ten thousand *zhōng*,
while a petty man is greedy for a *shēng* of food.
Thus it is said:
Quails and small birds travel in flocks,
without rest all day long;
they rise in confusion and gather together,
never leaving the wormwood and reeds.
The wild swan flies high,
separating from its mate and departing,
traveling thousands and tens of thousands of miles,
with its will set upon the marshes and ponds.
The Luan and Phoenix soar above the Huánglì mountains,
wandering in the midst of the Great Purity;
drifting with the auspicious winds,
sometimes rising or falling with composure,
yet their desires are still not satisfied;
they utter long cries,
kicking and calling while flapping their wings,
transcending the crimson clouds,
approaching the North Star,
breathing in the sun's dew,
going without food for ten days,
yet their minds are still as if unsatisfied.
These three types have different pursuits,
and each is at peace with what they do.
Therefore, Bó Yí gathered ferns and felt no regret;
Cháo Fù lived in a tree by his own wish.
From this perspective,
the will and capacity of a scholar
are indeed difficult to measure.
All gentlemen
should not use wealth and honor to be arrogant toward those in poverty and low status,
thinking that the poor and lowly must surely submit to them.
The *Shī* says:
"Virtue is as light as a feather,
yet few among the people can lift it."
There are four great difficulties in the world
which no one is able to practice:
the first is empathy,
the second is fairness,
the third is respect,
and the fourth is steadfastness.
Now, empathy is the root of benevolence;
fairness is the root of righteousness;
respect is the root of ritual propriety;
steadfastness is the root of trustworthiness.
When the four roots are established together,
the four conducts are then complete;
when the four conducts coexist,
this is called a true worthy.
If the four roots are not established,
the four conducts will not be formed;
if not one of the four conducts exists,
this is called a petty man.
What is called empathy
is for a gentleman
to consider others as he considers himself,
acting with a friendly voice.
Therefore, if a ruler does not open his absolute sincerity to show the worthy and loyal,
the worthy and loyal will have no way to reach him.
The *Yì* says:
"The King is enlightened,
and all together receive his blessings."
Thus, a loyal minister must wait for an enlightened ruler to manifest his integrity;
a good official must have a discerning master to achieve his merit.
If the ruler is not enlightened,
then the high ministers will conceal those below and suppress the loyal;
furthermore, the various officials will abandon the law and flatter the noble.
Now, loyal words are that which brings peace;
if they are not presented, there will surely be danger.
Laws and prohibitions are that which brings order;
if they are not upheld, there will surely be chaos.
Whether loyalty is presented or not,
whether the law is upheld or not,
the handle of these matters lies entirely with the ruler;
it is not something within the power of the subjects.
Therefore, the sage seeks it within himself
and does not blame those below.
For anyone who is a superior,
if the methods of law are clear and rewards and punishments are certain,
even without speaking, order will naturally prevail by the force of circumstance.
They value trade twofold
to elevate one another.
If one is able to attain wealth and honor,
even if they accumulate craftiness and evil,
people will compete to praise them,
and in the end, they will not be criticized;
if one stays in poverty and low status,
even if they are respectful and cautious, it is merely considered incompetence,
and in the end, they will not be affirmed.
This is how popular customs gradually decline,
and why ritual propriety and righteousness wither away.
There are three things in this world that are cause for distress.
What are these three?
It is said:
emotions are actually shallow while words claim depth;
intentions are actually negligent while writing feigns concern;
the heart has no intent to visit, yet outwardly a date is strictly promised.
If one does not believe them, one fears losing a worthy person;
if one believes them, one is misled.
This is the most loathsome thing in the worldly society.
Therefore, Kǒngzǐ disliked those whose words exceeded their deeds,
and the Shī lamented, "Easy and boastful words
come from the mouth.
Artful speech like a reed organ flute,
oh, the thickness of the face!"
In the social interactions of today's world,
people seek deep and solid bonds before they have observed and understood one another.
They bare their hearts and clasp wrists,
beat their chests and swear oaths,
merely wishing to protect each other in discussions;
but on the day they part ways,
after they have attained their goals,
they abandon and forget each other.
Some receive the grace and virtue of others,
initially being assisted or saved,
yet when they are unable to promote or elevate their benefactor,
they then defame them,
creating flaws and grievances,
clearly stating, "I spared no effort;
it's just that the person themselves was impossible."
The Shī says,
"Knowing I am like this,
it would be better never to have been born."
Joining first and then clashing,
having a beginning but no end—
it is not as good as never having had the intent to begin with,
rather than forcing oneself to swear oaths.
"When superior men frequently make covenants,
disorder is thereby prolonged."
The way of the great person
is to be universal and not partisan;
through subtle words they affect each other,
fitting together like matching tallies—
so what use is there for a covenant?
Kǒngzǐ was simple and sincere,
appearing as if he were unable to speak;
it is also said that his "courteous and frank speech,
was only out of caution."
A scholar values having refined words
but also hates being loquacious.
Therefore it is said:
"Only when refinement and substance are balanced
does one become a Jūnzǐ."
Compared to being unfaithful,
being firm, resolute, simple, and slow of speech
is closer to Rén.
Alas, how sad!
Generally, the people of today
have square words but round actions;
their mouths are upright but their hearts are wicked;
their deeds are inconsistent with their words,
and their hearts contradict their mouths.
When discussing antiquity, they know to praise Yí, Qí, Yuán, and Yán;
when talking about the present, they must focus on official ranks and positions.
In empty talk, they know to regard virtue and righteousness as worthy;
in recommendations, they must put clan prestige and seniority first.
Even if a commoner practices the conduct of Yán and Mǐn,
possesses a nature of diligent humility,
holds the talent of Yī and Lǚ,
and cherishes the way to save the people,
their not being supported by this world
is also already clear!
A saying goes:
"People should be old,
while vessels should be new.
Brothers grow distant over generations,
while friends grow closer over generations."
This is the principle of social interaction
and human sentiment.
Nowadays, it is not so;
many think of those far away and forget those near,
turning their backs on the old and facing the new;
some grow more distant over many years;
some abandon each other halfway,
ignoring the canons and warnings of former sages
and betraying the oaths of long-standing agreements.
What is the reason for this?
If one steps back and reflects on it,
one can understand.
Circumstances have their constant trends,
and principles have their inherent necessities.
When there is wealth and status, people compete to attach themselves to it;
this is the constant trend of circumstances;
when there is poverty and low status, people compete to leave it;
this is the inherent necessity of the principle.
Those who associate with the rich and noble
find use in being recommended above
and benefit from goods and wealth below.
Those who associate with the poor and lowly
find the great expense of providing relief and loans,
and the small loss of borrowing and lending.
Now, even if an official combines the evils of Jié and Zhí,
if they pass by a scholar with a team of four horses,
the scholar would still consider it an honor and turn toward them—
how much more so if they are actually beneficial?
Even if a commoner contains the worthiness of Yán and Mǐn,
if they visit a door wearing coarse hemp,
people will still consider it a disgrace and fear they will come again—
how much more so if they are actually a burden?
Therefore, wealth and status easily find appropriateness,
while poverty and lowliness find it hard to be suitable.
Good clothing is called extravagance and arrogance;
poor clothing is called poverty and distress;
walking slowly is called being hungry and starved;
walking quickly is called escaping responsibility;
not waiting is called being arrogant and rude;
coming frequently is called seeking food;
visiting empty-handed is seen as having no purpose;
presenting a gift is seen as wanting a loan;
being respectful and humble is seen as being unworthy;
being firm and expressive is seen as lacking virtue.
This is the constraints and thinness of a commoner's life,
the harsh suffering of poverty and low status.
One who dwells in a lowly position
harbors the deep sorrow of Běimén;
inside, they are blamed by wife and children,
and outside, they suffer the ridicule of scholars and officials.
At grand gatherings, they cannot follow the etiquette;
at farewell banquets, they cannot keep up with the crowd.
Their goods and wealth are insufficient to foster goodwill,
and their power and influence are insufficient to rely upon in times of urgency.
Even in long-standing joyful friendships,
if sentiments and bonds are neglected and not maintained,
then people will naturally become abandoned and distant for no other reason.
As they gradually grow distant, the lowly person becomes increasingly self-conscious and retreats day by day,
while the noble person becomes increasingly occupied with their own faction and forgets them.
For a lowly person who has become increasingly distant,
lying low in the lower reaches,
to gaze toward a noble person who forgets them day by day—
this is why Gǔfēng expresses internal heartbreak,
and why Jiè Tuī fled into the deep mountains.
Social interactions based on benefit lead to mutual closeness,
while those based on harm lead to mutual distance.
Therefore, those where long oaths are abandoned
must be of no use.
Those where interactions gradually become closer
must be beneficial.
In the interactions of worldly people,
where there is benefit, closeness arises;
accumulated closeness produces affection;
accumulated affection produces approval;
accumulated approval leads to regarding the person as worthy.
If the feelings regard them as worthy,
then unconsciously the heart becomes close to them
and the mouth praises them.
Where there is no benefit, distance arises;
accumulated distance produces resentment;
accumulated resentment produces disapproval;
accumulated disapproval leads to regarding the person as bad.
If the feelings regard them as bad,
then unconsciously the heart excludes them
and the mouth defames them.
Therefore, although wealth and status may be new,
the situation makes them closer day by day;
although poverty and lowliness may be old,
the situation makes them more distant day by day.
This is why a commoner cannot compete with an official.
The rulers of the world do not examine how friendships and associations are formed
and carelessly believe the words of noble ministers;
this is why pure scholars live in solitary obscurity,
and treacherous men form factions and flourish.
In the past, the retainers of Wèiqí
drifted to Wǔ'ān;
the officials of Chángpíng
moved to Guànjūn;
Lián Pō and Zhái Gōng
were at times crowded and at times deserted.
If even with the worthiness of these four lords,
and relying on the long-standing favors of their established nobility,
retainers still acted thus,
then how much more so for those born into poverty and low station?
Only those with the spirit of ancient heroes
and men of will and righteousness
would not act in this manner.
Where kindness is bound,
it will never be released throughout one’s life;
where the heart cherishes someone,
that devotion grows deeper even when they are in low station.
The *Shī* says:
"The virtuous gentleman,
his demeanor is consistent,
and his heart is as if firmly bound."
Therefore, only after the cold of the year arrives do we know that the pine and cypress are the last to wither;
only when the world is in hardship do we know a person’s steadfastness.
Hóu Yíng and Yù Ràng
gave up their lives to repay kindness;
Zhuān Zhū and Jīng Kē
risked their lives to be of service.
Thus, death can be accomplished;
it is the manner of facing it that is difficult.
Páng Xūn and Bó Diāo,
once they were received,
immediately acted in righteous repayment;
how much more so for those with long-standing ties?
Therefore, Zōu Yáng said of it:
"The dog of Jié can be made to bark at Yáo;
the retainers of Zhí can be made to stab Yóu."
How could these be empty words?
Common men are shallow and short-sighted,
anxious for what is right before them;
seeing benefit in rushing forward, they arrive first,
but considering something useless, they turn their backs.
Therefore, those who seek quick success
compete to promote those above and have no time to attend to those below;
they strive to chase those ahead and have no leisure to care for those behind.
For this reason, Hán Ānguó could give five hundred gold pieces to Tián Fén,
but could not relieve a single person in poverty;
Zhái Fāngjìn praised Chúnyú Zhǎng,
but could not recommend a single worthy scholar.
Now, Ānguó and Fāngjìn
were the loyal and good men of former times,
and yet they were like this;
then how much more so for the inferior men of these late and declining days?
This is why treacherous men pursue factional advancement,
while reclusive scholars become increasingly obscured.
If not for a bright and sagely ruler,
who could clearly observe this?
Furthermore, the birth of resentment and hatred
is like two people meeting.
If they face each other,
with kindness and affection directed toward one another,
pushing their intentions to the limit,
their sincerity shines upon each other,
penetrating the heart and reaching the marrow.
At the height of such love and joy,
they would lightly die for one another.
For this reason, Hóu Shēng and Yù Zǐ cut their throats without regret.
If they turn against each other,
their hearts and dispositions becoming divergent,
pushing their intentions to the limit,
they split and gallop in opposite directions,
reaching the farthest east and the extreme west,
yet their hearts are still not satisfied.
For this reason, Chén Yú and Zhāng Ěr in their old age completely destroyed each other without any feeling of pain.
From this perspective,
regarding the principles of social interaction,
the emotions involved are vast indeed.
This is not only true for friends;
it is the same for rulers and ministers, and for husbands and wives.
When they are in harmony,
even fathers and sons cannot come between them;
when they are at odds,
even enemies cannot surpass them in resentment.
Therefore, the sage is always cautious about the smallest beginnings in order to ensure a sincere end.
Wealth and status are not necessarily to be esteemed;
poverty and low station are not necessarily to be slighted.
Human hearts do not have the same preferences,
and their capacities differ by millions.
Xǔ Yóu relinquished the imperial throne,
while common men fight over a county office;
Mèng Kē declined a salary of ten thousand *zhōng*,
while petty men are greedy for a single *shēng* of grain.
Thus it is said:
Quails and small birds wander in flocks,
without resting all day long;
they rise up in confusion and perch together,
never leaving the mugwort and wild grass.
The great swan geese fly high,
parting from their pairs and diverging,
traveling over thousands and tens of thousands of miles,
for their will is set upon the lakes and ponds.
The *luán* and the phoenix soar above the heavens,
wandering within the Great Purity;
they drift with the auspicious breeze,
rising and falling at times with composure.
Their intent still not satisfied,
they let out a long, harmonious cry,
kicking and flapping their wings;
they surmount the vermilion clouds
and reach the Big Dipper and the Pole Star;
breathing in the solar dew,
they do not eat for ten days,
and yet their intent still feels unsatisfied.
These three have different pursuits,
each content in what they do.
Therefore, Bó Yí gathered ferns without regret,
and Cháo Fù lived in the trees of his own will.
From this perspective,
the will and capacity of a scholar
are truly difficult to measure.
All you gentlemen
should not use wealth and status to be arrogant toward the poor and lowly,
assuming that the poor and lowly must necessarily submit to you.
The *Shī* says:
"Virtue is as light as a feather,
yet few among the people are able to lift it."
In the world, there are four things of great difficulty,
which no one is able to practice:
first is reciprocity,
second is fairness,
third is reverence,
and fourth is steadfastness.
Reciprocity is the root of benevolence;
fairness is the root of righteousness;
reverence is the root of ritual;
steadfastness is the root of trustworthiness.
When these four are established together,
the four practices are complete;
when the four practices are all present,
one is called a true worthy.
If the four roots are not established,
the four practices will not be formed;
if not one of the four practices is present,
one is called a petty man.
As for what is called reciprocity,
a man who is a gentleman
considers others by empathizing with himself,
with every action and thought originating from the heart.
What he himself lacks,
he does not demand from his subordinates;
what he himself possesses,
he does not use to ridicule others.
Sensing his own desire for respect,
he treats scholars with ritual propriety;
sensing his own desire for love,
he treats others with kindness.
Desiring to be established himself, he establishes others;
desiring to attain success himself, he helps others to attain it.
Valuing others' care for him,
he is the first to toil for others;
hating that others might forget him,
he always keeps others in mind.
The ordinary sort is not like this:
they judge others without empathizing with themselves,
and their actions do not reflect their hearts.
What they lack themselves, they demand from others;
what they possess themselves, they use to ridicule others.
Lacking ritual propriety themselves, they demand respect from others;
lacking kindness themselves, they demand love from others.
In poverty and low station, they blame others for not caring about them;
in wealth and high status, it is they themselves who do not care about others.
Conducting oneself in such a manner,
it is difficult to be called benevolent.
What is called fairness
is to internally harbor the kindness of the Shījiū
and externally maintain a heart as smooth as a whetstone and as straight as an arrow.
The evaluation of scholars must be determined by their will and conduct;
criticism and praise must be verified by evidence.
One does not follow common customs to be identical to others
nor base arguments on following rumors.
If goodness is present,
one does not mock poverty or low status;
if evil is committed,
one does not fear wealth or nobility.
One does not flatter superiors while slighting inferiors,
nor does one tire of the old while respecting the new.
Common sorts are not so:
internally they are biased toward wives and children,
and externally they are misled by friends.
When they gain, they praise;
when they resent, they slander.
Their fair assessments have no standard;
their criticism and praise have no verification.
They flatter the noble to form cliques
and steal rumors to bark with the pack.
They serve the rich and noble like slaves
and view the poor and lowly like hirelings.
They visit the gates of the powerful a hundred times
but do not go once to the home of those without influence.
If the heart is held thus,
it is difficult to be called righteous.
What is called respect
is to internally not dare be arrogant toward one's family
and externally not dare be disrespectful to the Shì Dàfū.
One sees the lowly as noble
and looks upon the young as elders.
Etiquette is offered first;
words come forth later.
No kindness goes unrequited;
no respect goes unreciprocated.
Seeing the worthy, one does not place oneself above them
but yields to others.
In tasks, one takes the labor;
in dwelling, one follows simplicity;
in position, one is content with the lowly;
in sustenance, one is satisfied with the meager.
Common sorts are not so:
internally they are disrespectful to wives and children,
and externally they belittle friends.
Their intelligence does not distinguish truth from falsehood;
their minds do not distinguish good from evil.
Being foolish, they delight in being arrogant toward the worthy;
being young, they enjoy insulting elders.
Kindnesses are not reciprocated;
respect is not returned.
Seeing the worthy, they do not yield;
in gatherings, they cannot be humble.
In action, they seek ease;
in dwelling, they seek comfort;
in sustenance, they seek the richest;
in position, they fight for the highest.
Seeing others being humble,
they sneer at them;
seeing others being respectful,
they treat them with arrogance;
acting thus, they call themselves worthy, capable, and wise.
With conduct like this,
it is difficult to be called loyal.
What is called steadfastness
is the heart.
A man of measure
has focused and dedicated intent;
his mind perceives what is unique.
He is not driven by the customs of a treacherous world
nor confused by the many mouths of the crowd.
His intelligence is outstanding;
he holds his heart with profound depth.
He stands alone without fear
and withdraws from the world without regret.
His heart is as firm as gold or stone;
his will views the four seas as light.
Thus he guards his heart and achieves trustworthiness.
Common vessels are not so:
internally they have no principles;
externally they have no standards.
Biased and crooked,
they seek to conform to the world.
Their mouths have no fixed assertions;
they do not persist in virtue
and are inconsistent in their conduct.
With principles like this,
it is difficult to be called trustworthy.
These four conducts
are as light as a feather
and as heavy as a mountain.
The Jūn Zǐ considers them easy;
the Xiǎo Rén considers them difficult.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Is benevolence far away?
If I desire benevolence,
benevolence is at hand."
It is also said: "Those who know virtue are few."
The bias and cliquishness of common customs
have been so since ancient times,
not just today.
All sorts of Jūn Zǐ
compete in arrogance and excess,
craving pleasure and being disrespectful,
like merchants seeking double profit,
to outdo one another.
If one can attain wealth and status,
even if they accumulate cunning and evil,
people compete to praise them,
and they are never found at fault.
If one is in poverty and lowly status,
even if they are respectful and cautious,
they are merely considered unworthy,
and they are never seen as right.
This is why common customs gradually decay
and why ritual and righteousness wither away.
There are three things in the world to be worried about.
What are these three?
They are:
Sincerity is thin but words claim it to be thick;
concern is negligible but writing pretends to be worried;
the heart does not intend to come but externally one fixes a date.
If one does not believe them, one fears losing a worthy man;
if one believes them, one is misled.
This is the most loathsome type of common scholar.
Therefore, Kǒngzǐ detested those whose words exceeded their actions.
The Shī laments: "The boastful and grand words
come from the mouth.
Artful words are like a reed organ;
how thick is the face!"
In the social interactions of the current world,
before people have observed each other, they seek deep bonds,
reaching into their bosoms and grasping wrists,
patting their chests and taking oaths,
merely wishing to protect each other's reputations.
On the day they part,
or after they have gained what they wanted,
they abandon and forget each other.
Some receive kindness from others
and are initially helped across;
if they cannot be promoted,
they then slander their benefactor,
creating flaws and rifts,
openly claiming, "I spared no effort,
but alas, it simply wasn't possible."
The Shī says:
"Knowing I am thus,
it would be better not to have been born."
Agreeing first and then clashing,
having a beginning but no end—
it is better to have had no intention of friendship from the start
than to make forced oaths.
When Jūn Zǐ frequently make oaths,
disorder grows because of it.
The way of the Dà Rén
is to be inclusive and not cliquish;
they are moved by subtle words
and match like two halves of a tally.
What need then is there for oaths?
Kǒngzǐ was respectful
and appeared as if he were unable to speak;
he was also described as speaking "frankly and politely,
yet with caution."
A scholar values being articulate
but also hates being loquacious.
Thus it is said:
"Only when refinement and substance are balanced
is one a Jūn Zǐ."
Rather than being disloyal,
being resolute, steadfast, simple, and slow of speech
is closer to benevolence.
Alas, how tragic!
All the people of today
have square words but round actions;
their mouths are upright but their hearts are wicked.
Their conduct contradicts their words,
and their hearts are at odds with their mouths.
When discussing the past, they know to praise Bóyí, Shūqí, Yuán Xiàn, and Yán Huí;
when talking of the present, they only care for official rank and position.
In empty talk, they know to consider virtue and righteousness as worthy;
in recommendations, they certainly put family status and lineage first.
Even if a commoner practices the conduct of Yán Huí and Mǐn Sǔn,
possesses a nature of diligence and humility,
holds the talent of Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Shàng,
and harbors the way to save the people,
that they will not be supported by this world
is already clear!
Of the titles of a ruler,
none is greater than illumination;
of the reputations of a subject,
none is finer than loyalty.
These two virtues
are what rulers and subjects have collectively desired since ancient times.
However, illumination does not follow in succession,
and loyalty does not appear in one out of ten thousand cases,
not necessarily because they are stupid and dark and fail to attain them so that an evil name spreads,
but simply because the way they seek them is not the correct path.
Now, illumination arises based on those below,
and loyalty is accomplished by relying on the one above.
"When two people are of the same mind,
their sharpness can cut through gold."
Those who can achieve this
will possess both reputations.
The essential point lies in clearly exercising legal techniques and
holding the handles of power oneself.
What is called "technique"
is that which prevents subordinates from practicing deception;
what is called "power"
is that which prevents the situation from falling into disorder.
If technique is truly clear,
then even ten thousand lǐ away
or within the dark and hidden places,
effectiveness must be sought;
if power is truly employed,
then whether distant or near, kin or stranger,
noble or base, worthy or foolish,
none will not submit their hearts.
At the end of the Zhōu House, it was not so:
they departed from their techniques and abandoned their power,
being lazy themselves and relying on others.
Thus, the dukes and ministers did not think of loyalty,
the hundred officials did not exert their full strength,
the king was isolated and obscured above,
and the millions of commoners were oppressed and disordered below;
therefore, they eventually declined, were encroached upon, and could not recover.
For emperors and kings,
their benefits are heavy
and their awe-inspiring power is great.
Simply by hanging heavy benefits,
it is enough to encourage the good;
simply by establishing stern awe,
it is possible to punish the wicked.
If one spreads heavy benefits to entice the people
and wields great awe to drive them,
then the people of the whole world
can be made to face naked blades without regret
and rush into boiling water or fire without difficulty.
How could it be said that merely leading them to govern together would be inappropriate?
Take the hawk, a wild bird;
yet when a hunter controls it,
he can make it strike vigorously all day long without daring to be lazy.
How much more so should a subject be capable of being made to exert his full strength?
The Shī says:
"In hewing an axe-handle, in hewing an axe-handle,
the pattern is not far off."
The divine techniques
are within the ruler's own person,
yet the ruler neglects them;
therefore, he causes his subjects to clamp their mouths and tie their tongues, not daring to speak.
This is why ears and eyes are blocked and obscured,
and why clarity and intelligence are not attained.
The power to control subordinates
is displayed before the ruler every day,
yet the ruler lets it go;
therefore, he causes the various ministers to become lax and turn their backs on the court.
This is why awe and virtue do not shine,
and why merit and fame are not established.
The Shī says:
"Although I have different duties,
I am a colleague with you.
If I come to you with a plan,
you listen to me with arrogance."
Compassion is something all people have;
therefore, when the ear hears the sound of wailing and crying,
there is no one who does not feel miserable, sorrowful, and heartbroken for it.
When the eye sees a dangerous and critical matter,
there is no one who does not feel anxious and alarmed and rush to rescue it.
The righteousness between ruler and subject is heavy,
while the etiquette among strangers on the road is light.
Even in a passing encounter through the ears or eyes,
where there is neither favor nor virtue,
neither poverty nor wealth,
it is still like this.
How much more so for one who faces north, calls himself a subject, and receives favor?
Therefore, offering loyalty and assisting in times of danger
is the common desire of both the worthy and the unworthy.
If they truly desire it but their actions contradict it,
it is often because they suffer from the path being disadvantageous and harmful;
their words are not yet trusted, and their persons are already ruined.
Observing throughout history the ministers who loved their ruler, worried for their lord, and dared to speak out:
once the state of order is established,
the ruler himself cannot cause disorder,
let alone the subordinates.
If legal techniques are not clear and rewards and punishments are not certain,
then even if orders are issued daily,
the situation will naturally be in disorder.
Once the state of disorder is established,
the ruler himself cannot bring order,
let alone the subordinates.
Therefore, when the situation is orderly,
even if it is neglected, it does not become disordered;
when the situation is disordered,
even if one is diligent, it cannot be ordered.
Yáo and Shùn respected themselves and practiced non-action yet had abundance;
this was because the situation was orderly.
Húhài and Wáng Mǎng rushed about but were insufficient;
this was because the situation was disordered.
Therefore it is said:
"The skillful one seeks it from the situation
and does not demand it from individuals."
Thus, an enlightened king examines laws and measures and spreads instructions and orders;
he does not act selfishly to deceive the law,
nor does he defile instructions to disgrace his commands.
Therefore, subordinates respect his words and uphold his prohibitions,
exhausting their hearts and fulfilling their duties.
This is because legal techniques are clear and awe-inspiring power is exercised.
Technique as a way
is subtle and divine;
speaking of it is not enough,
but practicing it is more than sufficient.
Being more than sufficient,
it can thus encompass the four seas and illuminate the dark and hidden places.
Power as a strategic advantage
is strong, fierce, and great;
it does not depend on noble or base status;
the one who wields it is significant.
Being significant,
it can thus seize the lord's awe and make things go accordingly.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler never shows his techniques to others nor lends his power to subordinates.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"[One] may be granted power."
Therefore, the sage "manifests it in benevolence
and hides it in use."
"He is divine and transforms them,
making the people act appropriately."
Only then does he achieve order and accomplish his success.
When his achievements are effective among the people
and his fine reputation is transmitted to the world,
only then can the ruler be called enlightened
and the subject be called loyal.
This is what is meant by illumination arising based on those below,
loyalty being accomplished by relying on the one above,
and when two people are of the same mind,
their sharpness can cut through gold.
Of the titles of a ruler,
none is greater than illumination;
of the reputations of a subject,
none is finer than loyalty.
These two virtues
are what rulers and subjects have collectively desired since ancient times.
However, illumination does not follow in succession,
and loyalty does not appear in one out of ten thousand cases,
not necessarily because they are stupid and dark and fail to attain them so that an evil name spreads,
but simply because the way they seek them is not the correct path.
Now, illumination arises based on those below,
and loyalty is accomplished by relying on the one above.
When two people are of the same mind,
then their sharpness can cut through gold.
Those who can know this
will possess both reputations.
The essential point lies in clearly exercising legal techniques and
holding the handles of power oneself.
What is called "technique"
is that which prevents subordinates from practicing deception;
what is called "power"
is that which prevents the situation from falling into disorder.
If technique is truly clear,
then even ten thousand lǐ away
or within the dark and hidden places,
effectiveness must be sought;
if power is truly employed,
then whether distant or near, kin or stranger,
noble or base, worthy or foolish,
none will not submit their hearts.
At the end of the Zhōu House, it was not so:
they departed from their techniques and abandoned their power,
being lazy themselves and relying on others.
Thus, the dukes and ministers did not think of loyalty,
the hundred officials did not exert their full strength,
the king was isolated and obscured above,
and the millions of commoners were oppressed and disordered below;
therefore, they eventually declined, were encroached upon, and could not recover.
Regarding Dìwáng,
their benefits are significant,
and their authority is immense.
Merely by holding out great benefits,
it is enough to encourage the good;
merely by establishing strict authority,
one can punish the wicked.
If one spreads great benefits to entice the people
and wields great authority to drive them,
then the people of the whole world
can be made to face unsheathed blades without resentment
and rush into boiling water or fire without hesitation.
How can it be said that it is inappropriate to merely lead them in collaborative governance?
Even birds like hawks and wild fowl,
when a hunter controls them,
can be made to strike vigorously all day long without daring to be idle.
How much more so should it be possible to make ministers exert their full efforts?
The Shī says:
"In hewing an axe-handle, in hewing an axe-handle,
the pattern is not far off."
The divine methods
are entirely within the person of the ruler,
yet the ruler neglects them.
Therefore, he causes ministers to keep their mouths shut and tongues tied, not daring to speak.
This is why ears and eyes are obstructed
and why clarity and wisdom are not attained.
The power to control subordinates
is presented before the ruler daily,
yet the ruler relinquishes it.
Therefore, he causes the various ministers to become lax and turn their backs on the court.
This is why authority and virtue do not shine,
and why merit and fame are not established.
The Shī says:
"Although I have different duties,
I am a colleague to you.
I approach you with a plan,
yet you listen to me with indifference."
Compassion is something all people possess.
Therefore, when the ears hear the sound of wailing and crying,
there is no one who does not feel wretched, sorrowful, and pained at heart for them.
When the eyes see a situation of peril and danger,
there is no one who does not feel anxious and alarmed and rush to the rescue.
The duty between ruler and minister is heavy,
while the etiquette among strangers on the road is light.
Even in a passing acquaintance of the ears or eyes,
where there is no prior kindness or virtue,
and neither is worthy or noble,
it is still like this.
How much more so for those who face north as ministers and receive favor?
Therefore, offering loyalty and aiding in danger
are the common desires of both the worthy and the unworthy.
Truly, if they all desire it yet their actions differ,
it is usually because they suffer from the path being disadvantageous and harmful;
their words are not yet trusted before their own persons are ruined.
Looking back at the ministers throughout history who loved their rulers, worried for their masters, and dared to speak out,
their loyalty and trustworthiness were not yet understood
before they were investigated and interrogated by those close to the ruler.
Being overturned in their own time
and instead labeled as wicked, foolish, and depraved ministers—
how could they even be counted?
On the day Xiàochéng died,
he did not know the uprightness of Wáng Zhāng;
on the day Xiào’āi died,
he did not know the loyalty of Wáng Jiā.
Because of this, even though later worthies have feelings of concern for their rulers and sorrow for their masters,
and possess the integrity of loyalty and uprightness,
they still hesitate, observing and listening before acting.
"A crying crane is in the shade;
its young respond to it."
"Look at those birds;
even they seek a friend's voice."
Therefore, if the ruler does not open his sincerity to show the worthy and loyal,
the worthy and loyal will have no way to be understood.
The Yì says:
"The King is brilliant;
all together receive his blessings."
Thus, a loyal minister must wait for an enlightened ruler to manifest his integrity;
an excellent official must find a discerning master to achieve his merit.
If the ruler is not enlightened,
then high ministers will conceal subordinates and suppress loyalty,
and the various officials will abandon the law to flatter the powerful.
Loyal words are the means for safety;
if they are not presented, danger is certain.
Laws and prohibitions are the means for order;
if they are not upheld, chaos is certain.
Whether loyalty is presented or not,
and whether the law is upheld or not,
the handle for both lies with the ruler;
it is not something subordinates can control.
Therefore, the Sage seeks it within himself
and does not place the blame on subordinates.
Generally, for one who is a superior,
if the laws and methods are clear and rewards and punishments are certain,
then even without speaking, order will naturally be maintained by the force of circumstance.
Once the power of order is established,
the ruler himself cannot disrupt it,
much less the subordinates.
If the laws and methods are not clear and rewards and punishments are not certain,
then even if orders are issued daily,
the situation will naturally descend into chaos.
Once the power of chaos is established,
the ruler himself cannot govern it,
much less the subordinates.
Therefore, when the situation is orderly,
even if it is left alone, it does not become chaotic;
when the situation is chaotic,
even if one is diligent, it is not governed.
Yáo and Shùn were reverent and practiced non-action yet had more than enough;
this was because the situation was orderly.
Húhài and Wáng Mǎng rushed about but were insufficient;
this was because the situation was chaotic.
Therefore it is said:
the adept seeks it in the situation
and does not demand it of people.
Thus, the enlightened king examines laws and measures and spreads instructive commands;
he does not act out of private interest to deceive the law,
nor does he defile instruction to dishonor his commands.
Therefore, subordinates respect his words and uphold his prohibitions,
exhausting their hearts and fulfilling their duties.
This results from the clarity of laws and methods and the proper exercise of authority and power.
Method as a principle
is subtle and divine;
speaking of it is insufficient,
but practicing it leaves a surplus.
Because there is a surplus,
it can encompass the Four Seas and illuminate the dark and hidden realms.
Power as a force
is vigorous and grand;
it does not depend on noble or lowly status;
whoever wields it becomes significant.
Because they are significant,
they can seize the ruler's authority and follow the trends of the age.
Thus, an enlightened ruler never reveals his methods to others nor lends his power to subordinates.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"One can weigh things with them."
Therefore, the Sage "manifests it in benevolence
and hides it in application."
"Through divinity, he transforms it,
making it suitable for the people."
Only then can he achieve order and complete his merit.
When achievements benefit the people
and a fine reputation spreads through the world,
only then can the ruler be called enlightened
and the minister be called loyal.
This is what is meant by "Enlightenment relies on what is done below,
and loyalty depends on what is accomplished above;
when two people are of the same mind,
their sharpness can cut through metal."
In the ages of high antiquity,
at the time of the Great Simplicity,
the original Qi was profound and dark,
without form or sign.
All essences were merged,
chaotic and unified,
with nothing to control or govern them.
After a long time like this,
it suddenly transformed itself;
the clear and the turbid separated,
becoming Yīn and Yáng.
Yīn and Yáng took form,
truly giving birth to the Two Polarities.
"Heaven and Earth were intensely concentrated,
and all things were transformed in purity."
Harmonious Qi produced humans
to unify and govern them.
Therefore, Heaven is rooted in Yáng,
Earth is rooted in Yīn,
and Humans are rooted in Middle Harmony.
The Three Powers have different tasks
yet depend on each other for completion.
If each follows its way,
harmonious Qi will arrive,
and the astronomical instruments will be balanced.
The Way of Heaven is called bestowing,
the Way of Earth is called transforming,
and the Way of Man is called acting.
To act is what is called resonating with and penetrating *yīn* and *yáng* to bring about rare wonders.
Human actions move Heaven and Earth,
just as one drives a team of four horses upon a carriage,
or steers a boat from within a canopy.
Although we are covered and carried by them,
it also rests with us where we may go.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"At the proper time, ride the six dragons to control the heavens."
"Words and actions are the means by which the gentleman moves Heaven and Earth;
can one not be cautious?"
From this perspective,
Heaven displays its omens,
and Man arranges his achievements.
Thus the *Shū* says:
"Heaven’s work—let Man perform it on its behalf."
It is as if one governs affairs to harmonize the *qì* of Heaven,
thereby achieving its success.
Therefore, among the applications of the Way and Virtue,
none is greater than *qì*.
The Way
is the root of *qì*.
As for *qì*,
that which it transforms is Spirit;
it is the movement of *qì*.
At such a time,
when the correct *qì* is applied,
it is not only to humans,
but the hundred grains, the grasses and trees,
the birds and beasts, the fish and turtles,
all nourish their *qì* through their mouths.
Sounds enter the ears
to resonate in the heart;
men and women listen
to bestow their essence and spirit.
Relying on harmony to signal the coagulation of blood,
the embryos of the people
contain excellence to form their bodies.
When they are born,
harmony nourishes their nature,
and beauty is within them,
flowing through the four limbs
and filling the blood vessels.
Thus, in their hearts, natures, wills, and intentions,
as well as their ears, eyes, essences, and desires,
there are none who do not maintain integrity, incorruptibility, and purity in their thoughts and actions.
This is how the Wǔdì and Sānwáng were able to merely display laws and images and the people would not disobey,
and by rectifying their own virtue, the world was transformed of itself.
Therefore, laws, commands, punishments, and rewards
are only the means to govern the affairs of the people and bring about order;
they are not sufficient to promote great transformation and ascend to Tàipíng.
Those who wish to follow the unparalleled tracks of the Sānwáng
and attain the ultimate achievements of the Emperors and Sovereigns
must first trace the origin to the source and the root to the beginning,
promote the Way and bring about harmony,
and use pure and unadulterated *qì*
to give birth to simple and substantial people.
Manifest the outward signs of virtue and righteousness,
and create hearts of sincerity and generosity;
only then can transformation be beautiful and success be achieved.
In the age of high antiquity,
at the time of Tàisù,
the original *qì* was dark and obscure,
with no forms or signs yet.
The myriad essences were merged together,
blended into one,
with nothing to control or direct them.
After a long time like this,
it suddenly transformed of itself;
the clear and the turbid separated,
becoming *yīn* and *yáng*.
*Yīn* and *yáng* took form,
truly giving birth to the Liǎngyí.
Heaven and Earth became densely concentrated,
and the myriad things transformed into their pure states.
Harmonious *qì* gave birth to Man
to govern and order them.
Therefore, Heaven is rooted in *yáng*,
Earth is rooted in *yīn*,
and Man is rooted in Central Harmony.
The Sāncái have different functions
but rely on each other to be complete;
if each follows its way,
harmonious *qì* will arrive,
and the Jīhéng will be leveled.
The Way of Heaven is called bestowing,
the Way of Earth is called transforming,
the Way of Man is called acting.
To act
is what is called resonating with and penetrating *yīn* and *yáng* to bring about rare wonders.
Human actions move Heaven and Earth,
just as one drives galloping horses upon a carriage,
or steers a boat from within a canopy.
Although we are covered and carried by them,
it also rests with us where we may go.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"At the proper time, ride the six dragons to control the heavens."
"Words and actions are the means by which the gentleman moves Heaven and Earth;
can one not be cautious?"
From this perspective,
Heaven [displays] its omens,
and Man arranges his achievements.
Thus the *Shū* says:
"Heaven’s work—let Man perform it on its behalf."
It is as if one governs affairs to harmonize the *qì* of Heaven,
thereby achieving its success.
Therefore, among the applications of the Way and Virtue,
none is greater than *qì*.
The Way is the root of *qì*;
*qì* is the messenger of the Way.
There must be its root
for the *qì* to be born;
there must be its messenger
for transformation to be completed.
Therefore, as a thing, the Way
is supremely spiritual and subtle;
in its achievements,
it is supremely powerful and great.
That by which Heaven moves,
that by which Earth is still,
that by which the sun has light,
that by which the moon has brightness,
the four seasons and the Wǔxíng,
ghosts, spirits, and the people,
the myriad species,
changes, anomalies, and good and bad fortune—
what among these is not the result of *qì*?
Because of its perversity:
the nobility of Heaven can be split by *qì*,
the greatness of Earth can be shaken by *qì*,
the weight of mountains can be moved by *qì*,
the flow of water can be cut off by *qì*,
the sun and moon are divine, yet *qì* can eclipse them;
the stars and planets are in the void, yet *qì* can make them fall.
Mornings may have daytime darkness,
and nights have [light],
great winds can flip carriages and uproot trees,
crashing lightning can turn into ice,
warm springs can become boiling water,
the Lín, Lóng, Luán, and Fèng,
and pests and locusts—
all are the workings of *qì*.
From this perspective,
the movement and resonance of *qì*
are truly vast.
In the workings of transformation,
what can it not do?
That which it transforms is Spirit;
it is the movement of *qì*.
At such a time,
when the correct *qì* is applied,
it is not only to humans,
but the hundred grains, the grasses and trees,
the birds and beasts, the fish and turtles,
all nourish their *qì* through their mouths.
Sounds enter the ears
to resonate in the heart;
men and women listen
to bestow their essence and spirit.
Relying on harmony to signal the coagulation of blood,
the embryos of the people
contain excellence to form their bodies.
When they are born,
harmony nourishes their nature,
and beauty is within them,
flowing through the four limbs
and filling the blood vessels.
Thus, in their hearts, natures, wills, and intentions,
as well as their ears, eyes, essences, and desires,
there are none who do not maintain integrity, incorruptibility, and purity in their thoughts and actions.
This is how the Wǔdì and Sānwáng were able to merely display laws and images and the people would not disobey,
and by rectifying their own virtue, the world was transformed of itself.
Therefore, laws, commands, punishments, and rewards
are only the means to govern the affairs of the people and bring about order;
they are not sufficient to promote great transformation and ascend to Tàipíng.
Those who wish to follow the unparalleled tracks of the Sānwáng
and attain the ultimate achievements of the Emperors and Sovereigns
must first trace the origin to the source and the root to the beginning,
promote the Way and bring about harmony,
and use pure and unadulterated *qì*
to give birth to simple and substantial people.
Manifest the outward signs of virtue and righteousness,
and create hearts of sincerity and generosity;
only then can the likeness be beautiful and success be achieved.
In the governance of a sovereign,
there is nothing greater than the *Dào*,
nothing more magnificent than *dé*,
nothing more beautiful than instruction,
and nothing more spiritual than transformation.
The *Dào* is that by which it is sustained;
