*dé* is that by which it is encompassed;
instruction is that by which it is known;
and transformation is that by which it is achieved.
The people have a nature,
they have emotions,
they undergo transformation,
and they have customs.
Emotions and nature are of the heart-mind;
they are the root.
Transformation and customs are of conduct;
they are the branch.
The branch grows from the root,
and conduct arises from the heart-mind.
Therefore, the superior ruler pacifies the world
by prioritizing the root and only later the branch,
and by being cautious with the heart-mind to order conduct.
If the essence of the heart-mind is upright,
then wickedness and concealment have no place to arise,
and perverse intentions have no place to be carried.
Now, transformation changes the heart-mind of the people
just as government changes the physical bodies of the people.
When virtuous government is applied to the people,
then they are mostly pure and unhindered, handsome and fair, strong and long-lived;
when evil government is applied to the people,
then they are mostly exhausted and infirm, crippled and sickly, short-lived and muddled, plagued by pestilence and disease.
Thus, the *Shàngshū* praises "completing one's natural lifespan"
and dislikes "misfortune and premature death."
If the state has policies that harm clarity,
then the people will have many eye diseases;
that which exists
is the messenger of the *Dào*.
There must be its root
for its *qì* to then arise;
there must be its messenger
for transformation to then be completed.
For this reason, as a thing, the *Dào*
is supremely spiritual and subtle;
as for its achievements,
they are supremely powerful and great.
Heaven moves because of it,
Earth is still because of it,
the sun gives light because of it,
and the moon is bright because of it.
The four seasons and five elements,
spirits and people,
the myriad species of every kind,
anomalies and portents of good and ill fortune—
which of these is not so because of *qì*?
When it becomes contrary and rebellious:
as for the majesty of Heaven, *qì* splits it;
as for the vastness of Earth, *qì* moves it;
as for the weight of mountains, *qì* shifts them;
as for the flow of waters, *qì* cuts it off;
as for the spiritual sun and moon, *qì* eclipses them;
as for the stars in the void, *qì* causes them to fall.
At dawn there is midday darkness;
at night there is [light];
great winds fly carriages and uproot trees;
violent lightning becomes ice;
warm springs become boiling soup;
the *Lín*, *Lóng*, *Luán*, and *Fèng*;
the *máo*, *zé*, *yuán*, and locusts—
there are none that are not the workings of *qì*.
Viewed from this perspective,
the movement and resonance of *qì*
are indeed truly great.
As for the acts of transformation,
what thing can they not affect?
Therefore, the supreme sage does not strive to manage the affairs of the people but strives to manage the heart-mind of the people.
Hence it is said:
"In hearing litigations,
I am like anyone else.
What is necessary is to bring it about that there are no litigations!"
"Lead them with *dé*,
and align them with *lǐ*."
Strive to enrich their emotions and clarify principles by striving for *yì*;
when the people are affectionate, they have no intention to harm one another;
when their movements consider righteousness, they have no wicked or perverse heart-minds.
Such states as these
are not brought about by laws,
nor are they forced by awesome punishments;
these are the results of instruction and transformation.
If the state has policies that harm hearing,
then the people will have many ear diseases;
if there are policies that harm the worthy,
then the worthy will mostly suffer untimely deaths.
Now, the physical body and bones are solid and strong,
yet they still change according to government;
how much more so for the heart-mind and *qì*, which are subtle—can they not be nourished?
The *Shī* says:
"Thick are those reeds by the way,
let not the cattle and sheep trample them.
They are budding and taking shape,
their leaves are lush and soft."
It also says:
"The hawk flies to the height of heaven,
the fish leaps in the deep.
The joyful and easy-mannered lord,
how can he not inspire people?"
*Gōng Liú* had profound virtue;
his kindness reached the plants and trees,
and even the cattle, sheep, and six domestic animals
were moved by his virtue.
Reflecting on things in the heart-mind:
that which I lack,
I do not demand of subordinates;
that which I possess,
I do not use to mock others.
Feeling one's own desire for respect,
one treats scholars with *lǐ*;
feeling one's own desire for love,
one treats people with kindness.
"Wishing to be established oneself, one establishes others;
wishing to be prominent oneself, one makes others prominent."
Appreciating that people care for me,
I first labor for others;
disliking that people forget me,
I constantly think of others.
The common sort are not like this.
They judge others without being empathetic themselves;
their actions do not consider the heart-mind.
They demand of others what they lack themselves;
they mock others for what they possess themselves.
They lack *lǐ* but demand respect from others;
they lack kindness but demand love from others.
When poor and lowly, they blame others for not caring for them;
when rich and noble, it is they who do not care for others.
If one conducts oneself like this,
it is difficult to be called *rén*.
Those who are called "even-handed"
harbor the kindness of the *Shījiū* bird within
and maintain a heart-mind as straight as a whetstone or an arrow without.
Judging scholars must be fixed upon their intent and conduct;
slander and praise must be verified by evidence.
They do not follow the crowd or echo others;
they do not chase after rumors to base their opinions.
If goodness is present,
they do not mock the poor and lowly;
if evil is committed,
they do not fear the rich and noble.
They do not flatter superiors and slight subordinates;
they do not tire of the old and only respect the new.
The common sort are not like this.
They are biased toward their wives and children within
and are deceptive or deluded regarding friends without.
When they gain, they praise;
when they are resentful, they slander.
Their fair discussion has no target;
their mockery and praise have no evidence.
They fawn on the noble to form factions;
they mindlessly echo others like a pack of barking dogs.
They serve the rich and noble like slaves
and look upon the poor and lowly like hired laborers.
They visit the gates of those holding power a hundred times,
but do not visit the homes of those without influence even once.
If one holds a heart-mind like this,
it is difficult to be called *yì*.
What is called reverence
means not daring to be arrogant toward one's family internally,
and not daring to be disrespectful toward the Shìdàfū externally;
it is treating the lowly as the noble,
and regarding the young as the elder;
one's ritual gestures are performed first,
and one's words are spoken afterward;
no kindness goes unrequited,
and no ritual respect goes unreturned;
seeing the worthy, one does not position oneself above them,
but yields and defers to others;
in tasks, one takes on the labor,
in dwelling, one follows virtue,
in rank, one is content with the humble,
and in sustenance, one is satisfied with the meager.
Ordinary sorts of people are not like this:
internally, they are disrespectful and casual toward their wives and children,
and externally, they are slighting and insulting toward their friends;
their perception does not distinguish between the true and the false,
and their minds do not distinguish between the good and the ugly;
though foolish, they take pleasure in being arrogant toward the worthy,
and though young, they enjoy bullying their elders;
kindness is not reciprocated,
and ritual respect is not returned;
seeing the worthy, they do not yield to them,
and in gatherings, they are unable to defer;
in action, they desire to choose ease,
in dwelling, they desire to reside in comfort,
in sustenance, they desire to monopolize the rich,
and in rank, they desire to contend for the honorable;
seeing others practice humility and deference,
they consequently ridicule them;
seeing others practice reverence and respect,
they consequently treat them with arrogance,
and in this way, they consider themselves worthy, capable, wise, and intelligent.
When one's conduct is like this,
it is difficult for them to be called loyal.
What is called steadfastness
resides in the heart.
A man of measured principle
has focused and dedicated intentions;
his mind sees what others do not;
he is not driven by the customs of treacherous ruins,
nor is he confused by the talk of the masses;
his intelligence is far above the ordinary,
and he maintains a heart that is deep and profound;
he stands alone and without fear,
and withdraws from the world without distress;
his heart is as firm as metal and stone,
and his will regards the four seas as light;
thus he guards his heart and fulfills his trustworthiness.
Ordinary vessels are not like this:
internally, they have no self-discipline,
and externally, they have no standards of conduct;
they are tilting, devious, and biased;
they seek only to satisfy their own whims;
their words have no fixed conclusion;
"they do not remain constant in their virtue,"
and their actions are inconsistent.
When one's self-discipline is like this,
it is difficult for them to be called trustworthy.
As for these four types of conduct,
they are as light as a feather
yet as heavy as a mountain;
the Jūnzǐ considers them easy,
while the Xiǎorén considers them difficult.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Is Rén far away?
If I desire Rén,
then Rén arrives."
He also said, "Those who know virtue are few."
The bias and factionalism of common customs
have been so since ancient times;
it is not only today.
Among the many gentlemen,
they compete in arrogance and overstepping,
greedily seeking pleasure while being disrespectful and proud;
as loyalty and trustworthiness have not reached them,
they are constrained by those around them;
in the present age, they are overturned and covered;
those who have become ministers of wicked, foolish, and evil appearance
how could they be counted?
On the day of Xiàochéng's death,
he did not know the uprightness of Wáng Zhāng;
on the day of Xiào'āi's death,
he did not know the loyalty of Wáng Jiā.
Although later worthy men may have feelings of concern for their sovereign and sorrow for their lord,
and have the integrity of loyalty, sincerity, and uprightness,
they nonetheless hesitate, observe, and listen before acting.
"A crane calls in the shade,
and its chick responds."
"Look at those birds;
they even seek the voice of a friend."
If Rén is such that one cannot bear to tread upon living grass,
then how much more so for the people—how could they not be transformed?
The Jūnzǐ cultivates his virtue of joy and ease,
reaching up to the flying birds
and down to the fish in the depths;
none are not joyful and delighted,
so how much more so for the scholars and commoners—could there be any who are not benevolent?
The Sages deeply understood this;
they all strove to rectify themselves as a model,
and clarified ritual and righteousness as the teaching;
they harmonized the vital energy of virtue before birth
and corrected the principles of conduct after the first laugh.
When the people are in the womb,
they are formed by combining balance and harmony;
when they are born,
they are raised by establishing uprightness.
Therefore, the heart of Rén and righteousness, and the will for integrity and shame,
are attached to the bones and flow through the veins,
born together with the body;
there is no coarse or foul energy,
and no depraved or lewd desires.
Even if cast out beyond the Great Wilderness
or placed within the dark gloom,
in the end, there will be no conduct that violates ritual;
even if thrown into places of danger and ruin
or placed between the edges of blades,
in the end, there will be no mind to seek survival through dishonor.
If all the people in the world
acted in this way,
then where would there be wicked and rebellious people to be subjected to punishment?
"The workings of High Heaven
have neither sound nor smell;
take Wén Wáng as your model,
and the myriad states will have confidence."
This is how the Jī family promoted beauty in the past
and resulted in punishments being set aside afterward.
The Sages greatly honored virtue and ritual while disparaging punishments and penalties;
thus Shùn first charged Qiè to reverently spread the Five Teachings,
and afterward commanded Gāotáo to administer the Five Punishments and Three Residences.
Therefore, in all cases of establishing laws,
it is not to spy on the people's shortcomings and execute them for their errors,
but to prevent wickedness and evil and save them from disaster and ruin,
to restrain depravity and bring them into the correct path.
The Shī says:
"The people possess a constant nature,
and they love this admirable virtue."
Therefore, the people having hearts
is like seeds having a garden.
If they encounter harmonious energy, they will flourish and bear fruit;
if they encounter floods or droughts, they will wither and produce weeds.
If the people receive good transformation,
then they will have the hearts of scholars and Jūnzǐ;
if they are subjected to evil governance,
then they will harbor thoughts of wickedness and rebellion.
Thus, the way the good nurture the people of Heaven
is like a fine craftsman making leaven and fermented beans.
Activity and rest are according to the season,
and cold and warmth are properly adjusted;
then the entire batch of leaven and fermented beans will be beautiful and plentiful.
If they encounter a clumsy craftsman,
then the entire batch of leaven and fermented beans will become foul and spoiled and be thrown away.
Now the world is also like a single batch,
and the common people are like beans and wheat;
the "transformations and actions"
depend on those who lead.
If they encounter good officials, they will all harbor loyalty and trustworthiness and practice Rén and generosity;
if they encounter evil officials, they will all harbor wickedness and practice shallowness.
If loyalty and generosity accumulate, it leads to Great Peace;
if wickedness and shallowness accumulate, it leads to danger and ruin.
For this reason, sage emperors and enlightened kings
all emphasized transformation through virtue and downplayed the awe of punishment.
Virtue is that which is used to cultivate oneself;
awe is that which is used to govern others.
When those above are wise, then the people of low intelligence are few,
and the people of the middle way are many.
The birth of middle-class people in the world
is like molten metal in a furnace;
their transformation
follows only what the metalworker does;
square or round, thin or thick,
they follow the mold and the control.
Therefore, the goodness or badness of an age
and the shallowness or depth of customs
all depend on the ruler.
Supreme sages harmonize the virtuous breath to transform the hearts of the people,
and set right their own example to lead their subordinates.
Thus they can make the people such that every household is worthy of ennoblement;
Yáo and Shùn are examples of this.
The next rank of rulers personally embody the Way and Virtue and are earnest in kindness and love,
beautifying teachings and instructions and honoring ritual and deference.
Thus they can make the people free of contentious hearts and bring about the setting aside of punishments;
Wén and Wǔ are examples of this.
The next rank of rulers make clear their likes and dislikes and manifest laws and prohibitions,
balancing rewards and punishments without favoritism.
Thus they can make the people avoid wickedness and evil and pursue justice and fairness,
regulating weakness and disorder to achieve governance and strength;
the Zhōngxīng restorations are examples of this.
In governing the world,
those who place themselves in filth and give rein to their passions,
are negligent of the people's affairs and prioritize wine and pleasure,
keep company with the obstinate and ignorant while distancing themselves from the worthy and talented,
draw close to flatterers while shunning the upright,
increase taxes to reward those without merit,
and recklessly dispense joy or anger to harm the innocent—
thus they are able to disorder their governance and ruin their people,
corrupt their own persons and lose their states;
Yōu and Lì are examples of this.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"When three people walk together,
there must be a teacher for me among them.
I select what is good in them and follow it,
and for what is not good,
I correct it in myself."
The *Shī* praises "One should take warning from Yīn,"
and "Seeking many blessings for oneself."
Therefore, if a lord of the age could truly cause those within the six directions,
all the people of the world,
to all harbor upright and sincere sentiments
and be without shallow and mean evils,
each upholding a heart of justice and fairness
and without thoughts of treachery and danger,
then the customs of Xī and Nóng
would be seen here again,
and qílín, dragons, luán-birds, and phoenixes
would again be raised in the outskirts.
In the governance of a ruler,
nothing is greater than the Way,
nothing is more flourishing than Virtue,
nothing is more beautiful than teaching,
and nothing is more divine than transformation.
The Way is that which maintains things;
Virtue is that which encompasses things;
teaching is that which makes things known;
transformation is that which brings things to fruition.
People have a nature,
have emotions,
undergo transformation,
and have customs.
Emotions and nature
are the heart,
the root.
Transformation and customs
are the conduct,
the branches.
The branches grow from the root;
conduct arises from the heart.
Therefore, the superior ruler comforts the world
by prioritizing the root and following with the branches,
according with their hearts and regulating their conduct.
If the essence of the heart is truly upright,
then treachery and concealment will have nowhere to arise,
and heterodox intentions will have nowhere to be carried.
Indeed, transformation changes the hearts of the people,
just as government changes the physical bodies of the people.
When virtuous government is applied to the people,
then many will be pure, unhindered, beautiful, strong, and long-lived.
When wicked government is applied to the people,
then many will be weary, crippled, infirm, diseased, short-lived, or die from epidemics.
Therefore, the *Shàngshū* praises "Achieving a natural end to life,"
and detests "Calamity and short life."
If a state has governance that harms vision,
then many of its people will have eye diseases;
if it has governance that harms hearing,
then many of its people will have ear diseases;
if it has governance that harms the worthy,
then many of the worthy will die premature deaths.
The physical body and skeletal structure are meant to be strong,
yet they still change according to governance;
how much more so for the heart and spirit, which are subtle and delicate—can they not be nurtured?
The *Shī* says:
"Thick are those traveling reeds,
do not let the sheep and cattle trample them.
They are budding and taking shape,
their leaves are lush and soft."
It also says:
"The hawk flies up to heaven,
the fish leaps in the deep.
The joyful and easy-going gentleman,
how could he not inspire people?"
Gōng Liú's virtue was profound,
his kindness reached even the grass and trees;
sheep, cattle, and the six domestic animals
were still moved by his virtue.
His benevolence could not bear to trample the growing grass;
how much more so with the common people—would they not be transformed?
When a gentleman cultivates his joyful and easy-going virtue,
reaching up to the flying birds
and down to the fish in the deep,
none will not be joyful and pleased;
how much more so with the scholars and commoners—would they not be benevolent?
The Sages deeply knew this;
they all strove to rectify themselves to serve as an example,
and made ritual and righteousness clear to serve as teaching.
They harmonized the virtuous breath before birth,
and corrected conduct and demeanor after the first cough and smile.
When the people are fetuses,
they are formed by combining balance and harmony;
when they are born,
they are raised by establishing uprightness.
Therefore, the heart of benevolence and righteousness and the will of integrity and shame
are attached to the bones and flow through the veins,
being born together with the body,
and have no coarse or filthy breath,
no wicked or licentious desires.
Even if they are cast beyond the Great Wilderness,
or placed within the dark and obscure,
they will never have conduct that violates ritual;
even if thrown into places of danger and ruin,
or placed between the points of blades,
they will never have the heart to seek safety improperly.
If all the people of the age
acted in this way,
where would there be any treacherous or disorderly people to apply punishments to?
"The workings of high Heaven
have neither sound nor smell.
Take Wén Wáng as your model,
and the myriad states will have confidence."
This is why the Jī clan was honored and glorified in the past
and reached the point of setting aside punishments in the latter period.
For this reason, supreme sages do not strive to manage the affairs of the people but strive to manage the hearts of the people.
Therefore it is said:
"In hearing lawsuits,
I am like anyone else.
What is necessary is to cause there to be no lawsuits!"
"Lead them with virtue,
and align them with ritual."
Strive to make their sentiments thick and their principles clear;
if the people love one another, then there will be no intent to harm or injure one another;
if their movements consider righteousness, then there will be no treacherous or wicked hearts.
Cases such as this
are not caused by laws
nor forced by majestic punishments;
this is what is achieved through education and transformation.
The Sages greatly honored virtue and ritual and disparaged punishments;
therefore Shùn first charged Xiè to reverently spread the five teachings,
and only afterward ordered Gāoyáo to implement the five punishments and the three dwellings.
For this reason, all those who establish laws
do not do so to watch for people's shortcomings and punish their errors,
but to prevent treachery and evil and save them from calamity and ruin,
to check licentiousness and wickedness and lead them into the correct path.
The *Shī* says:
"The people possess a natural disposition,
to love this admirable virtue."
Therefore, that the people possess hearts
is like seeds having a garden.
When they encounter harmonious *Qì*, they flourish and bear fruit;
when they meet flood or drought, they wither and produce blight.
When the people receive good transformation,
then they possess the hearts of scholars and gentlemen;
when they are subject to evil governance,
then they possess thoughts of harboring treachery and disorder.
Thus, a good person's nurturing of the Heaven's people
is like a skilled craftsman's making of leaven and malt.
Rising and resting at the proper times,
obtaining the appropriate cold and warmth,
then the leaven and malt in one cellar will all be excellent and abundant.
If they encounter a clumsy craftsman,
then the leaven and malt in one cellar will all be foul, ruined, and discarded.
Now the *Liùhé* is also like one cellar;
the *Qiánshǒu* are like beans and wheat;
transformations and actions
depend on those in command.
Encountering good officials, they all harbor loyalty and trust and practice benevolence and thickness;
meeting evil officials, they all harbor treachery and wickedness and act with shallowness and meanness.
When loyalty and thickness accumulate, it leads to *Tàipíng*;
when treachery and meanness accumulate, it leads to danger and ruin.
Therefore, sage emperors and enlightened kings
all emphasize virtuous transformation and minimize awe-inspiring punishments.
Virtue is that by which one cultivates oneself;
awe is that by which one governs others.
People of the highest wisdom and the lowest stupidity are few,
while people of the middle way are many.
The lives of middle-tier people in this world
are like molten metal in a furnace;
following profound transformations,
it is solely what the smith makes of it;
square or round, thin or thick,
it follows the casting and control.
For this reason, the goodness or badness of the age,
the shallowness or thickness of customs,
all lie with the ruler.
The supreme sage harmonizes the virtuous *Qì* to transform the hearts of the people
and rectifies appearances and models to lead the subordinates;
thus he can make the people so that every house could be enfeoffed,
*Yáo* and *Shùn* were such.
The next level personifies the Way and Virtue and emphasizes compassion and love,
beautifies teachings and instructions and honors ritual and yielding;
thus he can make the people have no competitive hearts and cause punishments to be set aside,
*Wén* and *Wǔ* were such.
The next level clarifies likes and dislikes and makes laws and prohibitions manifest,
levels rewards and punishments without favoritism;
thus he can make the people avoid treachery and wickedness and hasten toward fairness and justice,
ordering weakness and disorder to achieve strong governance,
the *Zhōngxīng* eras were such.
In governing the world,
personally dwelling in filth and letting passions loose,
neglecting the people's affairs and being urgent for wine and pleasure,
associating with stubborn youths and distancing worthy talents,
being intimate with flatterers and keeping the upright at a distance,
increasing taxes to reward those without merit,
rashly adding joy or anger to harm the innocent;
thus he can throw his governance into chaos and ruin his people,
harming his person and losing his state,
*Yōu* and *Lì* were such.
*Kǒngzǐ* said:
"When three people walk together,
there must be a teacher for me among them.
I choose the good ones and follow them,
and as for the not good ones,
I correct them in myself."
The *Shī* praises: "It is fitting to take warning from *Yīn*,
and seek much fortune for oneself."
Therefore, if the ruler of the age can truly cause those within the *Liùhé*,
all the people of the world,
to all harbor upright and generous sentiments,
and have no shallow or mean wickedness,
each upholding a heart of fairness and justice,
and having no treacherous or dangerous thoughts,
then the customs of *Xī* and *Nóng*
will be seen again here,
and the *Lín*, *Lóng*, *Luán*, and *Fèng*
will again be kept and roam in the suburbs.
"Since ancient times of old,"
Heaven and Earth opened and split.
The *Sānhuáng* alternated their systems,
each establishing titles and posthumous names,
to record their eras.
Heaven mandated five generations,
the calendar returned three times.
Divine brightness was moved to birth them,
whereupon states were raised.
Perished through negligence,
extinguished through accumulated evil.
The spirit is subtle and refined,
Heaven's mandate is without limit.
Some relied on great majesty,
some continued the physical lineage.
Before *Tàiyì* it is remote.
From this point forward,
quite a bit can be recorded.
Although one applies refined thought,
deliberation often results in errors again.
Therefore, I have compiled ancient instructions
and written the *Wǔdézhì*.
The world passes down the *Sānhuáng Wǔdì*,
mostly taking *Fúxī* and *Shénnóng* as the *Sānhuáng*;
one of them is sometimes called *Suìrén*,
sometimes called *Zhùróng*,
sometimes called *Nǚwā*.
Whether these are correct or not
cannot yet be known.
I have heard that in antiquity there were *Tiānhuáng*, *Dìhuáng*, and *Rénhuáng*,
thinking perhaps it refers to these,
yet I also do not dare to be certain.
All these accounts,
regarding the *Wǔjīng*,
none have an authoritative text.
Therefore, I broadly follow the *Yìxì*,
recording from *Fúxī* onwards,
to leave for future worthies.
Although much may not be correct,
nevertheless, a few can wander and observe widely,
together seeking the truth.
A giant's footprint appeared at *Léizé*,
*Huáxū* stepped in it and gave birth to *Fúxī*.
His physiognomy featured a *Rìjiǎo*,
his era title was *Tàiyì*.
He dwelt in *Chén*.
His virtue was Wood,
recording years with the Dragon,
thus he was the Dragon Master and had Dragon names.
He created the *Bāguà*,
knotted ropes to make nets for fishing.
His descendant was *Dìkù*,
who succeeded the *Zhuānxū* clan.
His physiognomy featured a *Dàidǒu*,
his title was *Gāoxīn*.
His nature was divine and spiritual,
his virtuous conduct was reverent and solemn,
he welcomed and escorted the sun and moon,
obeying the laws of Heaven,
capable of arranging the Three Luminaries to aid the people.
He composed the music *Liùyīng*.
In his era, there were eight talented sons:
*Bófèn*, *Zhòngkān*, *Shūxiàn*, *Jìzhòng*, *Bóhǔ*, *Zhòngxióng*, *Shūbào*, and *Jìlí*,
they were loyal, solemn, respectful, and admirable,
spreading compassion and kind harmony,
the people of the world called them the *Bāyuán*.
His descendant was *Jiāngyuán*,
who stepped in the giant's footprint and gave birth to *Jī Qì*.
His physiognomy featured a *Pīyí*.
He served as the *Sītú* for *Yáo*,
and also spread the sowing of seeds,
farming and planting fine grains.
When *Yáo* encountered the flood disaster,
the myriad people were saved by him.
Therefore, *Shùn* named him *Hòujì*.
Previously,
when the *Lièshān* clan possessed the world,
his son was called *Zhù*,
who could plant the hundred grains,
therefore they established him as *Jì*,
sacrificing to him from the *Xià* dynasty upwards.
When the *Zhōu* rose,
they replaced him with *Qì*,
and have sacrificed to him until now.
*Tàirèn* dreamed that a tall man influenced her,
and she gave birth to *Wénwáng*.
His physiognomy featured four nipples.
He became the *Xībó*,
rising at *Qí*.
He settled the dispute between *Yú* and *Ruì* and began to receive the Mandate.
*Wǔwáng* had double-rowed teeth,
he defeated *Yīn* and stopped the killings,
completing the *Zhōu* Way.
The separate enfeoffments of the *Jī* clan were many:
*Guǎn*, *Cài*, *Chéng*, *Huò*, *Lǔ*, *Wèi*, *Máo*, *Dān*, *Gào*, *Yōng*, *Cáo*, *Téng*, *Bì*, *Yuán*, *Fèng*, *Xún*,
these were the *Zhāo* of *Wén*.
*Yú*, *Jìn*, *Yìng*, *Hán*,
these were the *Mù* of *Wǔ*.
*Fán*, *Jiǎng*, *Xíng*, *Máo*, *Zuò*, *Jì*,
were the descendants of *Zhōugōng*.
*Zhōu*, *Shào*, *Guó*, *Wú*, *Suí*, *Bīn*, *Fāng*, *Áng*, *Xī*, *Pān*, *Yǎng*, *Huá*, *Gào*, *Gōng*, *Mì*, *Róng*, *Dān*, *Guō*, *Yáng*, *Páng*, *Guǎn*, *Táng*, *Hán*, *Yáng*, *Gū*,
*Luán*, *Gān*, *Línyú*, and the *Wáng* clan,
were all of the *Jī* surname.
There was a divine dragon that appeared from *Chángyáng*,
moving *Rènsì*,
who gave birth to the Red Emperor *Kuíwéi*.
His personal title was *Yándì*,
his generational title was *Shénnóng*,
and he succeeded the clan of *Fúxī Shì*.
His virtue was regulated by fire;
thus he was the Master of Fire and named after fire.
Therefore, he hewed wood to make plowshares
and bent wood to make plow handles and hoes.
He established markets at midday,
bringing together the people of the world,
gathering the goods of the world,
so they could exchange and retire,
each obtaining their proper place.
His descendant *Qìngdū*
united in marriage with a dragon,
giving birth to *Yī Yáo*.
He succeeded the clan of *Gāoxīn Shì*.
His eyebrows had eight colors.
He was known to the world as *Táng*.
He composed the music *Dàzhāng*.
He first began the abdication of the throne.
When *Wǔ Wáng* conquered *Yīn*,
he enfeoffed his descendants at *Zhù*.
*Hánshǐ* swallowed a red pearl;
a prophecy said, "*Yùyīng* shall give birth to *Hàn*."
A dragon moved *Nǚ'ǎo*,
and *Liú Jì* arose.
Great lightning encircled the star *Chū* and illuminated the wilds,
moving *Fúbǎo*,
who gave birth to the Yellow Emperor *Xuānyuán*.
He succeeded the clan of *Yándì*.
His countenance was like a dragon,
and his virtue followed the element of Earth.
He was regulated by clouds;
thus he was the Master of Clouds and named after clouds.
He composed the music *Xiánchí*.
He first established the system of robes and garments.
His descendant *Wòdēng*
saw a great rainbow,
and by this influence gave birth to *Chónghuá Yú Shùn*.
His eyes had double pupils.
He served *Yáo*,
and *Yáo* then abdicated the throne, saying:
"Come, you *Shùn*!
The celestial succession rests upon your person.
Sincerely hold fast to the Mean.
If the people within the four seas fall into distress and poverty,
the heavenly bounty will forever end."
He then received the abdication at the Temple of the Accomplished Ancestor *Wénzǔ*.
He was known to the world as *Yǒuyú*.
He composed the music *Jiǔsháo*.
He abdicated the throne to *Yǔ*.
When *Wǔ Wáng* conquered *Yīn*,
he enfeoffed *Húgōng Guīmǎn* at *Chén*,
giving him his eldest daughter *Dàjī* in marriage.
A great star like a rainbow
flowed down to *Huázhǔ*;
*Nǚjié* dreamed of a union,
giving birth to the White Emperor *Zhì Qīngyáng*.
He was known to the world as *Shǎohào*.
He succeeded the clan of the Yellow Emperor
and established his capital at *Qǔfù*.
His virtue followed the element of Metal.
When he ascended,
a phoenix arrived;
thus he recorded offices by birds.
The *Fèngniǎo Shì* clan was the Regulator of the Calendar;
the *Xuánniǎo Shì* clan was the Master of the Equinoxes;
the *Bózhào Shì* clan was the Master of the Solstices;
the *Qīngniǎo Shì* clan was the Master of the Springs;
the *Dānniǎo Shì* clan was the Master of the Autumns.
The *Zhùjiū Shì* clan was the *Sītú*;
the *Jūjiū Shì* clan was the *Sīmǎ*;
the *Shījiū Shì* clan was the *Sīkōng*;
the *Shuǎngjiū Shì* clan was the *Sīkòu*;
the *Hùjiū Shì* clan was the *Sīshì*.
The five *Jiū* clans were those who gathered the people.
The five *Zhì* were the five Masters of Crafts,
who improved tools and implements
and managed the people.
Therefore, he created writing and contracts,
"so the various officials might be governed,
and the myriad people might be scrutinized."
There were four talented sons:
named *Zhòng*,
named *Gāi*,
named *Xiū*,
and named *Xī*.
They were truly able to manage the elements of Metal, Wood, and Water.
Thus *Zhòng* became *Gōumáng*,
*Gāi* became *Rùshōu*,
and *Xiū* and *Xī* became *Xuánmíng*.
They were reverent and diligent in their tasks,
not losing their offices for generations,
and finally providing relief to *Qióngsāng*.
His descendant *Xiūjì*
saw a falling star,
and by this influence gave birth to the White Emperor *Wénmìng Róng Yǔ*.
His ears had three openings.
He served as the *Sīkōng* for *Yáo*,
in charge of leveling the waters and lands,
naming the mountains and rivers,
charting the Nine Provinces,
and establishing the Nine Tributes.
When his work was accomplished,
he was granted the Black Jade Scepter *Xuánguī*
to report his achievements to Heaven.
*Shùn* then abdicated the throne,
with a command like the decree of *Yáo*.
*Yǔ* then ascended the throne.
He composed the music *Dàxià*.
He was known to the world as *Xiàhòu*.
He passed the succession to his son *Qǐ*.
*Qǐ*'s sons *Tàikāng* and *Zhòngkāng* were established in turn.
There were five brothers,
all of whom possessed dark virtues
and were unable to handle imperial affairs;
they descended to wait at the banks of the *Luò* and *Ruì* rivers;
these were called the Five *Guān*.
His grandson *Xiāng* succeeded to the throne,
and the Way of *Xià* gradually declined.
Thereupon *Hòuyì* moved from *Chú* to *Qióngshí*,
and by relying on the people of *Xià*, he took over the government of *Xià*
and destroyed *Xiāng*.
The consort *Hòumín* was then pregnant;
she escaped through a hole
and fled to *Yǒuréng*,
where she gave birth to *Shàokāng*.
He served as the *Mùzhèng* for the *Réng* clan.
*Yì* relied on his own archery,
neglected the affairs of the people,
and indulged in hunting wild animals;
he discarded *Wǔluó*, *Bóyīn*, *Xióngkūn*, and *Mángyǔ*,
and employed *Hán Zhuó*.
*Zhuó* was a slandering youth of the *Báimíng Shì* clan.
The *Báimíng Shì* clan loathed him and cast him out.
*Yì* of the *Yí* took him in,
trusted him, and employed him,
making him his chief minister.
*Zhuó* practiced flattery within the court
and distributed bribes outside,
deceiving the people
and keeping *Yì* amused in the hunting fields.
He planted deception and concealment
to seize the state,
and both those outside and inside submitted to him.
*Yì* still did not repent;
as he was returning from hunting,
his household retainers killed and cooked him,
to feed him to his sons.
His sons could not bear to eat him
and died at the gate of *Qióng*.
*Mǐ* fled to the *Yǒugé Shì* clan.
*Zhuó* took *Yì*'s wives and fathered *Jiāo* and *Yì*.
Relying on their slanderous malice and deceit,
they lacked virtue toward the people.
He sent *Jiāo* to lead an army
to destroy the *Zhēnguàn* and *Zhēnxún* clans.
He settled *Jiāo* in *Guò*
and settled *Yì* in *Gē*.
He sent *Jiǎo* to seek out *Shàokāng*.
*Shàokāng* fled to *Yǒuyú*,
where he served as the *Bāozhèng*.
*Yúsī* gave him his two daughters in marriage
and granted him the city of *Lún*.
Having one *chéng* of land
and one *lǚ* of followers,
he was able to spread his virtue
and initiate his plans,
thereby gathering the people of *Xià*
and comforting the officials.
*Mǐ* gathered the remnants of the two states from *Yǒugé*
to destroy *Zhuó*
and established *Shàokāng* as ruler.
He then sent *Nǚ'ài* to spy on *Jiāo*
and sent *Hòuzhù* to lure *Yì*;
they subsequently destroyed *Guò* and *Gē*,
restored the achievements of *Yǔ*,
performed the *Xià* sacrifices as a counterpart to Heaven,
and did not lose the old possessions.
After seventeen generations, *Jié* lost the world.
When *Wǔ Wáng* conquered *Yīn*,
he enfeoffed his descendants at *Qǐ*,
or some at *Zēng*.
He also enfeoffed the descendants of *Shǎohào* at *Qí*.
Jiāo’s talent and strength surpassed the masses,
but he relied on his bravery and was ultimately destroyed.
Therefore, Nángōng Kuò said:
“Yì was skilled in archery,
and Ào could propel a boat on land,
yet neither met a natural death.”
The Sì surname split into clans:
Xiàhòu, Yǒuhù, Yǒunán, Zhēnxún, Bómiǎo, Xīn, Bāo, Fèi, Gē, Míng, and Zēng,
all of whom were descendants of Yǔ.
The Yáoguāng star was as white as the moon
and moved Nǚshū in the palace of Yōufáng,
giving birth to the Black Emperor, Zhuānxū.
His appearance featured joined ribs.
His personal title was Gāoyáng,
and his lineage title was Gònggōng.
He succeeded the Shàoyì clan.
His virtue followed the element of Water,
and he regulated things by Water;
therefore, he established Water Officials and named them after Water.
He took over during the decline of Shàoyì,
when the Jiǔlí tribe disturbed virtue,
so he commanded Zhòng and Lí to punish and civilize them.
He calculated the movements of the sun and moon,
and determined the East, West, South, and North.
He composed the music Wǔyīng.
He had eight talented sons:
Cāngshū, Tuíkǎi, Dǎoyǎn, Dàlín, Pángjiàng, Tíngjiān, Zhòngróng, and Shúdá.
They were wise, broad, and deep,
clear, sincere, and honest;
the people of the world called them the Bākǎi.
The Gònggōng clan had a son named Gōulóng
who was able to level the nine lands;
thus he was titled Hòutǔ.
After his death, he became the God of the Soil,
and the world offers sacrifices to him.
Sōngjiǎn swallowed a swallow’s egg and gave birth to Xiè,
who served as Yáo’s Sītú.
His duty was to bring the people into harmony
and align the five social relationships.
Fúdū saw a white vapor piercing the moon
and her spirit was moved, giving birth to the son of the Black Emperor, Lǚ.
His appearance featured two elbows on each arm.
His personal title was Tāng,
and his lineage title was Yīn.
He brought about Great Peace.
Later, the dynasty declined,
and Wǔdīng was born.
Upon ascending the throne,
he remained silent and did not speak,
meditating on the Way for three years,
and in a dream, he obtained a wise man to be his teacher.
He then sent people to seek him in all directions among the lowly, based on the image in his dream,
and found Fù Yuè,
who was then working as a convict laborer building walls at Fùyán.
He promoted him to be Dàgōng
and had him provide guidance and remonstrance morning and night.
Fearing that he might be timid or negligent,
the king issued an edict saying:
“As with metal,
I use you as a whetstone;
as with crossing a great river,
I use you as a boat and oar;
as with a time of great drought,
I use you as a heavy rain.
Open your heart
to enrich my heart.
If medicine does not cause dizziness,
the illness will not be cured;
if one walks barefoot without looking at the ground,
one’s feet will be injured.
You must collectively correct me,
and do not abandon me!”
Therefore, he was able to achieve a restoration
and was titled Gāozōng.
It lasted until Dì Xīn and then perished;
the world calls him Zhòu.
Wǔ Wáng enfeoffed Wēizǐ in Sòng
and enfeoffed Jīzǐ in Cháoxiǎn.
The Zǐ surname split into clans:
Yīn, Shí, Lái, Sòng, Lè, Xiāo, Kōngtóng, and Běiduàn,
all of whom were descendants of Tāng.
In the past, the Sage Kings observed the images in Heaven and Earth,
examined the measures of the gods,
explored the coming and going of mandates and calendars,
and inspected the virtuous deeds of the various lords,
and thus bestowed surnames and designated clans
to manifest their virtues and achievements.
Tradition says that there were a hundred distinct offices for the people;
the descendants of kings and dukes who for a thousand generations could fulfill those offices
were bestowed surnames based on things,
and these were called the Bǎixìng.
Surnames had ten distinct grades,
and for the King, they were called the thousand grades.
In the past, Yáo bestowed the surname Zǐ upon Xiè,
and the surname Jī upon Qì;
he bestowed the surname Sì upon Yǔ,
whose clan was called Yǒuxià;
Bóyí was given the surname Jiāng,
and his clan was called Yǒulǚ.
Down to the Three Dynasties,
when offices had hereditary merit,
there were official clans;
fiefs were the same.
In later, declining generations,
these were taken as surnames
and could not be changed.
Thus some passed down the original surname,
some took clans from titles, fiefs, or posthumous names,
some from states,
some from peerage ranks,
some from offices,
some from courtesy names,
some from occupations,
some from residences,
and some from symbols.
As for the eras of the Five Emperors and Three Kings,
these are what are called titles;
Wén, Wǔ, Zhāo, Jǐng, Chéng, Xuān, Dài, and Huán
are what are called posthumous names;
Qí, Lǔ, Wú, Chǔ, Qín, Jìn, Yàn, and Zhào
are what are called states;
Wáng-shì, Hóu-shì, Wángsūn, and Gōngsūn
are what are called ranks;
Sīmǎ, Sītú, Zhōngháng, and Xiàjūn
are what are called offices;
Bóyǒu, Mèngsūn, Zǐfú, and Shūzǐ
are what are called courtesy names;
Wū-shì, Jiàng-shì, and Táo-shì
are what are called occupations;
Dōngmén, Xīmén, Nángōng, Dōngguō, and Běiguō
are what are called residences;
Sānwū, Wǔlù, Qīngniú, and Báimǎ
are what are called symbols.
All these surnames and clan names
emerged from lineages and cannot be fully recorded.
The Marquis of Wèi destroyed Xíng,
and Zhāo Gōng married someone with the same surname;
this implies they all shared the same ancestor.
From recent antiquity onward,
this is not necessarily the case.
Of the surnames bestowed in antiquity,
generally they can be used,
but for the rest, it is difficult.
The Zhōu House declined,
Wú and Chǔ usurped titles,
and down through the Seven States,
all of them called themselves Kings.
Therefore, the clans of Wáng, Wángsūn, Gōngsūn, and clans based on posthumous names or offices
existed in each state;
among eighteen hundred states,
posthumous names and offices numbered in the thousands,
so their origins cannot be the same.
As for those with the surname Sūn,
some were of the rank of royal grandsons,
and some were of the rank of various grandsons;
thus there are those with the same ancestor but different surnames,
and those with the same surname but different ancestors.
There is also confusion and mixing
where they changed and entered into one another;
some followed the mother’s surname,
and some changed to avoid enemies.
Determining surnames by blowing pitch-pipes
is something only a Sage can do.
Today the people have been dispersed for a long time,
and few can master the musical laws.
Heaven and the Lord rectify their ancestors.
Therefore, I will briefly record the prominent ones,
to wait for scholars to join in adding to or subtracting from it.
Fúxī was surnamed Fēng;
his descendants were enfeoffed in the four states of Rèn, Sù, Xūqú, and Zhuānyú.
They indeed managed the sacrifices to Tàiyì and the Jì River,
and served as the masters of Dōngméng.
Lǔ Xī Gōng’s mother, Chéngfēng,
was likely a daughter of Xūqú.
The Jì-shì clan wished to attack Zhuānyú,
and Kǒngzǐ criticized them.
The descendants of Yándì,
including Bóyí of the Sìyuè,
conducted the ceremonies for Yáo,
"restraining the people through punishment,"
and were enfeoffed in Shēn and Lǚ.
Among their descendants, Shàng was born,
who became the teacher of Wén Wáng.
He overthrew Yīn and was enfeoffed in Qí,
while others were enfeoffed in Xǔ and Xiàng,
or enfeoffed in Jì,
or enfeoffed in Shēn.
The city of Shēn was located north of Wǎn in Nányáng, at the foot of Mount Xù.
Therefore, the *Shī* says:
"Diligently, the Bó of Shēn,
the King recommended him for service.
In his city at Xù,
he became a model for the southern states."
Thirty li west of Wǎn lived Lǚwàng.
Xǔ was in Yǐngchuān,
which is the present-day Xǔ Xiàn.
The Jiāng Róng lived between the Yī and Luò rivers,
until Jìn Huì Gōng moved them to Lùhún.
The Zhōu, Bó, Gān, Xì, Lù, and Yí clans,
as well as the Guó, Gāo, Xiāng, Xí, Shìqiáng, Dōngguō, Yōngmén, Zǐyǎ, Zǐwěi, Zǐxiāng, Zǐyuān, Zǐqián, Gōngqí, Hàngōng, Hè, and Lú clans of Qí,
are all of the Jiāng surname.
Huángdì had twenty-five sons,
who were divided into twelve surnames:
Jī, Yǒu, Qí, Jǐ, Téng, Zhǎn, Rèn, Jū, Lǐ, Jí, and the Huányī clan.
During the Spring and Autumn period,
Jìn had Qí Xī,
who recommended his son and nominated his enemy for office,
becoming famous for his loyalty and uprightness.
The Viscount of Jǔ was of the Jǐ surname.
At the rise of the Xià,
there was Rèn Xī, who served as the Xià Supervisor of Chariots,
and was enfeoffed in Xuē.
Later they moved to Pī,
and his descendant Zhònghuì lived in Xuē
and served as the Left Minister to Tāng.
Wáng Jì’s consort Tà Rèn,
as well as the Xiè, Zhāng, Chāng, Cǎi, Zhù, Jié, Quán, Bēi, Yù, and Kuángdà clans,
are all of the Rèn surname.
A lady of the Jí clan was the first consort of Hòujì,
and she gave birth to the ancestors of the Zhōu.
The Jí clan was enfeoffed in Yān.
Zhèng Wén Gōng had a lowly concubine named Yān Jí,
who dreamt that a god gave her an orchid, saying:
"I am Bótiáo,
I am your ancestor.
With this, you shall have the national fragrance,
and people will submit to and admire you."
When Wén Gōng saw Jí,
he gave her an orchid and shared her bed.
Jí told him of her dream
and said:
"Your handmaid lacks talent.
If she is lucky enough to have a child,
others may not believe her;
may I use the orchid as proof?"
The Duke said:
"Very well."
Subsequently, she gave birth to Mù Gōng.
The branches of the Jí clan
include the Kàn, Yǐn, Cài, Guāng, Lǔ, Yōng, Duàn, and Mìxū clans.
Coming to the Hàn dynasty,
there was Zhì Dū in Hédōng
and Zhì Jūnzhāng in Rǔnán;
the pronunciation of their surname was the same as the ancient Jí,
though the character used to write it was different.
Both were famous in their time.
When the era of the Shǎohào clan declined,
the Jiǔlí disordered virtue.
Zhuānxū took over the rule
and ordered the Southern Commissioner Zhòng to oversee Heaven to handle the spirits,
and the Fire Commissioner Lí to oversee Earth to handle the people,
so that the old norms were restored
and there was no mutual infringement or profanation.
This was called severing the connection between Earth and Heaven.
Now, Lí was Wúhuí, a descendant of the Zhuānxū clan.
He served as Fire Commissioner for the Gāoxīn clan,
purifying and illuminating the light of Heaven and the virtue of Earth,
and shining over the four seas;
thus he was named Zhùróng.
Later, the Sānmiáo returned to the ways of the Jiǔlí.
Yáo, succeeding the descendants of Zhòng and Lí, did not forget the old traditions,
and Xībó governed them again.
Thus, the Zhònglí clan for generations ordered Heaven and Earth,
distinguishing their separate duties
throughout the Three Dynasties,
and were enfeoffed in Chéng.
During the Zhōu era,
they served as Grand Marshal for Xuān Wáng.
The *Shī* praises: "The King spoke to the Yǐn clan,
appointing Chéng Bó Xiūfù."
Later, they lost their position
and went to Jìn to serve as marshals;
Qiān claimed to be their descendant.
The grandsons of Zhùróng
were divided into eight surnames:
Jǐ, Tū, Péng, Jiāng, Yún, Cáo, Sī, and Mǐ.
The descendant of the Jǐ surname was Liù Shū'ān,
whose descendant was named Dǒngfù.
He truly loved dragons very much
and could understand their desires to feed them,
so many dragons flocked to him.
He then learned to tame dragons
to serve Dì Shùn.
He was granted the surname Dǒng
and the clan name Huànlóng,
and was enfeoffed in Zōngchuān.
Zōngyí and the Shìwéi of the Péng surname
were all those who could tame dragons.
Huànlóng Páng, because of his loyal remonstrance,
was killed by Jié.
Among the descendants of Zhùróng,
the branches of the Jǐ surname were
the Kūnwú, Jí, Hù, Wēn, and Dǒng clans.
For the Tū surname, the Zōngyí and Huànlóng clans
were destroyed by the Xià.
For the Péng surname, the Péngzǔ, Shìwéi, and Zhūjī clans
were destroyed by the Shāng.
The people of Kuài of the Jiāng surname
were destroyed by the Zhōu.
The descendants of the Yún surname were enfeoffed in Yān, Kuài, Lù, and Bīyáng.
The lord of Yān took Zhòng Rèn as his wife;
he was greedy and stingy,
disregarding the worthy and neglecting the capable,
and for this reason, the state was lost.
Kuài was located between the Hé and Yī rivers;
its ruler was arrogant, greedy, and miserly,
reducing ranks and cutting emoluments.
His ministers became humble and submissive,
and superiors and inferiors did not communicate.
The poets worried about this
and thus composed "Gāoqiú," expressing their grief and mourning,
and "Fěifēng,"
hoping the ruler would first provide instruction.
The ruler of Kuài did not awaken to this,
and the Zhòng clan attacked them.
Superiors and inferiors could not employ each other,
and prohibitions and punishments were not enforced,
so the state met its end.
Yīng'ér, the Viscount of Lù,
married the elder sister of Jìn Chéng Gōng as his consort,
but Fēng Shū governed and mistreated her.
Jìn Bó Zōng was angered
and consequently attacked and destroyed Lù.
Xún Yīng Wǔzǐ attacked and destroyed Bīyáng.
The Cáo surname was enfeoffed in Zhū;
a branch of Zhū Yánzǐ
became the state of Xiǎozhū;
both were destroyed by Chǔ.
Xióng Yán, a descendant of the Mǐ surname,
was enfeoffed in Chǔ by Chéng Wáng;
he was known as Yùxióng
and also called Yùzǐ.
He had four sons:
Bóshuāng, Zhòngxuě, Shūxióng, and Jìxún.
Jìxún succeeded as the Viscount of Xíng,
while others were enfeoffed in Kuí
or enfeoffed in Yuè.
Because the Viscount of Kuí did not offer sacrifices to Zhùróng and Yùxióng,
Chǔ attacked and destroyed them.

The royal clan included the Chǔjì, Lièzōng, Dòujiáng, Liángchén, Qí, Mén, Hóu, Jìróng, Zhòngxióng, Zǐjì, Yáng, Wúgōu, Wěi, Shàn, Yáng, Zhāo, Jǐng, Yán, Yīngqí, Lái, Láixiān, Jí, Shēn, Zhào, Shěn, Hè, Jiǎn, Jíbái, Wǔ, Shěnxiān, Yútuī, Gōngjiàn, Zǐnán, Zǐgēng, Zǐwǔ, Zǐxī, Wángsūn, Tiángōng, Shūjiān, Lǔyáng, and Hēigōng clans;
all are of the Mǐ surname.
Chǔ Jì was the great-grandson of Wángzǐ Áo.
Fénmào begot Wěi Zhāng,
who was Wángzǐ Wúgōu.
The Prime Minister Sūnshū Áo was the son of Wěi Zhāng.
The Left Marshal Shù was the great-grandson of Zhuāng Wáng.
The Lord of Shè, Zhūliáng, was the third younger brother of Shù.
The Chǔ grandmaster Shēn Wúwèi
was also of the Wén clan.
In the beginning,
Zhòu of the Yǒusū clan lost Yīn because of the woman Dájǐ.
In the time of Zhōu Wǔ Wáng,
Yǒusū Fènshēng served as Minister of Justice and was enfeoffed in Wēn.
Later, there was Sū Qín in Luòyì.
In the era of the Gāoyáng clan, there were eight talented men:
Cāngshū, Tuíkǎi, Dǎoyǎn, Dàlín, Pángjiàng, Tíngjiān, Zhòng廣, and Shūdá,
whom the people of the world called the Bā Kǎi.
A later descendant was Gāoyáo,
who served Shùn.
Shùn said:
"Gāoyáo!
The barbarians are disturbing the Xià,
and there are bandits, thieves, traitors, and villains;
you shall serve as the Judge."
His son Bóyì
was able to manage the common people to assist Shùn and Yǔ,
and he tamed birds and beasts;
Shùn granted him the surname Yíng.
Later there was Zhòngyǎn,
who had a bird's body and human speech,
and served as a charioteer for the Xià Emperor Tài Wù.
His descendants included Fèi Zhòng,
who fathered Èlái and Jì Shèng.
When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
he also killed Èlái.
Among the descendants of Jì Shèng was Zàofù,
who served King Mù of Zhōu with his skill in charioteering.
King Mù traveled to the Western Sea and forgot to return;
at that time, Xú Yǎn started a rebellion.
Zàofù drove the chariot,
covering a thousand lǐ in one day,
to go and suppress him.
The King enfeoffed Zàofù at Zhào Chéng,
and thus he took it as his lineage name.
Later, they lost their domain,
down to Zhào Sù,
who served as a Grand Master and Minister in Jìn.
Eleven generations later, they became Marquises,
and five generations after that was King Wǔlíng.
Five generations later, Zhào perished.
The Gōngshū, Hándān, Zǐrǔ, Yīngqí, Lóujì, Lú, and Yuán clans
were all of the Zhào Yīng lineage name.
Among the descendants of Èlái was Fēizǐ.
Because he was skilled at animal husbandry,
King Xiào of Zhōu enfeoffed him at Qín.
The generations followed the location and considered him the Grand Master of the Western Frontier,
which is the Qiān Qín Tíng.
Later, they were ranked among the feudal lords.
Five generations later, they took the title of King.
Six generations later, Shǐhuáng was born in Hándān,
which is why he was called Zhào Zhèng.
The Liáng, Gé, Jiāng, Huáng, Xú, Jǔ, Liào, Liù, and Yīng are all descendants of Gāotáo.
The Zhōnglí, Yùnyǎn, Tùqiú, Xúnliáng, Xiūyú,
Báizhì, Fēilián, Mìrú, Dōngguàn, Liáng, Shí, Bái, Bā, Gōngbā Gōngbā, Tán, Fù, and Pú clans
are all of the Yīng lineage name.
The descendants of Emperor Yáo were the Táotáng clan.
Later there was Liú Lěi,
who could rear dragons.
Kǒngjiǎ bestowed the lineage name Yùlóng upon him
to replace the descendants of Shǐwéi.
During the Zhōu, they became the Tángdù clan.
When the Zhōu declined,
Xíshú's son Wéi fled the troubles of Zhōu for the state of Jìn.
He fathered Zǐyú,
who served as an official
to maintain rectitude in the court.
Since there were no idle officials in the court,
his lineage name became the Shì clan.
He served as the Minister of Works
to maintain rectitude in the state.
Since the state had no failed achievements,
his lineage name became Sīkōng.
He received the fief of Suí,
so his lineage name became the Suí clan.
Shì Wěi's grandson Huì
assisted Dukes Wén and Xiāng
and was not hated among the feudal lords.
He served as a Minister
to support Dukes Chéng and Jǐng,
and the army had no failed policies.
He served as a commander
and held the position of Tutor.
He standardized punishments and laws
and collected instructional texts.
The state had no wicked people,
and the thieves of Jìn fled to Qín.
Thereupon the Marquis of Jìn requested ceremonial robes and caps from the King.
The King commanded Suí Huì to be a Minister,
thus he received Fàn
and was posthumously named Wǔzǐ.
Wǔzǐ was cultured;
he established the alliance between Jìn and Jīng,
brought fraternal states into submission,
and ensured there were no rifts.
Thus he received Xún and Lè.
From this, among the descendants of Emperor Yáo
are the Táotáng, Liú, Yùlóng, Tángdù, Xí, Shì, Jì, Sīkōng, Suí, Fàn, Xún, Lè, Zhì, Jì, Gǔ, Qiáng, Rǎo, Lí, and Fù clans. Chǔ's Prime Minister Jiàn once asked Wénzǐ about the virtue of Fàn Wǔzǐ.
Wénzǐ replied:
"The Master's household affairs were well-governed.
When he spoke in the state of Jìn,
he exhausted his sincerity without selfishness.
His ritual officers and chroniclers presented the truth without shame.
His household affairs were free from suspicion,
and his ritual officers and chroniclers did not pray for personal favors."
Jiàn returned
and reported this.
King Kāng said:
"Neither spirits nor men have resentment.
It is appropriate that the Master served as the right-hand man to five rulers
and became a leader of the feudal lords."
Therefore, regarding the Liú clan from Táng downwards and before the Hàn,
for virtue recognized in the world,
none was as prosperous as that of Fàn Huì.
This also shows the merit of cultivating oneself to bring peace to others.
When King Wǔ conquered Yīn,
he enfeoffed the descendants of Emperor Yáo at Zhù.
Emperor Shùn was surnamed Yú,
and also Yáo,
and lived in Guī.
When King Wǔ conquered Yīn,
he enfeoffed Guī Mǎn at Chén;
this was Duke Hú.
The Chén Yuán, Yǎo, Xián, Qìng, Xià, Zōng, Lái, Yí, Sītú, and Sīchéng clans
were all of the Guī lineage name.
Duke Lì's son Wán fled to Qí.
Duke Huán was pleased with him
and made him the Overseer of Craftsmen.
His descendants greatly won the hearts of the people
and eventually seized the throne for themselves.
This was King Wēi,
and they perished after five generations.
The people of Qí called the Chén clan the Tián clan.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn moved the various Tián families to Guānzhōng,
and there were the First through the Eighth clans.
Chancellor Tián Qiānqiū, Sīzhí Tián Rén,
as well as Tián Xiān of Dùyáng and Tián Xiān of Dàng,
were all descendants of Chén.
Emperor Wǔ granted Qiānqiū the right to ride a small carriage into the palace hall;
therefore, the world called him the Carriage Chancellor.
As for [Wáng] Mǎng, who claimed to be a descendant of Tián Ān,
he changed his lineage name because of the Wáng family.
Mǎng's deceitful actions
were truly in the style of Tián Cháng.
Among the branches of Jìngzhòng
were the Pí, Zhàn, Jǔ, Yǔ, Xiàn, Zǐ, Yàng, Wǔ, Fáng, Gāo, Máng, and Qín clans.
Emperor Yǐ's eldest son was Wēizǐ Kāi,
the elder brother of Zhòu by a concubine.
King Wǔ enfeoffed him at Sòng,
which is present-day Suīyáng.

The Sòng Kǒng, Zhùqí, Hánxiàn, Jìlǎonán, Jùchén, Jīng, Shìfù, Huángfǔ, Huá, Yú, Érdǒng, Ài, Suì, Jiūyí, Zhōngyě, Yuèjiāo, Wán, Huái, Bùdì, Jì, Niú, Sīchéng, Gāng, Jìn, Zhǐ, Cháo, Bó, Yòuguī, Sānyuàn, Wángfū, Yí, Zhēng, Zhèng, Mùyí, Lín, Zāng, Huǐ, Shā, Hēi, Wéiguī, Jì, Jù, Zhuān, Jǐ, Chéng, Biān, Róng, Mǎi, Wěi, Huán, Dài, Xiàng, and Sīmǎ clans
were all of the Zǐ lineage name.
Duke Mǐn's son Fǔfù Hé fathered Sòngfù,
Sòngfù fathered the Heir Apparent,
the Heir Apparent fathered Zhèng Kǎofù,
Zhèng Kǎofù fathered Kǒngfù Jiā,
and Kǒngfù Jiā fathered Zǐmù Jīnfù.
Jīnfù was reduced to the status of a scholar-official;
therefore, it is said his lineage rank was extinguished in Sòng.
Jīnfù fathered Qífù,
and Qífù fathered Fángshú.
Fángshú was pressured by the Huá clan
and fled to Lǔ,
becoming the Grand Master of Fáng;
therefore, he was called Fángshú.
Fángshú fathered Bóxià,
and Bóxià fathered Shūliáng Hé,
who was the Grand Master of Zōu.
Therefore, he was called Zōu Shūhé,
and he fathered Kǒngzǐ.
Crown Prince Jìn of King Líng of Zhōu
possessed accomplished virtue from childhood,
was intelligent and broad-minded,
and was gentle, respectful, sincere, and quick-witted.
When the Gǔ and Luò rivers flooded and fought each other,
and were about to destroy the royal palace,
the King wished to dam them.
Crown Prince Jìn remonstrated,
believing it did not accord with the heart of Heaven,
and that it would be better to cultivate governance.
Duke Píng of Jìn sent Shū Yù on a diplomatic mission to Zhōu,
who met the Crown Prince
and spoke with him;
five times he praised him, and three times he was at a loss for words.
He withdrew hesitantly
and upon returning, told Duke Píng:
"Crown Prince Jìn is only fifteen years old,
yet Yù was unable to keep up with him in conversation;
My Lord, please serve him."
Duke Píng sent Shī Kuàng to see Crown Prince Jìn.
Crown Prince Jìn spoke with him;
Shī Kuàng submitted to his virtue
and they formed a deep bond.
He then asked Kuàng:
"I have heard the Grand Music Master can know the length of a person's life."
Shī Kuàng replied:
"Your complexion is red and white,
and your voice is clear yet faint;
the color of fire suggests a short life."
Jìn said:
"Indeed.
In three years, I shall go up to be a guest of the Sovereign;
you must be careful not to speak of this,
or calamity will reach you."
Three years later, the Crown Prince died.
Kǒngzǐ heard of this and said:
"How regrettable!
It has killed my lord."
Because people of the world believed he knew the time of his departure beforehand,
a tradition arose calling him the immortal Wángzǐ Qiáo.
After he became an immortal,
his successors avoided the Zhōu calamities in Jìn
and made their home in Píngyáng,
taking Wáng as their clan name.
thereafter, for generations his descendants enjoyed the arts of nourishing one's nature and becoming an immortal.
Among the ducal clans of Lǔ,

there were the Jiǎo, Hòu, Zhòng, Zāng, Shī, Mèng, Zhòngsūn, Fú, Gōngshān, Nángōng, Shūsūn, Shūzhòng, Zǐwǒ, Zǐshì, Jì, Gōngchú, Gōngwū, Gōngzhī, Zǐgān, Huá, Zǐyán, Zǐqū, Zǐyǎ, Zǐyáng, Dōngmén, Gōngxī, Gōngshí, Shū, Zǐjiā, Róng, Zhǎn, and Yǐ clans;
all were of the Jī surname of Lǔ.
Among the ducal clans of Wèi,
the Shí, Shìshū, Sūn, Nìng, Zǐqí, Sītú, Gōngwén, Xīguī, Gōngshū, Gōngnán, Gōngshàng, Gōngmèng, and Jiāngzhě clans
also frequently held power and favor
and were noble ministers.
As for the Marquis of Liú, Zhāng Liáng,
he belonged to the Jī surname of the Hán ducal clan.
When Qín Shǐhuáng destroyed Hán,
Liáng’s younger brother died and was not buried;
Liáng dispersed his family fortune of ten million
to seek revenge for Hán.
He attacked Shǐhuáng at Bólàngshā,
but mistakenly struck the secondary carriage with a mallet.
Qín searched for the culprit urgently,
so Liáng changed his surname to Zhāng
and hid in Xiàpī,
where he met the divine man Huángshígōng,
who gave him the art of war.
When the Duke of Pèi rose up,
Liáng went to join him.
The Duke of Pèi sent him to assist Hán Xìn in capturing and pacifying the Hán lands,
establishing Chéng, the Lord of Héngyáng, as the King of Hán,
and appointing Liáng as the Hán Xìndū.
"Xìndū" means Sītú.
Commoners' pronunciation was previously incorrect;
they said "Xìndū,"
some said "Shēntú,"
or "Shèngtú,"
but they all essentially refer to the same Sītú.
Later biographers did not know the origin of "Xìndū,"
and willfully invented a meaning,
believing that this meant he was the King of Dài and moved to Xìndū.
All the descendants of Huánshū
included the Hán, Yán, Yīng, Huàyú, Gōngzú, and Zhāng clans;
these were all of the Jī surname following Hán.
Formerly, King Xuān of Zhōu also had a Marquis of Hán,
whose state was near Yān;
thus the *Classic of Poetry* says:
"Vast is that city of Hán,
completed by the armies of Yān."
Later, Hán Xī was also surnamed Hán;
he was attacked by Wèi Mǎn
and moved to dwell in the midst of the sea.
Bìgōng Gāo shared the same surname as Zhōu;
he was enfeoffed at Bì,
which became his clan name.
When the Duke of Zhōu passed away,
Gāo succeeded to his duties.
Later his descendants lost their position
and became commoners.
When Bì Wàn assisted Duke Xiàn of Jìn,
in the sixteenth year, the Duke sent Zhào Sù to drive the chariot
and Bì Wàn to be the right-hand guard,
and for destroying Gěng and Wèi, he enfeoffed Wàn;
this is the present-day Héběi County.
Wèi Kē also took the clan name Lìnghú.
Nine generations after Wàn, there was Marquis Wén of Wèi.
Marquis Wén’s grandson Yīng became King Huì of Wèi,
and the state perished after five generations.
Bì Yáng’s grandson Yù Ràng
served Earl Zhì;
Earl Zhì treated him as a distinguished scholar of the state,
and Yù Ràng repaid Earl Zhì for the grace of recognizing his talent;
the whole world records his righteousness.
The Wèi, Lìnghú, Bùyǔ, Yè Dàfū, Bóxià, and Wèiqiáng clans,
and the Yù clan, were all branches of the Bì clan
and were originally of the Jī surname.
Yǒu, the son of King Lì of Zhōu, was enfeoffed at Zhèng.
The descendants of Gòngshū of Zhèng
became the Gōngwén clan.
The Xuān, Jūn, Zǐqiáng, Qiángliáng, Juǎn, Huì, Yǎ, Kǒng, Zhàoyáng, Tiánzhāng, Gū, Wángsūn, Shǐguī, Qiāng, Qiāngxiàn, and Suì clans
were all of the Jī surname of Wèi.
The Xiè clan of the Jìn ducal family
was also ranked as Lǚ;
Xiè Ruì further followed the city name to become Jì;
later there was Lǚ Qǐ,
styled Jūbó.
Xiè Chóu took his sustenance from Kǔ
and was styled Kǔchéngshū;
Xiè Zhì took his sustenance from Wēn
and was styled Wēnjì;
each took these as their clan names.
Among the ranks of the Xiè clan,
there were the Zhōu and Qí clans.
Bózōng was killed for his forthrightness;
his son Zhōulí fled to Chǔ;
also, because Xiè Wǎn was forthright and harmonious,
he was envied by Zǐcháng
and was executed.
His son Pǐ fled to Wú to become the Grand Minister;
taking warning from his ancestors' conduct of meeting disaster through forthrightness,
he engaged in flattery and caused the downfall of Wú.
Among the ranks of the Xiè clan,
there were the Jì, Lǚ, Kǔchéng, Wēn, and Bó clans;
the grandson of Marquis Jìng, Luán Bīn,
as well as the Fù, Yóu, Jiǎ, Hú, Yángshé, Jìsù, and Jí clans,
along with Duke Xiāng’s grandson Sūn Yǎn,
were all of the Jī surname of Jìn.
Duke Mù of Jìn fathered Huánshū,
Huánshū fathered Hán Wàn,
who served as a grand master of Jìn;
ten generations later came Marquis Wǔ of Hán,
five generations later King Huì of Hán,
and after five more generations the state perished.
Xìn, the grandson of a concubine of King Xiāng,
was called Hán Xìndū by common people.
Gāozǔ considered Xìn a grandson of the Hán royal family
and made him King of Hán;
later he was moved to rule Dài,
was attacked by the Xiōngnú,
and surrendered to them.
Hàn sent General Chái to attack him,
and Xìn was beheaded at Cānhé;
Xìn’s wife and children fled into the Xiōngnú.
In the time of Emperor Jǐng,
Xìn’s son Tuídāng and grandson Chì came to surrender;
Hàn enfeoffed Tuídāng as the Marquis of Gōnggāo
and Chì as the Marquis of Xiāngchéng.
As for Hán Yān,
he was a Palace Attendant during Emperor Wǔ’s time,
uniquely noble and favored.
Hán Shuō, the Marquis of Àndào,
and Hán Zēng, the General of the Front,
were both prominent in Hàn.
Their descendants were distributed among Yánglíng, Màolíng, and Dùlíng according to the emperors of their times.
And the various Hán clans of Hànyáng and Jīnchéng
were all their descendants.
Other descendants of Xìn remained among the Xiōngnú.
The Sì, Fēng, Yóu, Guó, Rán, Kǒng, Yǔ, Liáng, and Dàjì clans.
The ancestors of these ten clans
were the sons of Duke Mù;
each took their courtesy names as their surnames.
Along with the Bóyǒu, Mǎshī, and Chǔshī clans,
they were all of the Jī surname of Zhèng.
Tàibó ruled Wú,
wearing his robes properly
to govern according to the rites of Zhōu.
Zhòngyōng succeeded him,
cutting his hair and tattooing his body,
and considering nakedness an ornament.
When King Wǔ conquered Yīn,
he enfeoffed their descendants in Wú,
ordering a great bestowal upon Northern Wú.
Jìzhá resided in Yánzhōulái,
hence he was called Jìzǐ of Yánlíng.
Hélǘ’s younger brother, King Fúgài, fled to Tángxī in Chǔ,
and took it as his clan name.
These were all of the Jī surname.
Féng Jiǎn Zǐ was a Grand Master of Zhèng.
Later, Hán had Féng Tíng,
who served as the Governor of Shàngdǎng.
He deflected misfortune onto Zhào,
which led to the disaster at Chángpíng.
Qín had General Féng Jié,
who was executed along with Lǐ Sī.
At the rise of Hàn,
there was Féng Táng,
who discussed generals and commanders with Emperor Wén.
Later there was Féng Fèngshì,
a native of Shàngdǎng,
who reached the rank of General.
His daughter was a Zhāoyí concubine of Emperor Yuán,
and thus the family settled in the capital.
His grandson was Yàn,
whose courtesy name was Jìngtōng.
He was devoted to learning and valued righteousness;
the scholars called him "The harmonious and dignified Féng Jìngtōng of virtuous conduct."
He wrote dozens of essays,
and Emperor Xiàozhāng loved and valued his writings.
Xún Xī, a Grand Master of Jìn, served Duke Xiàn.
His descendants commanded the Central Army,
so their surname became Zhōngháng,
and they received their fief in Zhì.
Zhì Guǒ advised Zhì Bó but was not listened to,
so he separated his clan in the Grand Historian's records as the Fǔ clan.
Sūn Bóyǎn, a Grand Master of Jìn, was truly in charge of the archives,
so his surname became Jí.
Xīn Yǒu had two sons, and the lineage was overseen by Dǒng,
so their surname became Dǒng.
The *Shī* praises King Xuān,
and first mentions that "Zhāng Zhòng was filial and friendly."
By the Spring and Autumn period,
Sòng had Zhāng Báimiè.
Only Zhāng Hóu and Zhāng Lǎo of Jìn
were truly a great family.
Zhāng Mèngtán assisted Zhào Xiāngzǐ in destroying Zhì Bó,
then escaped from merit and rewards
to farm at Yùshān.
Later, Wèi had Zhāng Yí and Zhāng Chǒu.
By the Hàn dynasty,
the Zhāng surname became increasingly numerous.
Zhāng Ěr, the King of Chángshān,
was a man of Liáng.
Chancellor Zhāng Cāng
was a man of Yángwǔ.
There was also the Marquis of Dōngyáng, Zhāng Xiāngrú.
Grandee of the Censors Zhāng Tāng
revised and added to the laws and ordinances
to prevent wickedness and evil,
which benefited the people.
He also liked to recommend worthy and prominent scholars,
and thus received blessings and protection.
His son Ānshì served as General of Chariots and Cavalry
and was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Fùpíng.
He was kind, benevolent, frugal, and modest;
he was reserved regarding power and fond of hidden virtues.
Because of this, his descendants flourished,
and every generation had worthy offspring.
They were further enfeoffed at Wǔshǐ,
and despite the chaos of Wáng Mǎng,
their state enjoyed continued existence.
The family produced a total of four Ducal Ministers
and through generations was famous for loyalty, filial piety, and righteous conduct.
Previously there were Chancellor Zhāng Yǔ
and Grandee of the Censors Zhāng Zhōng;
later there were Grand Marshal Zhāng Pú,
a native of Rǔnán,
and Grand Tutor Zhāng Yǔ,
a native of the State of Zhào.
Among the administrators of towns and neighborhoods,
there was no place without someone named Zhāng.
Xièyì in Hédōng has Zhāngchéng,
and there is a Western Zhāngchéng.
Could it be that the ancestors of the Jìn Zhāngs came from there?
The Yǎn surname includes Shǔyōng, Shǔjiū, Shǔlóng, Shǔgòng, Zhǐlóng, Lì, Yín, Shēn, Huì, Liù, Yuàn, Fěi, and Gāoguó;
the Qìng surname includes Fán, Yǐn, and Luò;
the Màn surname includes Dèng and Yōu;
the Guī surname includes Hú, Yǒu, and Hé;
the Zhēn surname includes Huá and Qí;
the Jǐ surname includes Qī and Shū;
the Yù surname includes Shǔ, Pān, and Tāng;
the Wéi surname includes Ráo, Rǎng, and Chà;
the Wěi surname includes the Red Di, and the Héng surname includes the White Di.
These are all very auspicious surnames.
Qí had Bǎo Shū,
whose family were Ministers and Grand Masters for generations.
Jìn had Bǎo Guǐ.
Hàn had Bǎo Xuān,
who was loyal and upright for generations
and was a famous official of Hàn.
Lì Shēng of Hàn was an envoy,
and his younger brother Shāng was a general.
Now the various Lì families of Gāoyáng are prominent surnames.
Long ago, Zhòng Shānfǔ also had the surname Fán.
His posthumous title was Mù Zhòng,
and he was enfeoffed in Nányáng.
Nányáng is in what is now Hénèi.
Later there was Fán Qīngzǐ.
The Màn surname was enfeoffed in Dèng,
and later they took it as their surname.
To the north of Shàngcǎi in Dèng County of Nányáng, there is the ancient Dèngchéng,
and to the north of Xīncǎi, there is another ancient Dèngchéng.
During the Spring and Autumn period,
King Wén of Chǔ destroyed Dèng.
In the Hàn dynasty, there were Dèng Tōng and Dèng Guǎng.
In Later Hàn, there was Dèng Yǔ of Xīnyě,
who was enfeoffed as Marquis of Gāomì for his primary merit in assisting the mandate.
His granddaughter, the Empress Dowager, was by nature compassionate, kind, strict, and brilliant.
She strictly ordered that none of the family members should hold power.
The capital was clean and quiet,
as if there were no noble relatives.
She diligently thought of and worried for the people,
never idling day or night.
Because of this, when facing the Qiāng soldier rebellion,
great floods, and famines,
she was able to restore the situation
and maintain order, peace, and abundance.
After the Empress Dowager passed away,
various wicked people conspired together,
competing to add slanders and embellishments
to destroy the Dèng family,
which the whole world lamented.
The family of Duke Zhāo of Lǔ's mother had the surname Guī.
In the Hàn dynasty, there was Wěi Xiāo Jìmèng.
Duǎn refers to the Quǎnjióng clan,
whose ancestors originally came from Huángdì.
Regarding the Xú, Xiāo, Suǒ, Zhángsháo, Táo, Fán, Qí, Jī, Fán, and Tú clans,
they are all ancient surnames of the Yīn people.
When Hàn arose,
Chancellor of State Xiāo Hé was enfeoffed as Marquis of Cuó.
He was originally a man of Pèi.
The Xiāo clan of Chánglíng today are his descendants.
General of the Front Xiāo Wàngzhī's lineage
and the Xiāo clans of Dōnghǎi and Dùlíng are his descendants.
Among the Grandees of the Censors, there was Fán Yánshòu,
a native of Xiāngyáng in Nánjùn.
The Fán clans of Dùlíng and Xīnfēng are his descendants.
The Zhōu, Shào, Bì, Róng, Shàn, Yǐn, Liú, Fù, Gǒng, and Cháng clans
were all families of Ducal Ministers and Grand Masters throughout the generations of the Zhōu house.
Zhōu and Shào
were the cadet sons of the Duke of Zhōu and Duke of Shào.
They received the fiefs of the two Dukes
and served as the chief officials,
so for generations, the houses of the Duke of Zhōu and Duke of Shào never ceased.
Yǐn was originally an official title,
like the Grand Tutor in Sòng,
or the Lìngyǐn and Zuǒyǐn in Chǔ.
Yǐn Jǐfǔ assisted King Xuān with great achievements.
The *Shī* says:
"The Grand Master of the Yǐn clan
is the foundation of Zhōu."
Dukes Mù, Xiāng, Qǐng, and Jìng of Shàn
possessed illustrious virtue through the generations,
with talent second only to sages.
Therefore, Shùxiàng praised them, saying that they would surely multiply and flourish in later times.
Kǔchéng is the name of a city
located northeast of the Salt Lake.
Later people wrote it sometimes as "Kū";
when people of Qí heard its sound,
they wrote it as "Kùchéng";
when those in Dùnhuáng saw its written form,
they called it "Chēchéng";
those in Hànyáng,
not liking the characters "Kū" or "Kǔ,"
changed the writing to "Gǔchéng clan."
Tángxī is the name of a valley
located in Xīpíng of Rǔnán.
The courtesy name of Yǔ was Zǐqǐ.
"Qǐ" is a character meaning "to open."
Former people mistakenly wrote "Tángxī" as "Qǐ,"
and later people changed it,
and then it was written as "Kāi."
In the case of the ancient Qīdiāo Kāi and Gōngyě Cháng,
former people wrote "Diāo" using the "Yì" radical,
abbreviating it to "Zhōu,"
and they also mistakenly wrote "Yě" as "Gǔ,"
which later generations passed down as "Gǔ,"
or they further split into the Gǔ, Chéng, Táng, Kāi, Gōng, Yě, Qī, and Zhōu clans.
These several clans
all have the same origin but different developments.
Generally, the merging, changing, and dividing of surnames
are mostly of this kind.
This serves as an illustration;
it is difficult to record them all.
The *Yì* says:
"The gentleman classifies groups to distinguish things,"
"Gains extensive knowledge of previous words and past deeds to accumulate virtue,"
"Learning to gather it,
questioning to distinguish it."
Therefore, I have briefly observed the records of the world,
collected from the classics,
followed the lands,
and referenced clear records,
to praise the descendants of sages and worthies,
to rank the ancestors of various clans,
to speak of the origins of lineages and surnames,
and arranged these two chapters of *Jiǎyì*
to bequeath them to the later worthies of today.
Living in the present world,
it is noble to be able to achieve great success;
at the highest level, there is establishing virtue,
and below that, there is establishing words.
Being mediocre and untalented,
and not having the capacity and ability for official duty,
having never served in such a role,
I have nowhere to demonstrate my merit.
My heart is occasionally moved,
so I take up the brush to record several passages,
using words to connect my humble feelings,
merely so that they are not neglected or forgotten.
Though the words of woodcutters are humble and lowly,
the former sages also consulted them.
Roughly drafting the accounts of former sages,
in thirty-six chapters,
to continue previous teachings,
like Zuǒ Qiūmíng’s works on the *Wǔ Jīng*.
Of the legacy left by former sages,
none is greater than their teachings.
Be broad in learning and extensive in knowledge;
when in doubt, think to ask.
Wisdom and clarity are what bring achievement;
virtue and righteousness are what are established.
Fùzǐ loved learning
and was "tireless in teaching others."
Therefore, "Extolling Learning" (*Zàn Xué*) is arranged first.
In the learning of a scholar,
the fundamental is valued and the superficial is held cheap.
The great man does not prioritize flowery display;
the gentleman strives for substance.
Although the Rites act as a matchmaker,
they must be conveyed through ritual gifts.
The customs of the time trend toward the superficial;
I fear the destruction of the arts.
Therefore, "Attending to the Fundamentals" (*Wù Běn*) is arranged second.
People all possess wisdom and virtue,
but suffer from being clouded by profit.
Acting foully to seek glory is like
wearing a basin and looking at the sky.
"To practice benevolence, one does not become wealthy;
to be wealthy, one is not benevolent."
If one wishes to cultivate virtuous conduct,
one must be cautious of its source.
Therefore, "Restraining Profit" (*È Lì*) is arranged third.
The world does not understand discourse
and changes according to the masses.
They do not ask about will or conduct,
but only record official rank and title.
Wealth and honor gained through unrighteousness
were what Zhòngní felt shame for.
Grieved by the decline of customs,
which have drifted far from the sages' descriptions.
Therefore, "On Honor" (*Lùn Róng*) is arranged fourth.
That which is a hardship for the worthy,
and what is feared regarding jealousy,
is that all envy those who surpass them
and take it as a deep resentment.
Either based on flaws or provocations,
or creating trouble out of nothing.
It is painful that the ruler does not investigate
and believes slanderous words.
Therefore, "The Difficulty of the Worthy" (*Xián Nán*) is arranged fifth.
Tracing the source of clarity
and describing where darkness arises;
where rejecting admonition leads to failure,
and where calamity and chaos are formed.
Those in power
all wish to monopolize the ruler,
blocking and obscuring worthy scholars
to usurp the sovereign's power.
Therefore, "Clarity and Darkness" (*Míng Àn*) is arranged sixth.
Looking up to the former kings
and how they achieved Great Peace,
their evaluations and promotions
are written in the *Wǔ Jīng*.
The reality of punishment and reward
is not based on empty names.
If virtuous sounds are clearly prepared,
why ask about the palace court?
Therefore, "Evaluation of Performance" (*Kǎo Jì*) is arranged seventh.
When a ruler selects scholars,
he always seeks wisdom and ability.
But the various officials offer recommendations,
competing to promote inferior talents.
"Hating those who are grasping and oppressive,"
how can any official govern well?
Buying medicine and getting wild geese,
it is difficult to act as a physician.
Therefore, "Longing for the Worthy" (*Sī Xián*) is arranged eighth.
To trace the origins of Heaven and Man
and their interconnected causes,
the key to achieving harmony
lies in the ruler.
Upholding the law and selecting the worthy,
the state begins with oneself.
When the treacherous steal positions,
who will oversee them?
Therefore, "The Root of Governance" (*Běn Zhèng*) is arranged ninth.
