Observing the past and present,
and even looking into books and records,
rulers all desire order,
while ministers often delight in chaos.
Loyalty and sycophancy are muddled together,
each advancing with its own kind.
Often suffering from a lack of clarity,
the ruler believes treacherous discourse.
Therefore, "Latent Sighs" (*Qián Tàn*) is arranged tenth.
Status arises from virtue,
and virtue is established through valuing loyalty.
It is what the state relies upon,
and where safety and danger are tied.
Without being upright and honest,
kind, compassionate, and harmonious,
serving the ruler like Heaven,
and looking upon the people like children,
one cannot preserve rank and position
nor complete a good name.
Therefore, "The Value of Loyalty" (*Zhōng Guì*) is arranged eleventh.
The former kings managed wealth
to "prevent the people from doing wrong."
The *Hóng Fàn* worries for the people;
the *Shī* satirizes the pursuit of profit.
Those who are superficial and false are many;
fundamental agriculture must decline.
Regulate it with systems;
how could one not discuss this?
Therefore, "Superficial Extravagance" (*Fú Chǐ*) is arranged twelfth.
Accumulating small things harms conduct;
seeking comfort ruins one's name.
The clear-sighted should not indulge desires
without showing a look of remorse.
Being enough to reject admonition
and not following good advice when hearing it,
small comforts invite humiliation,
and in the end, there must be misfortune.
Therefore, "Being Cautious of the Minute" (*Shèn Wēi*) is arranged thirteenth.
An enlightened ruler thinks of the good
and exhausts his spirit for the worthy and wise.
But the various officials act with favoritism
and do not verify truth or falsehood.
They merely exalt empty reputation
to deceive and dazzle one another.
When they occupy offices and take on duties,
they have no results or achievements.
Therefore, "Actual Recommendations" (*Shí Gòng*) is arranged fourteenth.
Sages nurture the worthy
as well as the myriad people.
The systems of the former kings
were all sufficient to replace plowing.
If rank is increased but stipends are reduced,
there must be a collapse of standards.
First increase the officials' salaries,
then peace can be achieved.
Therefore, "Ranking Stipends" (*Bān Lù*) is arranged fifteenth.
The ruler worries and the ministers toil;
this is the universal principle of past and present.
The superior thinks of achieving peace;
the subordinate should exhaust his kindness.
Upright and good, faithful scholars
all feel pained by frequent amnesties.
Evil and treachery flourish
solely because of amnesties.
Thus, "On Amnesty" (*Shù Shè*) is arranged sixteenth.
When the former kings governed the world,
they wielded both majesty and virtue;
for rewards, they established marquises,
and for punishments, they had severe penalties.
When rewards are heavy and prohibitions are strict,
the ministers then respect their duties.
To cultivate great peace,
one must follow this law.
Therefore, *Sānshì*, chapter seventeen, is narrated.
The people are the foundation of the state;
grain is the lifeblood of the people.
If their daily labor leaves them no leisure,
how can grain be abundant?
High officials and ministers
"tire and toil the common people,"
lightly seizing the people’s time;
this is truly something to be indignant and remonstrate about!
Therefore, *Àirì*, chapter eighteen, is narrated.
Observing what officials govern,
brawls and lawsuits are the most numerous.
Tracing the origin of where the disaster arises,
it is the work of deceit and fraud.
To cut off the branches,
one must block the source.
When the people do not deceive or lie,
the world will then be at peace.
Therefore, *Duànsòng*, chapter nineteen, is narrated.
Among the *Wǔdì* and the *Sānwáng*,
there are differences in quality and sentiment.
Although one wishes to surpass the *Huáng*,
one must first achieve peace.
"Benevolence must follow after a generation,"
is the canon of *Zhòngní*.
Encountering decline and wicked shepherds,
how can one not use punishments?
Therefore, *Shuāizhì*, chapter twenty, is narrated.
Sagely kings worry about encouragement,
selecting and training generals and commanders,
granting them the ceremonial axe,
and vesting them with power and nobility.
Truly, if many are obscured and ignorant,
not recognizing shifting circumstances,
and rewards and punishments are not clear,
how could they not be defeated?
Therefore, *Quànjiàng*, chapter twenty-one, is narrated.
The *Mányí* disturb the *Huàxià*,
a trouble from ancient times to the present.
*Yáo* and *Shùn* worried for the people;
*Gāoyáo* managed the rebels.
King *Xuān* achieved a restoration;
*Nánzhòng* campaigned on the borders.
Now the people die daily;
how can they not flourish?
Therefore, *Jiùbiān*, chapter twenty-two, is narrated.
The nature of the common people
is different from and contrary to that of the ruler;
they cannot plan far ahead,
being restricted to a single system.
If they harbor private opinions
to serve as national policy,
one should investigate their words
to cross-examine what they mean.
Therefore, *Biānyì*, chapter twenty-three, is narrated.
Since the borders are far from the capital gates,
the *Tàishǒu* arrogate power.
The *Táigé* does not investigate,
believing their treacherous words,
ordering the destruction of commanderies and counties
and driving the people to migrate inward.
Now they are again mounds and wilderness;
anxiety will surely arise in their hearts.
Therefore, *Shíbiān*, chapter twenty-four, is narrated.
Heaven produces divine objects,
and "the sage takes them as a model."
Milfoil and tortoise shells for divination
serve to resolve doubts and suspicions.
Common practitioners are shallow in their origins;
none exhaust their potential.
Those who are self-important but not wise,
how are they worthy of trust?
Therefore, *Bǔliè*, chapter twenty-five, is narrated.
The *Yì* has scribes and shamans;
the *Shī* has masters and invokers.
The sage completes it first;
the people exert effort later.
When the millions are encouraged and joyful,
the spirits then grant blessings.
*Kǒngzǐ* did not pray,
in order to make clear that blessings reside in virtue.
Therefore, *Wūliè*, chapter twenty-six, is narrated.
The *Wǔxíng* and the *Bāguà*
are produced by *Yīnyáng*.
Receiving *qì* in thin or thick amounts,
it manifests in their form.
Heaven inscriptions those signs;
Man indeed receives and completes them.
If one does not cultivate their conduct,
fortune and prosperity will not arrive.
Therefore, *Xiàngliè*, chapter twenty-seven, is narrated.
The *Shī* mentions auspicious dreams,
and historical records also contain many;
observing the course of events,
the prognostications are not false.
Fortune comes from goodness;
disaster arises from the decay of virtue.
The response of good or ill fortune
matches one’s conduct.
Therefore, *Mèngliè*, chapter twenty-eight, is narrated.
Arguments and challenges arise everywhere,
making the *Dào* impassable.
Later students are confused
and do not know what to follow.
Since the *Gēngzǐ* year of old,
there have been those who criticized, saying,
"How could I be fond of disputation?"
I do so to clarify the truth.
Therefore, *Shìnàn*, chapter twenty-nine, is narrated.
In the relations between friends,
righteousness resides in the *Liùjì*;
"upholding them with dignified mien,"
they lecture on and practice the *Wángdào*,
valuing the long-standing agreement,
unchanging through wealth or poverty.
Now the people have long migrated,
and none can uphold this.
Therefore, *Jiāojì*, chapter thirty, is narrated.
The ruler has a beautiful reputation,
and the minister has a fine name;
when two people are of one heart,
their desires are fulfilled.
Treasuring authority and divine methods,
do not reveal them to those below.
Once the situation of governance is fixed,
in the end, nothing can topple it.
Therefore, *Míngzhōng*, chapter thirty-one, is narrated.
Sentiment between Man and Heaven is connected;
their *qì* resonates and harmonizes.
Good and evil manifest in each other
through portents and transformations.
The sage operates them
as if steering a boat or chariot.
Cultivating the spirit of the people,
none fail to contain excellence.
Therefore, *Běnxùn*, chapter thirty-two, is narrated.
In the rule of a bright king,
nothing is greater than personal transformation.
Virtue and the *Dào* are the root;
benevolence and righteousness are the assistants.
When thoughts and hearts follow the governance,
and the people are urged to be diligent and broad,
the Four Seas are governed;
how can there be waxing or waning?
Therefore, *Déhuà*, chapter thirty-three, is narrated.
Observing remote antiquity,
the movement of the *Wǔxíng*;
consulting the *Shī* and the *Shū*,
and examining former instructions.
When the *qì* ends and the cycles are exhausted,
later generations come forward again.
Although not necessarily correct,
one may rely on tradition and inquiry.
Therefore, *Wǔdézhì*, chapter thirty-four, is narrated.
A gentleman has much knowledge
of "former words and past deeds."
"Sorting clans and distinguishing things,"
such surnames existed of old.
Seeing widely and identifying commonalities ◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇.
Therefore, *Zhìshìxìng*, chapter thirty-five, is narrated.
